By placing him on IR before the final roster cuts, this means he is gone for the year. There are conditions under which he could return very late, but with the type of injury he has, he won’t return until next spring. Bisontis was in a tight battle for the starting right guard spot with Isaiah Adams. He is the second rookie to be placed on season-ending IR along with DT Kaleb Proctor. RELATED: GARRETT WILLIAMS ACTIVATED OFF PUP LIST The team made some other moves. Also placed on IR are TE Jameson Geers with a thumb injury and LB Austin Keys with an undisclosed injury he suffered against the Las Vegas Raiders. The Cardinals also waived/injured TE Kenny Yeboah with an injury settlement. Cardinals rookie running back Jeremiyah Love is dealing with a high ankle sprain, per sources. It makes it unlikely that Love plays again this preseason, with the team hoping he can return for the Sept. 13 regular-season opener vs the Chargers. pic.twitter.com/H0vb0R7x4k — Adam Schefter (@AdamSchefter) August 17, 2026 In other injury news, the coaching staff has decided to keep rookie RB Jeremiyah Love out of the remaining preseason games because of his high ankle sprain he sustained in the Raiders’ contest. In corresponding moves, the franchise signed TE Baylor Cupp, RB Tre Stewart, and DT Keveion’ta Spears. Cupp (6’-6”, 243 pounds) came out of high school as a 5-star recruit and attended Texas A&M and then went into the transfer portal and chose Texas Tech. He went undrafted in 2024 and signed with the Kansas City Chiefs. He has a 30” vertical jump with a wingspan of 6’-8 ¼”. He spent the majority of 2024 on the Chiefs’ practice squad. He then inked a deal with the Baltimore Ravens but was waived during final cuts. He then spent the season with the Dallas Renegades of the UFL, where he had 15 targets, 8 catches for 73 yards, and 0 touchdowns. He is considered a blocking tight end and is known as being injury-prone. Stewart (5’-10”, 192 pounds) is showing up to a very full running back room. He played for Jacksonville State, earned First-Team All-Conference USA honors, and posted back-to-back 200-yard games. In 2024, he ran for 1,604 yards with 23 TDs and 3 fumbles lost. This spring, he played for the Orlando Storm of the UFL. He played in just five games with 28 attempts for 115 yards, 0 touchdowns, and 0 fumbles. Spears (6’-4”, 313 pounds) went to Louisiana Tech, Memphis, and finally SMU. This past season, he played in all 13 games with 15 tackles, 2.5 tackles for loss, 0 sacks, 1 hurry, and 4 batted passes.

title: What to know about Falcons – Colts in preseason Week 2
summary: Depending on your perspective, this is either going to be the worst week of preseason or the best. With joint practices being the priority this week, starters will be sitting in this one for the Falcons, which means it’ll be reserve and roster hopefuls from opening kickoff to the final seconds. If you’re invested in […]
full_text: WESTFIELD, IN - AUGUST 20:Indianapolis Colts defensive back Hunter Wohler (30) knocks a way a pass intended for Atlanta Falcons tight end Jack Velling (84) during the Indianapolis Colts and Atlanta Falcons joint training camp practice on August 20, 2026 at the Grand Park Sports Campus in Westfield, IN. (Photo by Zach Bolinger/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Depending on your perspective, this is either going to be the worst week of preseason or the best. With joint practices being the priority this week, starters will be sitting in this one for the Falcons, which means it’ll be reserve and roster hopefuls from opening kickoff to the final seconds. If you’re invested in roster battles more than the relatively settled starting lineup and think this preseason game will help sort those battles out, there will be plenty to pay attention to. If you view this as the least important one because the starters get some tuning up again in Week 3 and final impressions matter, you’ll likely view this as a Saturday slog. Either way, we’re spending our Saturday afternoon with the Falcons, so let’s hope for an interesting afternoon with some surprisingly good football. Here’s what you need to know. Roster battles to monitor QB3 Cooper Rush was not great in his first preseason action, and probably needs a bounceback effort against Indianapolis. Jack Strand has done enough to stick around as a practice squad quarterback, I firmly believe, but will need Rush to continue to muddle while he excels to actually grab the QB3 role. RB3 It’s Tyler Goodson’s job, more than likely. Trey Sermon is injured, Cash Jones is more of an interesting versatile option as a fourth running back/seventh receiver/special teamer than a legitimate third option, and Goodson has been showing out while Nate Carter has had quieter practices and a forgettable first preseason effort. WR5/6 Vinny Anthony looked good as a returner and solid enough as a receiver to think he’s got a real shot of sticking, while Chris Blair and Dyland Drummond logged a ton of work and Blair once again looked good. I haven’t seen any indication the Falcons are leaning toward one or two of the many options they’ve assembled here, but Anthony and Blair had looked the best thus far. C2 Corey Levin looked better in pass protection than James Brockermeyer, but neither one was a standout in Week 1. I’d like to see another full game from both, but Levin’s experience and familiarity with Bill Callahan still presumably has him in the driver’s seat for now. ILB2 It’s starting to feel like Kendal Daniels has this job. He’s wearing the green dot in games, making standout plays in practice, and holding his own in preseason action. Christian Harris is his most serious competition and has been fine, while Harold Perkins Jr. is stumping for a role CB2/3 Without Avieon Terrell or Billy Bowman Jr. playing, it’s Mike Hughes at CB2 despite some struggles and…maybe Darnay Holmes for the nickel? Holmes has been a summer standout with energy, physicality, and solid coverage, which continued into this week’s joint practices with the Colts. Until Terrell and Bowman are out there, that’s the pecking order heading into the season. What’s new with the Colts? Like the Broncos, the Colts didn’t make sweeping organizational changes in 2025. Unlike with the Broncos, it’s a little bit harder to call that an unqualified good decision, but they did also look outside the organization a little more after re-signing Daniel Jones, Alec Pierce, and Mo Alie-Cox. They traded linebacker Zaire Franklin to the Packers for defensive tackle Colby Wooden, hoping to further shore up a tough rotation up front, and added Jerry Tillery and Derrick Nnadi to the interior as well. Arden Key gives them more pass rushing punch at defensive end alongside fellow addition Michael Clemons, and if nothing else, the Colts took their need to be tough up front very seriously. Most of their other signings outside wide receiver Keenan Allen and linebacker Akeem Davis-Gaither were depth moves, but I’m the last person to knock quality depth acquisitions. The draft brought in two likely starters in linebacker CJ Allen, a player I know more than a few Falcons fans were interested in, and safety AJ Haulcy. The Colts still bet heavily on their core and their coaching staff, a risky move considering Jones’ long history of injuries and streaky play and the fact that this team has gone 9-8, 8-9, and 8-9 over the past three seasons. Perhaps this will be their breakout year, but it’s a big bet, even though this is a talented roster on paper. What to know about Saturday The starters aren’t going to play, as mentioned, so this is truly an opportunity for roster hopefuls to make their case in game action. While I don’t think battles will be decided based on this effort—the joint practices are quite important to Stefanski and company—standouts can only help their chances. While after the first game there was concern about rust and how dominant the Broncos looked against Atlanta’s starters, after this one we really have to focus on individual performances and take from them what we can. Atlanta is not, unless things go terribly awry, ever going to put their full second team on the field at the same time the way they will in this one, and most of their third and fourth stringers will be on the practice squad or looking for work elsewhere. The result is far less important than seeing, for example, whether Harris or Daniels is out there to start this one, which reserve receiver takes off, and whether Rush or Strand can create some daylight in the quarterback competition. That’s what you should focus on, especially after the football inevitably gets a bit dreary. Let us know what you’ll be looking for tomorrow!

title: Falcons news: What we learned about QB position from joint practices with Colts
summary: I’m just going to cut to the chase here — obviously, we’re going to focus on the Falcons’ joint practices with the Colts today. I’ve spent the past two days in Westfield, Ind. covering those practices, and I have a lot of thoughts to share in the Opening Drive — mostly about the quarterback situation. […]
full_text: WESTFIELD, IN - AUGUST 20: Atlanta Falcons quarterback Tua Tagovailoa (1) runs through a drill during the Indianapolis Colts and Atlanta Falcons joint training camp practice on August 20, 2026 at the Grand Park Sports Campus in Westfield, IN. (Photo by Zach Bolinger/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images I’m just going to cut to the chase here — obviously, we’re going to focus on the Falcons’ joint practices with the Colts today. I’ve spent the past two days in Westfield, Ind. covering those practices, and I have a lot of thoughts to share in the Opening Drive — mostly about the quarterback situation. The layout of the practice fields at the Grand Park Sports Complex where the Colts hold their training camp practices made it really difficult to monitor everything that was happening, but the Falcons beat had a fantastic contingent on the ground in Indianapolis, and I’ve linked out to everyone else’s coverage below , too. If you want a well-rounded perspective on the whole team’s performance vs. the Colts in joint practices, I’d strongly recommend checking out everyone’s coverage. And don’t miss the Falcoholic Community Question of the Day at the end of the post! A sneak preview: If you were in charge of writing the Atlanta Falcons’ mission statement for the 2026 season, what would it say? Falcons Opening Drive: What we learned during joint practices with the Colts In the past four days, I’ve spent time in six different states — Georgia, North Carolina, Tennessee, Kentucky, Ohio, and Indiana. I’ve driven about 900 miles, with about 700 more to get home tomorrow. I’ve gotten sunburned, in INDIANA of all places; I’ve woken up at 1:41 a.m., mistaken the streetlight outside my hotel window for daylight, and panicked, thinking I was late for a 3 p.m. practice; and I have watched the Falcons starters take a lot of reps against the Colts. As I write this on Thursday night, in my hotel in downtown Indianapolis, Ind. mulling this trip over, I have to say that it was all well worth it. You can learn a lot about a team by observing them in an unfamiliar environment and unusual circumstances. Tua Tagovailoa had an up-and-down couple of days, but it’s important to remember that even though these were padded practices and they were pretty physical, tackling to the ground was not allowed, and any player’s performance in joint practices is not necessarily an indicator of how they’ll play in the regular season. I know we all wanted to see Tua deliver a — I hate to say it, but a Daniel Jones-on-Wednesday type of performance . I don’t think any of us wanted that more than Tua himself did. Tua responded to his poor performance in the first preseason game against the Broncos, and a rocky performance in Wednesday’s practice, with a workmanlike attitude, a lack of ego, and a commitment to getting it right — and he did look better on Thursday. Now that Jawaan Taylor is healthy enough to be on the field, the offensive line should have a chance to develop the chemistry and timing they’ll need to keep Tua upright. Michael Penix Jr. updated the media on his medical status on Thursday, and I don’t think anyone’s surprised that Tua will most likely be the Week 1 starter. Starting Tua and giving Penix as much time as possible to get fully healthy is the right call. I do think Penix is close based on how fluidly he moves in 1-on-1s and 7-on-7s, and I won’t be surprised if he ends up starting later in the season. But for now, we have to hope Tua’s able to stack up some wins as the Falcons’ starter. And after what I’ve seen and heard from Tua these past two days in Westfield, Ind., I know he’ll do everything in his power to make that happen. Now, let’s get to the Falcons coverage you absolutely must read, watch, or listen to today: Daniel Flick, AJC: Day 1 , Day 2 Josh Kendall, The Athletic: Day 1 D. Orlando Ledbetter, Bowtie Sports: Day 1 , Michael Penix hopes to be cleared after call with his doctor Thursday night Will McFadden, AtlantaFalcons.com : Day 1 , Day 2 Daniel Jones looked disturbingly good (my words, not the writer’s) against the Falcons passing defense on Wednesday, as Stampede Blue’s Jon Spradley notes. Day 2 recap from Stampede Blue’s Thomas Butler-Guerrero . Joint Practices in Indy underway for Falcons and Colts pic.twitter.com/TCOCCbIqu5 — Victor Prieto (@victorprieto_11) August 19, 2026 Bijan Robinson getting lots of cheers and attention from the crowd (like always) pic.twitter.com/2LRfq9UEU3 — Victor Prieto (@victorprieto_11) August 19, 2026 Matt Ryan’s still got it pic.twitter.com/bvYOEVIfNJ — Victor Prieto (@victorprieto_11) August 20, 2026 Divine Deablo, Kendal Daniels and Falcons linebackers at joint practice with Colts pic.twitter.com/wTGaaMkLOh — Victor Prieto (@victorprieto_11) August 20, 2026 From the Falcoholic Community I thought this was great insight from FalconsFaninMaine in the comments on Wednesday’s Opening Drive . Obviously we’re all just guessing at this point of the preseason, but this is a very well reasoned take. I hope Atlanta wins more games than this — I think we all do — but I can’t argue with any of the points Maine made here. Maine’s notes about kicking in particular stood out to me because Folk looked so great in joint practices on Wednesday. And I have to think the offensive coaching will be improved, because I am not sure it could be more predictable than last season. Join the conversation! title: Ravens discussion: who will be Baltimore’s Week 1 starting center?
summary: Ravens center Danny Pinter, who appeared to be leading the team’s starting competition, suffered a knee injury that is expected to sideline him for “an extended amount of time,” according to head coach Jesse Minter. Baltimore will now need to choose a Week 1 starter from their remaining options. Jovaughm Gwyn and Ethan Pocic are […]
full_text: Jul 29, 2026; Owings Mills, MD, USA; Baltimore Ravens lineman Jovaughn Gwyn (54) during practice at the Under Armour Performance Center. Mandatory Credit: Mitch Stringer-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Ravens center Danny Pinter, who appeared to be leading the team’s starting competition, suffered a knee injury that is expected to sideline him for “an extended amount of time,” according to head coach Jesse Minter. Baltimore will now need to choose a Week 1 starter from their remaining options. Jovaughm Gwyn and Ethan Pocic are the next men up, both with solid cases for the starting job: Zach’s take: Right now, it’s hard to imagine anybody else besides Gwyn starting at center Week 1. While this isn’t an issue for the starting lineup, it is for depth. Gwyn looked to already be pushing for the starting role against Pinter and it wouldn’t have been surprising if he had won it. But that would have made Pinter the top backup. Now, the Ravens have to hope Pocic’s health picks up in time for the regular season. Pocic has been relatively limited so far while he gets back up to speed following his Achilles injury last season. Corey Bullock is an option if Pocic’s health doesn’t hold up but he was moved to guard before Pinter’s injury and is now moving back to center. But for now, the clear option if Gwyn to play Week 1 and that’s not a bad thing. Dustin’s take: Even though Gwyn flashed with a great preseason performance against the Eagles, I still think the Ravens would prefer if Pocic was the starting center against the Colts in Week 1. The question with Pocic is if he’s physically ready for the role as he continues to ramp up from a torn Achilles in December of last year. I was really impressed with Gwyn’s physicality and ability to reach and seal off second-level defenders in the run game against Philadelphia, but playing center requires more than just physical ability. The mental side of the position is where Pocic’s experience as a seasoned veteran could give him the edge to start right away. Gwyn played just 11 regular season snaps in 2025, while Pocic is familiar with the physical nature of AFC North football due to his time with the Browns. However, if Gwyn has another strong performance against the Vikings on Saturday, it will become increasingly hard for Baltimore to deny him the opportunity to snap the ball come Week 1. Now, it’s your turn! Who do you think will start at center for the Ravens in Week 1? Let us know in the comments section below!

title: Ravens rookie film review: defensive draft picks make promising debuts
summary: The Ravens’ 2026 draft class played a significant role in Baltimore’s preseason opening win over Philadelphia. While preseason production only tells part of the story, these games give us our first opportunity to see how the coaching staff plans to deploy its rookies, what areas they are emphasizing in their development, and how their college […]
full_text: BALTIMORE, MARYLAND - AUGUST 15: Zion Young #9 of the Baltimore Ravens lines up before the snap during an NFL preseason football game against the Philadelphia Eagles at M&T Bank Stadium on August 15, 2026 in Baltimore, Maryland. (Photo by Perry Knotts/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Ravens’ 2026 draft class played a significant role in Baltimore’s preseason opening win over Philadelphia. While preseason production only tells part of the story, these games give us our first opportunity to see how the coaching staff plans to deploy its rookies, what areas they are emphasizing in their development, and how their college traits translate to the NFL. Here’s what stood out from Zion Young, Rayshaun Benny, and Chandler Rivers in their first preseason action. EDGE Zion Young (Round 2, No. 56 overall) 22 snaps | 16 pass rush | 4 run defense | 2 coverage Young’s stat sheet may not jump off the page, but his 22 snaps were much more interesting from a developmental standpoint. Baltimore kept him on the field deep into the fourth quarter and used the opportunity to expose him to several different responsibilities. Young was asked to rush the passer, defend the run, drop into coverage, and work from multiple stances. That last part was particularly noteworthy. Young was most comfortable at Missouri rushing from a three-, three-and-a-half-, or four-point stance, but Baltimore gave him several snaps standing up as a traditional outside linebacker. That appears to be intentional developmental work as the Ravens try to expand what he can do within their defensive front. One of his best plays came against a screen to the near side. Young diagnosed the play, pursued into space and finished with an excellent open field tackle. For a 6-foot-6 edge defender, seeing that kind of movement and ability to finish in space was encouraging. Definitely a varying level of comfortability between Zion in a 3 point/ 4 point stance vs 2 point Flashes a nice cross chop as well as speed to power. Seems like ravens were asking him to wear different hats role wise pic.twitter.com/mU0JFLqIHL — Yuri (@Yuri_Ravens) August 17, 2026 As a pass rusher, Young also showed some variety. He flashed a cross-chop, which was notable because his college pass-rush plan was heavily built around power, particularly his long arm and bull rush. He also had a good speed-to-power rep, showing the pocket compressing ability that was one of his best traits coming out of Missouri . There has been some skepticism surrounding Young’s performance because he didn’t consistently generate immediate pressure, but the context matters. Philadelphia’s quarterbacks were getting the ball out quickly, and Baltimore wasn’t simply asking Young to pin his ears back and rush every snap. This looked like a developmental game for Young, with the Ravens deliberately putting different responsibilities on his plate. Postgame takeaway: The production was quiet, but the usage was encouraging. Baltimore appears focused on developing Young into a more versatile edge defender rather than limiting him to the power-rushing role he excelled in during college. The cross chop, open field tackle and stand-up reps were the biggest things to take away from his debut. Related: Zion Young’s post-draft scouting report CB Chandler Rivers (Round 5, No. 162 overall) 14 coverage snaps | 1 target | 0 receptions allowed | 1 pass breakup Of the three defensive rookies, Rivers may have had the most immediately noticeable performance. He was targeted only once across 14 coverage snaps and forced an incompletion on the play. Baltimore primarily played zone coverage, so there weren’t many opportunities to evaluate Rivers’ pure man coverage traits, but his processing and closing ability showed up. On his pass breakup, Rivers read the play, drove downhill on the football and attacked through the receiver’s frame at the catch point. That’s exactly the type of decisive play you want to see from a defensive back operating in zone coverage. Ravens 5th round pick Chandler Rivers impressed physically last week Did a nice job tackling in the open field and drove on a pass catcher to force an incompletion. He posted the second highest pff coverage grade pic.twitter.com/4mbj29cEgp — Yuri (@Yuri_Ravens) August 19, 2026 Rivers’ tackling was arguably even more impressive. He was forced to make several plays in space and consistently finished. That carried over to special teams, where he worked around a blocker on kickoff coverage and made the tackle. For a rookie defensive back competing in a crowded secondary, those special-teams reps could be extremely important when Baltimore eventually has to make its roster decisions. Rivers primarily operated from the nickel in his debut. As the preseason progresses, it will be interesting to see whether Baltimore expands his responsibilities and gives him opportunities outside or at safety. His college tape suggested that positional flexibility could eventually become part of his value. Postgame takeaway: Rivers had a strong debut. The coverage numbers were clean, he made a decisive play on his lone target, and his open-field tackling consistently stood out. His ability to contribute on special teams only strengthens his case for a roster spot. Related: Chandler Rivers’ post-draft scouting report DT Rayshaun Benny (Round 7, No. 250 overall) 15 snaps | 13 pass rush | 1 run defense | 1 coverage Benny looked very similar to the player we saw at Michigan. His power immediately translated. Benny had multiple pass rush reps where he generated movement with his bull rush, getting underneath offensive linemen and using his leverage to compress the pocket. He may not always be the player who finishes the rush, but his ability to move the line of scrimmage can create opportunities for everyone around him. What stood out most was his work on stunts and twists. Benny was effective when asked to crash into offensive linemen and create space for another defender looping behind him. He covered a surprising amount of ground on some of those exchanges and showed that he can be useful as more than simply a straight-line interior power rusher. Ravens DT Rayshaun Benny vs the eagles Power rush/ pocket compression and set a few picks for stunts/ twists pic.twitter.com/Q0dMj2qdx7 — Yuri (@Yuri_Ravens) August 17, 2026 We didn’t get many opportunities to evaluate Benny against the run because he logged only one official run defense snap, but his ability to occupy blockers still showed up. He prevented offensive linemen from cleanly climbing to the second level, allowing Baltimore’s linebackers to remain clean, flow toward the football and finish plays. That ability doesn’t always show up in the box score, but it is extremely valuable in the Ravens’ front. Postgame takeaway: Benny’s power translated immediately. His bull rush and ability to create opportunities for teammates on games up front were the highlights of his debut. Week 2 should hopefully give us a larger sample size, particularly against the run, where his ability to control blockers could become one of his biggest strengths. Related: Rayshaun Benny’s post-draft scouting report Final Thoughts The biggest takeaway from Baltimore’s defensive rookies wasn’t necessarily raw production it was how the Ravens used them. Young was treated like a developmental chess piece, working from different stances and handling responsibilities beyond simply rushing the passer. Benny immediately showed how his power can affect the entire defensive front, particularly when Baltimore runs stunts and twists. Rivers looked comfortable in the nickel, tackled extremely well and showed immediate special-teams value. There is still a long way to go before Week 1, but all three gave Baltimore something encouraging to build on. For Week 2, the three things I’ll be watching most closely are Young’s pass rush development from a two point stance, Benny receiving more opportunities against the run, and Rivers getting snaps at…

title: Bills sign Greg Gaines to veteran salary benefit contract, but what does that mean?
summary: The Buffalo Bills added some veteran experience to their defensive line this week, signing defensive tackle Greg Gaines to a one-year contract ahead of their second preseason game. Gaines joins Buffalo as an experienced interior defensive lineman entering his eighth NFL season. The 6-foot-1, 312-pound defensive tackle was originally selected by the Los Angeles Rams […]
full_text: The Buffalo Bills added some veteran experience to their defensive line this week, signing defensive tackle Greg Gaines to a one-year contract ahead of their second preseason game. Gaines joins Buffalo as an experienced interior defensive lineman entering his eighth NFL season. The 6-foot-1, 312-pound defensive tackle was originally selected by the Los Angeles Rams in the fourth round of the 2019 NFL Draft. He spent his first four seasons with the Rams and was part of Los Angeles’ Super Bowl championship team during the 2021 season. Gaines then spent the last three seasons with the Tampa Bay Buccaneers from 2023 through 2025. On the surface, the contract is fairly straightforward. According to Spotrac , Gaines signed a one-year, $1.3 million Veteran Salary Benefit contract with Buffalo that includes $137,500 guaranteed signing bonus and a $50,000 Week 1 roster bonus. Gaines’ experience is important when looking at his contract. He has seven credited NFL seasons, which establishes his minimum salary for 2026. But the actual mechanics of the deal are a little more interesting than the $1.3 million number suggests. Thanks to the NFL’s Veteran Salary Benefit (VSB), the Bills can pay Gaines the veteran minimum appropriate for his experience while carrying a substantially smaller number against their salary cap. For a team where every bit of cap space matters, it’s another example of how NFL teams can use the collective bargaining agreement to add an experienced player without paying the full cap price. What is the NFL veteran minimum salary in 2026? NFL minimum base salaries increase depending on the number of credited seasons a player has accumulated. For the 2026 season, the minimum salaries are: Rookie (0 credited seasons): $885,000 1 credited season: $1,005,000 2 credited seasons: $1,075,000 3 credited seasons: $1,145,000 4-6 credited seasons: $1,215,000 7+ credited seasons: $1,300,000 Gaines entered the NFL in 2019 and has accumulated seven credited seasons from 2019 through 2025. That puts him in the highest veteran-minimum category. His minimum base salary for 2026 is therefore $1.3 million. How does a player earn a credited season? A credited season is not simply determined by whether a player was under contract with an NFL organization. Generally, a player earns a credited season by being on a team’s active roster, inactive list, Injured Reserve (IR) or Physically Unable to Perform (PUP) list for three or more regular-season or postseason games. A player can also qualify after being released through an injury settlement if the financial compensation is equivalent to at least three regular-season game checks. Time spent exclusively on a practice squad or the Commissioner’s Permission List does not count toward a credited season. Those distinctions matter because credited seasons determine several benefits under the collective bargaining agreement, including a player’s applicable minimum salary. For Gaines, seven credited seasons means Buffalo couldn’t simply sign him for the $1.075 minimum that would apply to an experienced younger player with only 2 credited seasons. That’s where the Veteran Salary Benefit comes into play. So what is the NFL Veteran Salary Benefit? The NFL’s Veteran Salary Benefit, previously known as the Minimum Salary Benefit, is designed to make experienced players more financially competitive with younger players when teams are filling out their rosters. Without it, there’s an inherent salary-cap disadvantage to signing an experienced veteran. Consider Gaines. His minimum salary is $1.3 million because he has seven credited seasons. A player with two credited seasons has a 2026 minimum salary of only $1.075 million. If both players counted dollar-for-dollar against the salary cap, Buffalo would have a $225,000 cap incentive to sign the younger player, even before considering bonuses. This scenario across the NFL means older role players could find themselves priced out of jobs simply because their collectively bargained minimum salaries are higher. The Veteran Salary Benefit helps level that playing field. The VSB allows teams to offer qualifying players with at least four credited seasons a one-year contract at the minimum base salary applicable to their experience. For the 2026 season, the contract may also contain up to $187,500 in additional compensation, such as signing bonuses, roster bonuses or incentives. The key is how the contract is treated for salary-cap purposes. Instead of counting the veteran’s full minimum base salary against the team’s cap, an eligible VSB contract receives a reduced cap charge based on the minimum salary for a player with two credited seasons. In 2026, that’s $1.075 million. So Gaines still receives his $1.3 million veteran base salary. The Bills simply don’t have to count all $1.3 million of that base salary against their salary cap. Breaking down Greg Gaines’ Bills contract According to Spotrac, Gaines’ one-year deal breaks down this way: Veteran minimum base salary: $1,300,000 Guaranteed at signing: $137,500 Week 1 bonus: $50,000 Maximum cash: $1,487,500 Dead Cap: $137,500 The $137,500 and $50,000 bonuses combine for $187,500, exactly the amount of additional compensation permitted under a qualifying Veteran Salary Benefit contract in 2026. That means Gaines can receive as much as $1,487,500 in cash under the deal. But that isn’t what Buffalo has to count against the salary cap. Because Gaines’ contract qualifies for the Veteran Salary Benefit, his $1.3 million base salary is treated as the $1.075 million minimum applicable to a player with two credited seasons for cap purposes. Buffalo’s cap calculation therefore looks like this: Gaines’ actual base salary: $1,300,000 VSB-adjusted base salary for cap purposes: $1,075,000 Guaranteed bonus: $137,500 Week 1 bonus: $50,000 Total cap charge: $1,262,500 Dead Cap: $137,500 So while Gaines can collect $1,487,500, the Bills carry a cap charge of only $1,262,500. For Buffalo, the cap math becomes: $1,075,000 + $137,500 + $50,000 = $1,262,500. The Bills effectively save $225,000 in salary-cap space compared with what Gaines’ contract would otherwise cost. Why does the NFL have the Veteran Salary Benefit? The easiest way to understand the rule is to look at the decision Buffalo would otherwise face. Suppose the Bills are choosing between Gaines and a younger defensive tackle with two credited seasons. The younger player’s minimum salary is $1.075 million. Gaines, because he has survived seven seasons in the NFL and earned the corresponding veteran minimum, must receive at least $1.3 million. Without the Veteran Salary Benefit, that would mean Gaines costs Buffalo an additional $225,000 against the salary cap simply because he’s more experienced. That creates an unusual problem. The NFL’s minimum salary structure rewards players for remaining in the league, but without a corresponding cap mechanism, those raises could simultaneously make experienced veterans more expensive to employ than younger players. The VSB addresses that problem. It essentially allows a team to pay the veteran according to his experience without taking the entire additional cost of that experience against the salary cap. For teams, it creates an inexpensive avenue for adding proven depth. For veterans, it helps keep experience from becoming a financial liability when they’re competing against younger, cheaper players for roster spots. And Gaines’ contract is a nearly perfect example of how the mechanism works. Gaines is low-cost bet on experience for Buffalo This isn’t the kind of August transaction that’s going to reshape Buffalo’s salary cap or dominate the offseason transaction ledger. But it’s a useful one. Gaines has played seven NFL seasons, appeared in a Super Bowl-winning defense, and missed only two regular-season games during his three years in Tampa Bay. Buffalo is getting an experienced 312-pound interior defensive lineman at a point in the calendar when…

title: Pick the play that defines Bills’ Wild Card playoff win over Jaguars
summary: The 2025 Buffalo Bills’ season has been written, but the book is incomplete. Before we cast our full attention toward the 2026 season, let’s take one last glance back over our shoulder for our annual look at the Plays That Defined the prior campaign. For any newcomers, first and foremost; Welcome! When it comes to […]
full_text: JACKSONVILLE, FLORIDA - JANUARY 11: Cole Bishop #24 of the Buffalo Bills intercepts a pass intended for Jakobi Meyers #3 of the Jacksonville Jaguars during the fourth quarter in the AFC Wild Card Playoff game at EverBank Stadium on January 11, 2026 in Jacksonville, Florida. (Photo by Megan Briggs/Getty Images) | Getty Images The 2025 Buffalo Bills’ season has been written, but the book is incomplete. Before we cast our full attention toward the 2026 season, let’s take one last glance back over our shoulder for our annual look at the Plays That Defined the prior campaign. For any newcomers, first and foremost; Welcome! When it comes to the “rules” of this exercise, we’re not voting for our favorite highlight necessarily, but the one that best captures the essence of the game. Put differently, if you had to choose just one play to show someone to explain as much of the contest as possible, which would you choose? Wild Card Round: Buffalo Bills at Jacksonville Jaguars The Buffalo Bills, in the (lately) unusual position of being an NFL Wild Card contestant, traveled to Florida to take on the AFC South champion Jacksonville Jaguars. The two teams traded blows, with seven lead changes during the game. The Jaguars came in focused and shut down Buffalo’s incredible rushing attack. That was nearly enough, but a last-minute (almost literally to the second) touchdown put the Bills ahead and their defense shut the door. Fourth-down stop (Q2; 11:21) Plays That Defined 2025 – Wild Card – Fourth-down stop pic.twitter.com/htiiEPJNNW — Kuebiko (@Kuebiko_Kami) July 14, 2026 In a game this close, there’s so many plays where the “what if” can haunt you. For Jacksonville, this might be the one. Though a missed field goal and a handful of other plays could make a case. Trevor Lawrence scrambles left with the Jaguars going for it. He basically just needs to hit the line of scrimmage and fall forward. He’s centimeters short. Bills’ ball. No points for the Jaguars who were already in field goal range. Run for no gain (Q2; 8:32) Plays That Defined 2025 – Wild Card – Run for no gain pic.twitter.com/nnmfp9wkuc — Kuebiko (@Kuebiko_Kami) July 14, 2026 The Bills have a reputation for running, and James Cook was the 2025 NFL rushing champion. That meant the Jaguars knew what to stop. Keeping the Bills to three yards a carry was huge, and honestly pretty insane. Even more nuts is that there were no tackles for a loss except for a lone sack of Josh Allen. They just did not allow yards on the ground. Brandin Cooks’ big catch (Q4; 2:26) Plays That Defined 2025 – Wild Card – Brandin Cooks' big catch pic.twitter.com/AbK2KON0Eo — Kuebiko (@Kuebiko_Kami) July 14, 2026 The passing game was needed to make up the difference, and did they ever. Allen completed two passes of 36 yards (one earlier to Keon Coleman). Allen had a potent long game, but was also brutally efficient with an 80% completion rate. The pass helped set up the game-winning touchdown. Josh Allen’s TD (Q4; 1:05) Plays That Defined 2025 – Wild Card – Josh Allen touchdown pic.twitter.com/zlME8vLbJq — Kuebiko (@Kuebiko_Kami) July 14, 2026 And here is the game-winning touchdown. Allen had two rushing scores, and only one passing. While the ground game stalled for yards and the passing attack thrived, the scoring opportunities flew in the face of that trend. Cole Bishop’s INT (Q4; 0:59) Plays That Defined 2025 – Wild Card – Cole Bishop interception pic.twitter.com/t0XBZRQlUe — Kuebiko (@Kuebiko_Kami) July 14, 2026 Jacksonville had no timeouts and about a minute to work with, which isn’t wonderful odds. Then again, they only needed a field goal to continue the game. The tipped pass by Tre’Davious White put the football into Cole Bishop’s hand, and Buffalo would advance to the next round. Which play best defines the Bills’ victory?

title: Buffalo Bills 2026 scouting report: tight end Dalton Kincaid
summary: Back in the early aughts, when the Buffalo Bills were firmly mired in the midst of a long, miserable playoff drought that was still going to be worse before it was better, I used to read a lot of Bill Simmons’ work. Admitting that now feels far less cool then it was at that point—or […]
full_text: ROCHESTER, NEW YORK - JULY 29: Dalton Kincaid #86 of the Buffalo Bills makes a catch during training camp at St. John Fisher University on July 29, 2026 in Rochester, New York. (Photo by Joe Hrycych/Getty Images) | Getty Images Back in the early aughts, when the Buffalo Bills were firmly mired in the midst of a long, miserable playoff drought that was still going to be worse before it was better, I used to read a lot of Bill Simmons’ work. Admitting that now feels far less cool then it was at that point—or at least as it seemed, anyway—but Simmons had a unique way of blending humor, pop culture, and sports together to create entertaining bits of writing. One of his bits that has always stuck with me centered on the “if Player X can stay healthy” trope that often surrounds the discussion of athletes. He began talking about injuries that way in earnest with a young Detroit Lions quarterback named Matthew Stafford, a player who hadn’t reached his potential due to a slew of early-career injuries. But the player it always stuck out most with to me was former Tampa Bay Buccaneers quarterback Josh Freeman. Simmons used to call him “Josh Freeman If He Can Stay Healthy” as if it were his actual name. The joke, of course, wasn’t really at the expense of the player, but instead at the expense of fans, pundits, fantasy football players, and others with a rooting interest in the player performing to a level he had yet to unlock. Much of that discourse amounted to something like, “If Freeman can stay healthy, he can be a top producer in the league.” In today’s edition of “91 players in 91 days,” we discuss a tight end who can be a top producer in the NFL…if he can just stay healthy. _____________________________________________________________________________ Name: Dalton Kincaid Number: 86 Position: TE Height/Weight: 6’3” 246 lbs. Age: 26 (27 on 10/18/2026) Experience/Draft: 4; selected by Buffalo in the first round (No. 25 overall) of the 2023 NFL Draft College: Utah Acquired: First-round draft choice Financial situation (per Spotrac): Kincaid enters the fourth year of his rookie contract, and he carries a cap hit of $4,272,234 for the season. The Bills have already picked up the fifth-year option on his deal, so he’s under contract for 2027 with a cap hit of $8.162 million, as well. 2025 Recap: After missing time in 2024 thanks to a PCL tear, Kincaid started the 2025 season on a great pace. In Buffalo’s first five games, he totaled 20 catches for 287 yards and three touchdowns. Extrapolating that out to 17 games, it would have put him on pace for a 68/976/10 for the season. However, Kincaid missed Buffalo’s Week Six loss at the Atlanta Falcons due to an oblique strain, and he wasn’t the same upon his return. Kincaid had one big game—Buffalo’s 28-21 win over the Kansas City Chiefs in Week Nine where he caught six passes for 101 yards and a score—but that single contest made up nearly all of his remaining regular season production. A hamstring strain caused him to miss three games in November, as well. In Kincaid’s final seven games, he caught 19 passes for 284 yards and two scores. That comes out to a 46/690/5 pace over 17 games, which is remarkably close to what his regular-season numbers ended up being. In 12 games, Kincaid totaled 39 catches for 571 yards and 5 touchdowns on 49 targets. In the playoffs, he was exceptional, totaling nine catches for 11 yards and two scores on 11 targets. For his efforts, he was named to the Pro Bowl Games, replacing Chiefs’ tight end Travis Kelce when he dropped out. After the season, it was confirmed that Kincaid never had surgery to repair his PCL after the 2024 injury, instead dealing with the tear and rehabbing the injury through joint-strengthening physical therapy options. Positional outlook: Kincaid is one of five tight ends on Buffalo’s current roster. Shane Zylstra, Keleki Latu, Jackson Hawes, and Dawson Knox are the others. 2026 Offseason: Kincaid played in Buffalo’s preseason opener, but he was not targeted in the 29-14 victory. He held up well as an in-line blocker on at least one long play, as he took on outside linebacker Trevis Gipson and gave Josh Allen time to hit Khalil Shakir downfield on a second-quarter touchdown drive. He also was instrumental blocking downfield on a long gain for James Cook on a toss on that same drive. 2026 Season outlook: Kincaid definitely bulked up this offseason, as I admittedly had a hard time figuring out whether it was him or Dawson Knox on the field during Buffalo’s preseason opener. It used to be a little easier—just look for the bulkier fella and it was Knox—but with some added muscle, Kincaid looks much stronger entering his fourth season. He’s going to need that strength to translate to durability if he’s going to reach his full potential. When Kincaid is on the field, Buffalo’s offense is extremely hard to stop. He was the single best tight end target in the game last season in terms of quarterback rating, as Bills quarterbacks had a 149.2 rating when targeting Kincaid in the passing game. He also led all tight ends in yards per catch, notching 14.6 yards per reception. The issue for Kincaid has never been his ability; it has always been his availability. With San Francisco 49ers wideout Ricky Pearsall undergoing PCL surgery this offseason, a procedure that is likely to sideline him for 9-12 months, we see why Kincaid chose a more conservative treatment plan to mitigate his injury. Granted, we don’t know if the two issues are exactly the same, but they do impact the same ligament. Kincaid understandably wanted to play last season, and while he was certainly limited by his knee injury and the other muscle issues he encountered over the course of the season, he still showed himself to be an elite receiver when he was on the field. If he can become a better blocker—and early returns are certainly encouraging—then he can take the next step towards becoming the player Buffalo thought he would be when the chose him No. 25 overall in 2023. All of it starts with one thing, though, and it’s the Bill Simmons corrolary to Kincaid’s actual surname. With any luck, “Dalton Kincaid If He Can Stay Healthy” can become a thing of the past just like it did with Matthew Stafford. Less pain for Dalton Kincaid plus an alpha wideout in DJ Moore equals more pain for opposing defenses. That’s the kind of math equation I can get behind heading into the 2026 NFL season.
author: Sean Murphy

title: Panthers 34 Jaguars 17: Everything got better from last week
summary: The Carolina Panthers bounced back from a dreadful showing against the Bills to beat down the Jacksonville Jaguars, 34-17. First Quarter The Panthers won the toss and took the ball first to give their first team offense a chance to redeem themselves after last week’s struggles. To their credit, they did improve by getting one […]
full_text: JACKSONVILLE, FLORIDA - AUGUST 21: Bryce Young #9 of the Carolina Panthers congratulates AJ Dillon #28 on his touchdown against the Jacksonville Jaguars during the first half at EverBank Field on August 21, 2026 in Jacksonville, Florida. (Photo by Mike Carlson/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Carolina Panthers bounced back from a dreadful showing against the Bills to beat down the Jacksonville Jaguars, 34-17. First Quarter The Panthers won the toss and took the ball first to give their first team offense a chance to redeem themselves after last week’s struggles. To their credit, they did improve by getting one first down on their first drive. That came on a pass interference where Bryce Young attacked a mismatch that Tetairoa McMillan had against a linebacker. The drive would stall there, but it set up a brilliant punt from Sam Martin. The Jaguars called three straight run plays that Carolina stopped to get the ball right back. That set up a scoring drive. Jonathon Brooks picked up a big chunk on his first carry of the drive, then Young found Tommy Tremble for another nice gain. Two completions to McMillan set the Panthers up on the one, and Brooks was able to punch it in from there. The Jaguars answered with a very similar drive of their own. They marched down the field, but the defense stepped up in the red zone. Princely Umanmielen and Pat Jones combined to force a sack on Nick Mullens and force a field goal. Second Quarter The first string got pulled after their good work. The second string didn’t carry the momentum with their first drive. They went three and out, but the defense held up their end and forced the same out the Jaguars. Kenny Pickett was able to lead a scoring drive on the next possession. Jimmy Horn Jr. ripped off a 39 yard run to make up the most of it. Pickett made a nice throw to David Moore on a deep out, but it was called back for a hold. That effectively ended the drive, and Ryan Fitzgerald banged home the field goal attempt. On the third play of the ensuing Jaguars drive, quarterback Carter Bradley committed one of the cardinal sins of quarterbacking. He threw off his back foot across his body into the middle of the field, and that allowed Chau Smith-Wade to dive in for a highlight interception. Pickett found Horn inside the ten, then AJ Dillon ran it home for the touchdown. The Jaguars were able to put together another scoring drive. A couple of decent gains and a defensive penalty got them into Panthers territory, but inaccurate throws and lack of play making from the wide receivers stymied the drive in the red zone and forced another field goal. The Panthers tried to steal another score. A roughing the passer gained 15 yards. Jimmy Horn couldn’t reel in a tough catch in traffic then David Moore dropped a slant route, meaning Fitzgerald was counted on to make a 61 yard field goal. Clearly he did lots of leg work in the offseason, because he knocked it through without issue. Third Quarter DeVonta Smith knocked the ball free from DeeJay Dallas to end what was a promising Jaguars drive. Pickett connected with John Metchie III a number of times to move the Panthers into scoring range. The drive stalled out at the border of the red zone, and Fitzgerald badly pulled the short field goal. The Jaguars went three straight runs again, and Elijah Garcia blew up the third down run to force a punt. Metchie made a risky pickup on a punt and almost fumbled but was fortunate to be ruled down by contact. The Pickett to Metchie connection came back to carry the Panthers down the field with some help from Anthony Tyus. On third down from the 16, Pickett threw a contested ball to Roc Taylor, who reeled it in for the touchdown. Fourth Quarter Joey Aguilar hit a few deep passes to work deep into Panthers territory. But once again, the defense stiffened up with their back against the wall. They nearly picked off a pass, then Jackson Kuwatch blew up a draw on 3rd and 10 to force a field goal. Kyle Trask took over at quarterback and led a quality scoring drive in response. He made a couple nice throws in the interymediate area of the field while Anthony Tyus had another couple of bulldozing runs. A 17 yard pass to Casey Washington got the Panthers into the red zone. Two plays later, Washington caught a pass off a curl route, shrugged off a defender, then cruised into the end zone to put the Panthers up 34-9. Aguilar led another touchdown drive in garbage time but no one really cared. The game technically went into a weather delay at the two minute warning, but the teams elected to just end the game there. Overview It was a total 180 from last week’s performance against the Bills. The offense looked crisp. Bryce Young completed some passes down the field and Jonathon Brooks was able to find a little bit of space to operate. The defense limited what was largely the Jaguars second team offense, but it was still nice to see them have success. We got to see good performances from depth guys like John Metchie and Casey Washington out wide and several defenders took turns stringing together a couple of stops. There wasn’t much to complain about, and it seemed like everyone came out of the game healthy. That’s about all you can ask for in a preseason game. The Panthers will wrap up the preseason next week at home against the Texans.

title: Brian Answers: Bryce Young, Haynes King, Pat Jones, roster decisions, and more!
summary: Hello CSR! Welcome to Brian Answers, part two of your weekly Panthers fan mailbag for everyone! We got flooded with questions after a generally bad preseason outing. Let’s dive right in to everything you want to talk about! facepalmjedi: What can I do about my dread of watching Bryce Young stink up the field for […]
full_text: CANTON, OHIO - AUGUST 06: Haynes King #16 of the Carolina Panthers celebrates after scoring a five-yard touchdown to defeat the Arizona Cardinals 33-30 in the 2026 Pro Football Hall of Fame Game at Tom Benson Hall Of Fame Stadium on August 06, 2026 in Canton, Ohio. (Photo by Nick Cammett/Diamond Images via Getty Images) | Diamond Images/Getty Images Hello CSR! Welcome to Brian Answers, part two of your weekly Panthers fan mailbag for everyone! We got flooded with questions after a generally bad preseason outing. Let’s dive right in to everything you want to talk about! facepalmjedi: What can I do about my dread of watching Bryce Young stink up the field for the next two, maybe more, seasons? I don’t think one preseason game is worth bringing up these kinds of thoughts. Lets all revisit at least a few weeks into the season, when the teams are playing real football and not just trying to log reps in games that don’t matter. I’m sorry if this answer feels targeted, you just happened to be the first one to ask a question this week! schrodingersblackcat: It seems most fans I’ve seen making predictions have us carrying 3 QBs on the final 53. And after what we’ve seen from King, I can’t imagine cutting him. There’s no way he would clear waivers. Considering we’re also looking heavy at WR and hard up for roster spots, is there any scenario where we cut Pickett and roll with King at QB2? I wouldn’t be surprised if the Panthers did cut Haynes King and hope they can stash him on the practice squad, but after that Hall of Fame game performance, I’m definitely leaning more towards them carrying 3 QBs and trying to stash another depth pieces (WR, CB, LB) on the practice squad. I don’t see them moving on from Kenny Pickett, but its not something I couldn’t entirely envision either. But my money is on 3 QBs on the final 53. Coach_K: make or break year for Evero? Probably not. I’m not sure what fans’ issues with Ejiro Evero are right now. He managed to field a middle of the pack defense with basically zero solid inside linebackers and a complete lack of pass rush. Now, if with all the pieces they added his off-season, he fields a WORSE defense, that would be cause to consider his future in Carolina. But I just don’t see it, and I don’t know why Evero is a topic of conversation right now in fan circles. DannyLimes: what/who are you most excited to see with the remainder of pre-season. Who has the most to gain, who has the most to lose? Princely Umanmielen is someone I have been watching heavily, as he could have a very important role as a designated pass rusher now that he’s basically the 3rd edge on the roster. I very much want to see if the work he’s put in during the off-season pays dividends with on field production. He absolutely has the most to gain. I’m also excited to see more from the young DBs this team has accumulated over the last couple of seasons. Will Lee and Corey Thornton at CB, Lathan Ransom and Zakee Wheatley at S, all have much to gain by continuing to make plays. On offense, I’d like to see Jonathon Brooks get a fair shot at running the ball instead of getting swallowed up by the opposing defense right away every play. He very much seems to factor into the team’s plans on offense during the regular season, and I’d love to see him pop a long run just to show he’s back. Bull123: Brian…legit question, is Pat Jones gonna be a player for us this year? I actually really liked what I saw from Pat Jones before he got hurt last season. He showed a relentless motor getting after the quarterback and he’s going to have a large role in this defense as the run setting EDGE rusher. I actually think he’s going to be a nice comeback story if he can remain healthy, and luckily he has some solid pieces around him to lighten the load. @WTMealey: Do you feel like the comments on this site have discussed BY ad nauseum or is there still aspects of his skills or lack of or contract that you still find interesting? I love the Panthers and think I am realistic about BY with a healthy amount of homer bias while still seeing the flaws in his game namely consistency. But I get the groundhog day effect sometimes with folks who fail to acknowledge his successes. Maybe they feel the same way about me. Anywho do you enjoy the debate or are you over it? I’m very much over the debate about Bryce Young as a starter this season, he’s going to be the starter barring an injury or a severe regression. One preseason game is not going to change that. There’s really no reason to be talking about a new contract either as the team has made it very clear they aren’t making a decision on that until next off-season, possibly later since he’s still on the 5th year option next season. We’ve seen high level play and absolute dog water play from him at times throughout his career, I’m just looking to see something more consistent and that’s all I’m focused on in regards to Bryce this coming season. Revshawn: Honestly, I don’t have any questions this week. I’d rather take this time to let everybody here know how much I appreciate you all. This is the best blog on the internet, Panthers or otherwise. It makes me happy that ya’ll are around. Thank you Brian and staff as well for being caretakers of this place. Thanks Rev! Hopefully we can have some more positive vibes around this team sooner than later, but I took thank this community for being one of the most active SB Nation NFL sites. It takes a long time to grow a community like this one! dayneb12: Will Zavala be a preseason cut? There can’t be any reason this dude makes the 53, right? This coaching staff definitely doesn’t have any ties to Chandler Zavala, but he also had one good preseason game and one horrific preseason game. I wouldn’t be surprised if he got cut, but the Panthers do need the depth if they have belief in him still. schrodingersblackcat: Another Final 53 related question: If you’re GM, what do you do with XL when there are so many WRs deserving of a roster spot? This question gets much harder if Chris Brazzell isn’t sent to season ending IR. By my count there’s maybe 8 WRs who could make the final roster, so if the Panthers carry 7, that puts Xavier Legette, John Metchie, David Moore, and Jimmy Horn Jr at odds for those final spots. I think its more likely they move on from Metchie, Moore, or Horn before they let Legette go. They could try to trade him, but I just don’t see it at this juncture. positivebob: Don’t hear too much about STs. Who’s looking good for KR and PR? Gunners, PP. Any ST aces out there? Looks like Jimmy Horn Jr or Trevor Etienne will be primary returners, though somebody like Ja’Seem Reed could find his way ontou the roster as a returner. Brycen Tremayne is likely a roster lock for his work on special teams as well. I think Jackson Kuwatch could also find his way onto the roster with proper special teams play. That’s all for this week, Panthers fans! Enjoy the Jaguars preseason game, and hopefully we’ll have some more positive things to talk about next week. KEEP POUNDING!

title: 2026 Season Opener Countdown: 23 Days Remaining
summary: Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener by for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to […]
full_text: 29 November 2009: Panthers' guard Travelle Wharton #70 reacts during a play in a game between the New York Jets and the Carolina Panthers at Giants Stadium in East Rutherford, New Jersey as the New York Jets defeated the Carolina Panthers by the score 17-6. (Photo by Duncan Williams/Icon SMI/Icon Sport Media via Getty Images) Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener by for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to change that up a bit by counting down our own list of the Top 100 Panthers of all time. This does not correspond to jersey number, does not need to be somebody who wore a jersey, and will in no way be controversial. #23. Travelle Wharton Travelle Wharton is Carolina through and through. He was born in Greenville, South Carolina, went to high school in Simpsonville, South Carolina, and attended the University of South Carolina in Columbia. As fate would have it, he stayed in Carolina for the start of his pro career after the Panthers drafted him with the 94th overall pick in the 2004 NFL Draft. He started out as a reserve as a rookie but eventually took over after Week 5 as the Panthers mixed and matched guard combinations. He would not relinquish that starting spot for nearly a decade outside of a couple of injury-shortened seasons, though he’d shift around here and there. He played a season at left tackle while Jordan Gross kicked over to right tackle. Eventually, the Panthers would settle on Gross at left tackle and Wharton at left guard, and that duo became a staple of the offensive line for several seasons. While Wharton never earned the accolades of his teammate, he was equally important to providing stability and quality to the left side of the line. He was only flagged for 23 penalties during his 115 games as a Panther and only three false starts. Wharton ventured outside the boundaries of the Carolinas in 2012 after his release from Carolina and signed with the Bengals, but he suffered knee injury in camp and never suited up for Cincinnati. He was released the following summer and found his way back to Carolina, where he played one final season as the Panthers’ left guard before calling it a career. He’s stayed involved with the team since his retirement. He spent a couple of seasons on staff as an assistant offensive line coach before he was let go along with most of Ron Rivera’s staff after the latter was fired in 2019. He’s also done media with the Panthers, teaming up with his former linemate Jordan Gross to do a local TV show for a spell. In all, his 115 games played for the Panthers is fourth in franchise history among offensive lineman. That longevity along with his reliability and Carolina connections land him at number 23 on the list of top 100 Carolina Panthers of all time.

title: ESPN is wrong about the Chicago Bears
summary: In my day job, I am an English professor. This is relevant because in my hobby of writing about football, I frequently encounter people who forget that words mean things. ESPN just released a ranking of NFL positional groups that includes this statement: “you would be surprised by what you can learn sitting down and […]
full_text: In my day job, I am an English professor. This is relevant because in my hobby of writing about football, I frequently encounter people who forget that words mean things . ESPN just released a ranking of NFL positional groups that includes this statement: “you would be surprised by what you can learn sitting down and objectively grading and/or ranking each positional unit of all 32 teams.” This is probably true. The author of the article should try it some time. “Objectively,” per Merriam-Webster, involves “evaluation with a basis in observable facts rather than feelings or opinions.” He then proceeds to just rattle off a bunch of rank lists without actually providing any criteria for how the lists were composed. To be clear–this is an author writing to the standard of “trust me bro” and vibes, and it says a lot about the state of ESPN and sports journalism in general. Because a detailed analysis of everything wrong with the article would take framing and analysis that exceeds what the low quality of its argumentation deserves, I am simply going to focus on three Bears-centric rankings that make me wonder whether or not the author was even bothering. Running Backs ESPN ranks Chicago’s running back room as 24th in the NFL. In 2025, Chicago had the 4th-best rushing attack in the league by EPA/run, and it was one of only ten teams in the league that had positive value in EPA per run. Not only was Chicago third in total rushing yards, it was one of only three teams in the league with two running backs (Swift and Monangai) with at least 25 attempts in the top twenty in terms of success rate and EPA per rush. Those two were 12th and 21st in terms of yards per carry in terms for backs with at least 50 rush attempts, and 3rd and 19th in terms of total EPA. Either would be the basis of a rushing attack above 24th in the league, and Chicago has both of them. By any objective standard, Chicago has a 1-2 punch at running back that is near the top of the league. If the concern is that Chicago’s third running back is going to bring down the rest of the group, we would need to believe that 23 teams in the NFL have third-string running backs sufficient to make up the difference over this pairing. Wide Receiver Apparently, Chicago also has the 24th-best wide receiver room in the league, which makes me think that the author simply ranked a few teams and sort of just copy-pasted tables otherwise. Yes, DJ Moore has left Chicago. It is absolutely okay to have feelings about that. But remember, ESPN claims to be giving us an objective evaluation. Luther Burden was 4th in yards per route run in 2025, and their next three receivers (Odunze, Walker, and Raymond) also placed above 97th-place DJ Moore (traded away). Moore was productive, but he was the 61st-highest target share in the league but his production per route did not match that. Thus, Chicago’s 9th-best league passing attack in terms of EPA per pass did lose a high-volume receiver, but to suggest that they are in the lower third of the league seems to come down to a writer who went by big names and not actual production. Edge Rusher It is not simply homerism that causes me to push back against ESPN, though, because somehow they believe Chicago has the 22nd-best edge rusher room in the league. I. Martzing. Wish. Montez Sweat was 31st in total pressures in the league, and even among edge defenders he himself wasn’t even 22nd. But it’s about the entire room, and that’s where it gets even more bleak. Austin Booker wasn’t even in the top fifty. The Bears didn’t have another edge after him in the top hundred. It gets better in sacks, because there, at least, Sweat is in the top twenty. True, there’s a cliff after that before getting to Booker (again outside of the top fifty), but this is the closest to factual that this analysis can get. After those two men in rotation? Dayo Odeyingbo, who is paid like a quality starter and who plays like Dayo Odeyingbo. Also there’s Shemar Turner, who might or might not be healthy enough at some point to learn a new position. There seems to be no consistency to the ranking system, because if Sweat is enough to keep the Bears edge rushers out of the cellar, then Burden and Swift should elevate the receivers and running backs more. Chicago did record the 21st-most sacks per game, which makes it possible that ESPN simply used that as the basis of this ranking, but if so they seem to have forgotten that sacks come from places besides the edge and that sacks matter little if the next time the passer is allowed to complete without pressure or if the other team can run to the outside. Summary Stay in school, kids. At worst, use an AI engine–or a dictionary–to define some key words. Maybe trust in more than vibes to make an argument. Most importantly, remember that just because someone claims to be making an objective review or providing fact-based content doesn’t make it true.

title: Question of the Day: Should Chicago Add a Running Back?
summary: With Chicago’s RB1B out with an injury for the near future and the depth at running back behind D’Andre Swift and Kyle Monangai pedestrian at best, it got me thinking about potential options to add to the room now that more roster cuts are being reported. Let’s take a look at some of those options […]
full_text: PITTSBURGH, PENNSYLVANIA - OCTOBER 12: Kaleb Johnson #20 of the Pittsburgh Steelers warms up against the Cleveland Browns before the game at Acrisure Stadium on October 12, 2025 in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Joe Sargent/Getty Images) | Getty Images With Chicago’s RB1B out with an injury for the near future and the depth at running back behind D’Andre Swift and Kyle Monangai pedestrian at best, it got me thinking about potential options to add to the room now that more roster cuts are being reported. Let’s take a look at some of those options to consider. Kaleb Johnson, Steelers It seems almost daily that reports are coming out of Pittsburgh that say the former Iowa Hawkeye, and my 5th-rated RB in the 2025 class, is unlikely to make the final 53-man roster come opening weekend. With Kaleb Johnson entering the contest AFTER journeyman and former Bear Travis Homer, those reports appear to hold some weight. Clearly Kaleb has fallen out of favor in the Steel City, and thus, a change of scenery could be mutually beneficial. But would he succeed in Ben Johnson’s scheme here in Chicago is another question. Trey Benson, Cardinals Benson is another young, talented back who seems to have fallen out of favor with the team that drafted him just a few seasons ago. Before drafting All-World stud Jeremiyah Love with the 3rd overall pick this past April, the Cardinals re-signed James Conner and added bruiser Tyler Allgeier in free agency. Granted, Benson’s issues have been more his inability to stay on the field than his ability during the game, but alas – he, too finds himself on the roster bubble and could be available at a super cheap price in a trade or added post cuts. Malik Davis, Cowboys Despite winning the RB2 job last season and going on to post impressive numbers, including a 100-yard effort (5.2 ypc) in his only game with more than 8 carries, Davis finds himself on the roster bubble in Dallas, mainly due to two other young, promising backs in Jaydon Blue and Phil Mafah. If Davis gets cut, Chicago would be wise to look into this 27-year-old. Kendre Miller, Saints Let’s just say that 24-year-old RBs who are 5’11”, 220 lbs, and who run in the 4.5 range with the collegiate production of Miller don’t grow on trees. Were it not for injury, he’s another guy who wouldn’t be available – but alas, instead he is yet another young, talented back who finds himself on the roster bubble. Though New Orleans added Travis Etienne to pair with Alvin Kamara, the latter of the two has been dealing with his own injuries so Miller’s price might be more than the others. Either way, he would be worth considering for Chicago. Noah Whittington, Texans Though Whittington was #7 on my rankings of 2026 RBs pre-draft , he’s the only back on my list to go undrafted. Houston wisely scooped him up, but he’s currently behind former Bear David Montgomery, 2nd-year player Woody Marks, and former 6th-rounder Jawhar Jordan. If they foolishly let him go, I would be thrilled if Chicago brought him in. Personally, I would love to see Kaleb Johnson or Noah Whittington added before the regular season – assuming they become available. Both are healthy and would add another element to our RB room and, in my opinion, immediately be one of the top 3 most talented on the roster. What about you? Should Chicago add any of these backs? Or maybe a different one? Or are you content with Salvon Ahmed, Brittain Brown and Roschon Johnson if Swift or Monangai miss any time?

title: Bengals make the top 5 in a unique but important category
summary: One thing that makes the NFL unique is that the best teams don’t always play in the biggest markets. Consider that the Seahawks, the reigning Super Bowl champions, play in Seattle. The Chiefs, winners of three Super Bowls since 2019, play in Kansas City. In addition, the team with the longest active streak of seasons […]
full_text: CINCINNATI, OH - OCTOBER 16: Cincinnati Bengals fans react during the game against the Pittsburgh Steelers and the Cincinnati Bengals on October 16, 2025, at Paycor Stadium in Cincinnati, OH. (Photo by Ian Johnson/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images One thing that makes the NFL unique is that the best teams don’t always play in the biggest markets. Consider that the Seahawks, the reigning Super Bowl champions, play in Seattle. The Chiefs, winners of three Super Bowls since 2019, play in Kansas City. In addition, the team with the longest active streak of seasons reaching the Playoffs is the Bills, who play in Buffalo. Seattle (13th), Kansas City (33rd), and Buffalo (54th) are all outside the Top 10 in the 2025 Nielsen DMA (Designated Market Area) Rankings, according to the United States TV Database. This is why the NFL is the greatest league in the world. You don’t have to be in a big market to have the best fanbase. The Seahawks, the Chiefs, and the Bills all have great fanbases. As do the Bengals, with Cincinnati ranking 37th in the aforementioned rankings. The Nielsen Scarborough NFL Fandom Index recently unveiled its top five teams, with the Bengals checking in at No. 4 on the list. It’s the first year of the study, which, as Cincinnati Enquirer Sports Editor Jason Hoffman notes , is a “comprehensive study that moves beyond simple headcount to identify where the sport’s pulse beats strongest, revealing that America’s most avid fans are often found in the heart of its mid-sized legacy markets.” Also in the top five are Buffalo, Kansas City, Green Bay, and Philadelphia. The Packers are as historic a franchise as they come, but they play in Green Bay, the 68th market in the USTVDB rankings. That’s how great the NFL is. The fact that the Bengals are in the same top five as Philadelphia is impressive, considering it’s Philadelphia (the No. 5 DMA market), and the Eagles’ fanbase is, for my money’s worth, the most passionate fanbase in America. According to Nielsen, both cities are in the top five because “Neither market leads a single metric outright, yet both land in the top five on five of the eight questions the index tracks. That breadth, rather than any one standout behavior, is what pushes the two cities to No. 5 and No. 4 overall.” The eight metrics used to compile these rankings include: apparel purchases, general interest levels, live event attendance, betting intent, social media engagement, radio listenership, streaming habits, and linear TV viewership. Social media engagement and radio listenership are very strong parts of the Bengals’ fanbase. Bengals’ Twitter is incredibly passionate, and their radio network is incredible. In addition, Paycor Stadium has seen strong attendance in recent seasons due to the popularity of Joe Burrow and Ja’Marr Chase. That attendance will only continue to grow with the ongoing renovations. This is a great list for the Bengals to be in the top five on, and I’m looking forward to seeing where they rank next year.

You will see plenty of takeaways, but it is important to remember this is still just practice for both sides. No one is game planning for each other or anything yet. ‘This is it’: Bengals’ Joe Burrow tired of waiting, targets Super Bowl “You can keep pushing it down the road or you can talk about it now and say this is the year,” Burrow said Thursday. “You know, I’m tired of saying, ‘Next year, next year, next year.’ This is it. Your life is too short to keep pushing things down the road. I’m trying to instill some urgency and some intensity in everybody to go and be great every day and try to make it happen.” Can’t wait for this to be the quote that is taken out of context for the next year. Burrow’ simply is tired of falling short, and earlier in the press conference took on some of the blame for inconsistencies. This is not a “win or I am gone” quote. He simply wants to win. NFL News 2026 NFL Preseason, Week 2: What We Learned from Thursday’s games Statistically speaking, Fernando Mendoza didn’t glisten. However, the most worrisome aspect of the game was Mendoza largely getting pummeled by the Texans backup defense. It’s arguable that Houston’s defensive reserves could be as good as some teams’ starters, but it’s still troublesome that the 2026 NFL Draft’s No. 1 overall pick was hit five times, pressured on 37.5% of his dropbacks and sacked once. Not the easiest test for any rookie. Even if they are backups the Texans’ defense is still fearsome. NFL Network: Ravens center Danny Pinter suffers torn patellar tendon Pinter exited Wednesday’s session on a cart and underwent imaging to determine the severity of his knee injury. Testing revealed the worst news for Pinter, who was on track to earn a starting job for the first time since he joined the league as a fifth-round pick by the Colts in the 2020 draft. The Ravens’ injury luck unfortunately continues to be poor. This is one coming at a spot they are trying to fill after Tyler Linderbaum left in free agency. Jaguars two-way star Travis Hunter tries hand at placekicking during joint practice The two-way stud took his shot at placekicking during Wednesday’s special teams session at joint practice with the Carolina Panthers. Hunter took five field goal attempts from 27 yards out, per Garry Smits of The Florida Times-Union, with the first four missing badly, including a couple that barely got off the ground. He should get some pointer from Chad Johnson if he really wants to never leave the field.

Mandatory Credit: Petre Thomas-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Sports used to be so simple. College and the Olympics were amateur sports; the rest was professional. While everyone might have an opinion about what is “right” and what is “wrong,” in the end, each sport, league, or institution will set its own rules based on what it is legally allowed to do. For the Cleveland Browns, a legal ruling on Wednesday seemed to put TE Dae’Quan Wright on the path toward returning to Ole Miss . Wright was added in free agency on August 11th , but had been absent for the last few days of training camp. On Thursday, while the Browns hosted the Buffalo Bills in a joint practice, Wright submitted his name to the NCAA’s transfer portal. Cleveland made a move at tight end on Thursday as well , but Wright remains a part of the team’s 90-man roster at this point. On Friday, Wright’s path to return to college hit at least a speed bump, perhaps a wall, as Wednesday’s ruling was placed on hold (in Jared’s layman’s terms): BREAKING: The Tenth Circuit has GRANTED the NCAA’s stay request in Wisne v. NCAA. Judge Sweeney’s nationwide injunction is now stayed pending appeal, meaning qualifying Class of 2022 athletes lose its federal fifth-season protection for now. pic.twitter.com/i3ASE2TmHi — Austin Massey (@austinmasseySBI) August 21, 2026 Given that the Browns have kept Wright on their roster, despite a need at tight end, it seems they are hopeful for his return to practice soon. Friday’s ruling may allow for that and give him a week of practice and the third preseason game to stake a claim to a 53-man roster spot. Or another legal ruling will change everything, once again. If so, DBN will keep you as up to date as we can (while running the legalese through folks with lawyer backgrounds on the SB Nation team).
