title: Kyle McCord Should Fix One Thing
summary: When it comes to backup quarterbacks, I have two profiles that I prefer. The first is the hyper-athlete, along the lines of Malik Willis, because with an extremely shifty, mobile quarterback, at least you can do SOMETHING if he’s forced into the game. Willis is perhaps the best possible version of this quarterback because he […]
full_text: When it comes to backup quarterbacks, I have two profiles that I prefer. The first is the hyper-athlete, along the lines of Malik Willis , because with an extremely shifty, mobile quarterback, at least you can do SOMETHING if he’s forced into the game. Willis is perhaps the best possible version of this quarterback because he also has an absolute cannon, which is why he’s now getting a chance to start. But if I can’t have Malik Willis, I’ll happily take Kyle McCord , as McCord does a lot of difficult things well. McCord was an extremely accurate college quarterback, both at Ohio State (where it’s easy to be accurate due to all of the amazing receivers) and at Syracuse. His ball placement is very good, pushing elite. He’s not afraid of pressure in the pocket and steps up when appropriate. He’s not very mobile, but he can move enough to pick up a first down here and there . And he trusts himself to make big throws when needed. The only real problem with Kyle McCord is raw arm talent. The most glowing review of his arm I could find came from Dane Brugler, who wrote in The Beast : “ Solid arm talent — throws with adequate velocity and adds some arc when needed ” There are a lot of backup quarterbacks who would be starters if not for arm strength. For Packer fans, the quintessential example is probably Matt Flynn , who was essentially great at every quarterback soft skill, but had an arm that was just borderline enough to hold him back (especially post-injury). If Flynn is the borderline example, former Badger and Packer Scott Tolzien is probably the “barely an NFL player at all” borderline example, as he was a very smart quarterback who just couldn’t push the ball at all. I write a lot (probably too much) about quarterback arm strength because I find it maddening that we lack a publicly available ranking of everyone’s relative arm talent. I am a big baseball fan, and in baseball, the idea that we could possibly have a scenario where we don’t know how hard pitchers throw is laughable. Throwing a football isn’t the same as throwing a baseball of course, but I guarantee that if you put baseball nerds in charge of quarterback scouting for five seconds, they’d immediately have tape-based analysis of the MPHs on throws under pressure, over the middle, deep, to the sideline, etc., and a chart comparing them. And yes, it’s easy to tell that Josh Allen has an incredible arm, but I’d like to have a clearer picture of, say, Jordan Lover versus Jared Goff. Or Jayden Daniels versus Jaxson Dart. For the middle of the bell curve, we’re all just guessing. Anyway, in my subjective evaluations of quarterbacks, I use baseball’s 20/80 scale as best I can (for more on the 20/80 and how it is supposed to work, see here ), while also incorporating the opinions of draft analysts like Dane Brugler (and others), and by cohorts here at APC. I think a starting NFL quarterback needs to be a 50 (Backups can be 35-45) and I think the starter with the worst arm of late has been Tua Tagovailoa. That said, when he’s not horribly concussed, Tua compensates for that lack of arm strength with the league’s fastest release. Brock Purdy is right there with him. I think McCord is about on par with Tua and Purdy in terms of raw arm talent; however, he lacks the fast release to compensate, and that’s not something that is easily fixed. McCord is an extremely accurate thrower, and if you mess with his mechanics to speed things up, you probably also mess with his accuracy. But all is not lost, because the one thing we definitely CAN do these days is improve raw arm strength, and I’m always surprised borderline quarterbacks don’t do so more often. Baseball has been doing this for at least a decade now as part of the Driveline revolution . Even if you don’t really follow baseball, there’s a good chance you’ve heard of Milwaukee Brewer Jacob Misiorowski , who sits at about 101 mph and routinely hits the high 104s, but it’s not really just Miz. Almost EVERY major league pitcher now sits in the mid-90s , and while some of this is the result of going max effort more frequently and shorting outings, modern training techniques like weighted ball programs also can make meaningful increases to max velocity. And there is no practical reason why this cannot work in football. The Kyle McCords of the world should be especially interested in this specific improvement. McCord is, I think, a true borderline case. His arm strength isn’t terrible; it’s just not quite good enough to be a starter. As he exists today, I suspect he will be a more than competent backup for as long as he wants to play. But McCord does most of the truly hard stuff well. Most struggling quarterbacks don’t possess his inner clock (McCord’s pressure-to-sack ratio was well under 20%, even at Syracuse), and most don’t throw with as much precision. McCord has one of the only major QB defects with a proven remedy. I’ll be keeping a close eye on him tonight just to see if he has enough to stick around. If he does, maybe another offseason or two can push him to starter caliber.

title: Packers to watch in the preseason Broncos matchup
summary: The NFL regular season is quickly approaching, but a few Green Bay Packers players are facing big moments in the preseason, including in Friday night’s contest against the Denver Broncos. Whether it’s players fighting for starting/rotational roles on either side of the ball, or under-the-radar names simply trying to make the 53-man roster, there’s still […]
full_text: PITTSBURGH, PENNSYLVANIA - AUGUST 13: Murvin Kenion III #39 of the Green Bay Packers in action during the game against the Pittsburgh Steelers at Acrisure Stadium on August 13, 2026 in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Joe Sargent/Getty Images) | Getty Images The NFL regular season is quickly approaching, but a few Green Bay Packers players are facing big moments in the preseason, including in Friday night’s contest against the Denver Broncos. Whether it’s players fighting for starting/rotational roles on either side of the ball, or under-the-radar names simply trying to make the 53-man roster, there’s still plenty for a number of players to be playing for in the preseason, especially against a formidable team like Denver. Let’s dive into a few of those names to keep an eye on during Friday night’s contest. Skyy Moore Both Matt LaFleur and Brian Gutekunst have said enough positive things about Skyy Moore to suggest that his spot on the 53-man roster is safe. However, it’s interesting to see which offensive units he’ll see time on to determine whether or not he’ll be a featured receiver on offense. The initial expectation when the Packers signed Moore this offseason was that he’d be strictly a return specialist. However, with a strong training camp, Gutekunst and LaFleur have suggested that the 25-year-old could also play a role on offense. Don’t worry as much about the numbers Moore puts up against the Broncos. Instead, pay attention to which offense he’s playing with. If he sees some reps with Jordan Love and the first-team unit, it’ll be a strong indicator that he’ll have a role to play beyond just returning kicks and punts in 2026. Jager Burton Jager Burton run blocks at guard (LG) pic.twitter.com/4bg69Rf2Ol — Justis Mosqueda (@JuMosq) August 19, 2026 The Packers have a long track record of finding great value on Day 3 of the NFL Draft with offensive linemen. Zach Tom was a fourth-round pick, while former mainstay left tackle Rasheed Walker wasn’t selected until the seventh round out of Penn State. Fifth-round rookie Jager Burton has a chance to be that next OL gem the Packers uncovered. A high-wasted, tenacious blocker out of Kentucky, Burton still looks a bit robotic at times, and can struggle keeping his feet moving after contact in pass protection. However, the flashes we saw in his preseason debut were very encouraging. Burton’s anchor looked strong in pass pro, and he was quickly displacing defensive linemen in the run game. Burton appears to be in an active competition for a starting guard spot , presumably opposite of Aaron Banks, against Jacob Monk and Anthony Belton. With another strong performance on Friday, he might win that starting job outright. Murvin Kenion III I’m absolutely fascinated by Murvin Kenion III, an undrafted rookie who has a real shot at making the final 53-man roster. A 25-year-old rookie typically isn’t that interesting, but Kenion’s journey to the NFL is fascinating. His college career includes stops at City College of San Francisco, Idaho, Sacramento State, and Nevada before finally going pro. While Kenion didn’t hear his name called in the 2026 NFL Draft, he made a strong final college impression at Nevada in 2025 with 59 tackles, five tackles for loss, five interceptions, three pass breakups, and two forced fumbles. Kenion brought some of that playmaking ability early in his preseason debut against Pittsburgh, and with another strong performance against the Broncos, he has a chance to have enough film to find a spot on Green Bay’s initial 53-man roster. Kyle McCord I won’t lie. I wasn’t expecting much when Kyle McCord rolled out onto the field in Week 1 of the preseason. But I came away pleasantly surprised with what the former Ohio State and Syracuse QB was able to do with the backups. McCord completed 12-of-16 passes for 102 yards last week, but beyond the box score, seemed more than comfortable running Green Bay’s offense. While he doesn’t have top-tier physical tools, He has solid size at 6-foot-3 and 218 pounds, and significant starting experience in college that helps him understand defenses and what they’re trying to do against. This isn’t to say that McCord is a starting-caliber QB, but another strong performance on Friday could allow him to stick around in Green Bay as a backup for the long haul.

title: Packers tease new uniform reveal coming next Tuesday
summary: The wait for the Packers’ long-anticipated/long-feared “Rivalries” uniform reveal is almost over. The team posted a short teaser video today, announcing the reveal of new alternate uniforms will be coming on Tuesday, August 25. The Packers are getting their new look courtesy of the dual NFL/Nike “Rivalries” uniform venture, duplicating similar initiatives in both the […]
full_text: GREEN BAY, WI - OCTOBER 20: The Green Bay Packers rolled out an all white helmet for their game between the Green Bay Packers and the Houston Texans at Lambeau Field on October 20, 2024 in Green Bay, WI. (Photo by Larry Radloff/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The wait for the Packers’ long-anticipated/long-feared “Rivalries” uniform reveal is almost over. The team posted a short teaser video today, announcing the reveal of new alternate uniforms will be coming on Tuesday, August 25. The Packers are getting their new look courtesy of the dual NFL/Nike “Rivalries” uniform venture, duplicating similar initiatives in both the NBA and MLB. Last year the NFC West and AFC East kicked the program off , and this year the NFC North and AFC South get the somewhat dubious honor of having new alternate uniforms forced upon them. The Packers are slated to wear their new uniforms during their Week 5 matchup with the Chicago Bears . The Bears themselves will wear their new alts when they face the Packers on Christmas. The team hasn’t done much to tip its hand concerning what the new uniforms could look like, but Packers president Ed Policy did give some oblique hints last fall. In November 2025, he said the uniforms were “not based on a historic uniform, but is inspired by one of the most unique and defining pieces of Packers history,” and followed that up with some truly mild praise (at best) this spring, offering that “this truly alternate uniform will celebrate owners and emphasize our uniqueness.” The teaser video shows very little of the actual uniform; there are just two extremely brief glimpses of anything the player (possibly/probably Jordan Love) is wearing. At around the seven-second mark, we see two very short shots of a player walking away from the camera wearing light colored shoes (white or a cream color) with gold trim paired with dark socks. That’s very little to go on, but it does align with a post from last month confirming the colorways of the shoes expected to be released in conjunction with the new uniforms. The Packers’ colors are traditional green and gold with cream and black added in. Based on @fashion_nfl 's list of RIVALRIES shoe colorways, and research on what each Nike color looks like, here's what should be each team's Air Max colorway👇 pic.twitter.com/S4rtmjWu48 — Texans Uniforms (@TexansUnis) July 3, 2026 Beyond that, all we have is speculation, but I think based on Policy’s previous comments , we’re going to get a uniform that pays homage to the many Packers shareholder certificates they’ve issued over the years. There’s nothing more unique about the Packers than that, since no other team in the NFL is publicly owned in any meaningful sense. You can kind of see a green and cream color scheme of sorts if you look at a few of the old certificates , and the 2012 offering certainly points in that direction . But there’s also quite a bit of gold lighting in the teaser video, which might hint toward another possibility I raised in previous writing about these uniforms: that they could include a nod toward the mighty Cheesehead. The Packers themselves now own the company that produces the most famous hat in sports, so they could go that direction as well. We’ll probably get a new helmet to go with these new uniforms, too. The Packers currently have three helmets in rotation: their traditional gold helmets, their alternate “Winter Warning” white helmets, and their throwback hand-painted faux-leather helmets, which they debuted last year. That’s quite a lineup. No matter what they wear, though, based solely on the teaser video it looks like Nathaniel Hackett would have loved them .

title: Green Bay Packers News: Packers’ cornerback battle is getting interesting
summary: Keisean Nixon, Carrington Valentine, Brandon Cisse and Benjamin St-Juste have all gotten first-team snaps during camp, and as Justis Mosqueda recently noted, it seems like the competition at corner is really opening up.  So as Green Bay takes the field against the Denver Broncos on Friday night, noting the cornerback rotation will be particularly interesting […]
full_text: Green Bay Packers cornerback Keisean Nixon (25) celebrates defeating the New Orleans Saints during their football game Sunday, September 24, 2023, at Lambeau Field in Green Bay, Wis. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co Keisean Nixon, Carrington Valentine, Brandon Cisse and Benjamin St-Juste have all gotten first-team snaps during camp, and as Justis Mosqueda recently noted , it seems like the competition at corner is really opening up. So as Green Bay takes the field against the Denver Broncos on Friday night, noting the cornerback rotation will be particularly interesting (preseason-relativity caveat for “interesting”). Which corners are on the field and when? Who gets the most meaningful snaps? Who does it seem like they trust the most? Those questions also carry additional weight now that we’ve recently heard some chatter about possible trade conversations. Recent reporting indicates teams have called the Packers about Valentine, while other reports have connected Green Bay to the broader cornerback market. That’s not confirmation that a trade is coming, but smoke usually means fire, so it’s worth keeping an eye on. If Cisse or St-Juste continues to look ready for an expanded role, the Packers could feel increasingly comfortable making a difficult decision involving one of their veterans. Conversely, if the younger corners struggle, Green Bay may decide its current group needs reinforcement. So as I watch tonight’s game, my thirty thousand foot lens will be fixed on any indications of whether the team seems poised to try to solve cornerback from within, or bank on looking elsewhere. ICYMI: Packers corner competition is opening up Justis Mosqueda’s recent training camp recap highlights OL and CB position battles. Packers are possible suitor for Joey Porter Jr. Rumors are circulating that the Packers might be in the Joey Porter Jr. market. Teams calling Packers about Valentine A few weeks out from final cutdowns, Packers’ Carrington Valentine has begun to generate trade buzz. Jordan Morgan finally gets his shot at the Packers’ left tackle job For two seasons, the Packers force-fit Morgan into guard, but now appear primed to give him a shot at tackle. title: Opportunity knocks for Packers edge rusher Brenton Cox
summary: Brenton Cox Jr. has been a model citizen for more than three years in Green Bay. Now he has a rare — but brief — opportunity to let his talent shine. Any discussion about Cox should begin with that first point; since arriving in Green Bay as an undrafted free agent in 2023, he’s been […]
full_text: GREEN BAY, WISCONSIN - SEPTEMBER 07: Brenton Cox Jr. #57 of the Green Bay Packers walks off the field after the Packers beat the Detroit Lions 27-13 at Lambeau Field on September 07, 2025 in Green Bay, Wisconsin. (Photo by Patrick McDermott/Getty Images) | Getty Images Brenton Cox Jr. has been a model citizen for more than three years in Green Bay. Now he has a rare — but brief — opportunity to let his talent shine. Any discussion about Cox should begin with that first point; since arriving in Green Bay as an undrafted free agent in 2023, he’s been exactly what any coach could hope for. He’s handled his work well, performed when called upon, and hasn’t made so much as a peep off the field. And that’s significant because of the circumstances under which he made his way to the Packers. Cox was certainly a draftable talent. He’d performed well at both Georgia and Florida, and has enviable (if not elite) physical tools. But he wasn’t drafted, and the only reason he spent time at both Georgia and Florida was because he was asked to leave first one program and, ultimately, the other. “He wears you down with his antics,” according to an anonymous scout who gave their appraisal to The Athletic’s Dane Brugler prior to the 2023 NFL Draft. Cox was Brugler’s 39th ranked edge rusher in that year’s edition of The Beast — again, certainly good enough to be drafted — but his name was never called, and those “antics” were likely the reason why. It wasn’t any one big thing, though a misdemeanor arrest for marijuana possession in April 2019 probably sped his departure from Georgia along. But an “accumulation” of issues (to quote Florida head coach Billy Napier) ended up bringing Cox’s time as a collegian to an end earlier than expected, turning him loose to ply his trade at the NFL level. And that’s exactly what he’s done. A solid pass rush prospect coming out of his time in college, Cox has shown some significant pass rush juice in his limited opportunities with the Packers. But now opportunity knocks, and it’s a high-stakes chance for Cox to make his mark. Micah Parsons is on the shelf for the first month or so of the 2026 season, and there’s no reason Cox can’t be one of the players who leads the charge in his absence. I’d push back on any analysis that says the Packers lack options on the edge. Lukas Van Ness was a first round pick for a reason, Barryn Sorrell has a solid scouting profile and was good enough as a rookie in 2025, Dani Dennis-Sutton was a steal in the fourth round, Collin Oliver is a traits-y, toolsy hybrid player, and Cox is no slouch in his own right. But it’s fair to say none of them has distinguished himself to this point. There are snaps available for the taking, and the first player to step up and grab himself a role might hang onto it well beyond when Parsons returns. Cox has a chance to make a real impact, which could pay significant dividends as he heads toward free agency next spring. But Cox’s window will close quickly. Parsons won’t be out forever, and he’ll eat up a ton of snaps when he returns. And with Cox on a short-term contract, he’s vulnerable. With players like Sorrell, Dennis-Sutton, and Oliver under contract into 2028 and beyond, the Packers don’t have much incentive to drop developmental resources into Cox; while players on their rookie contracts are cost-locked, he’s only going to get more expensive if he performs at a high level. Still, the opportunity is there. Cox has a chance to make a real difference for the Packers this season, making himself a lot of money in the process. The extent to which he can do that might secure his future as well as helping the Packers in the present.
author: Jon Meerdink

title: What is the Packers’ plan for Anthony Belton?
summary: Under Matt LaFleur, the Packers have never been afraid to move offensive linemen around. As we head into his eighth season as head coach, constant shifting up front has become commonplace. Guards become tackles, tackles become guards, anybody can play center at any time, and players flip flop from one side to another and back […]
full_text: PITTSBURGH, PENNSYLVANIA - AUGUST 13: Anthony Belton #71 of the Green Bay Packers in action during the game against the Pittsburgh Steelers at Acrisure Stadium on August 13, 2026 in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Joe Sargent/Getty Images) | Getty Images Under Matt LaFleur, the Packers have never been afraid to move offensive linemen around. As we head into his eighth season as head coach, constant shifting up front has become commonplace. Guards become tackles, tackles become guards, anybody can play center at any time, and players flip flop from one side to another and back again at the drop of a hat. It’s worked in the past. During the early years, in particular, the Packers got the most out of their offensive line talent with flexibility, and LaFleur’s “best five” mantra rang true. Getting the best five on the field was more important than having a well-defined depth chart of guards, tackles and centers. Positions mattered less than performance. The “move anybody, anywhere, anytime” approach has also failed in the past, too. The 2021 Divisional Round loss to the 49ers is the peak example. The Packers started Billy Turner at left tackle in that game despite Turner having not played that spot in more than a year, opting to try him at left tackle and itinerant Ricky Wagner at right tackle rather than rolling with Yosh Nijman, who had capably held down the left side most of that season. It’s also backfired with the Packers’ recent handling of Jordan Morgan. Despite being a dyed-in-the-wool left tackle, the Packers installed Morgan at guard as a rookie and never really let him out of that box until this season, even as Rasheed Walker struggled in 2025. The Packers seem to have rightly identified that Morgan was more versatile than Walker, but I think it was a mistake to get better depth at guard rather than getting stronger at tackle. Furthermore, the constant movement seems to have stunted Morgan’s development in his first two seasons. LaFleur himself all but admitted this last year , conceding they spread Morgan too thin last year, especially when asking him to play multiple different spots in a single game. And now that we’re 300-something words into this piece, I have to say I can’t help but wonder if the same thing is playing out with Anthony Belton. Belton is the latest practitioner — or perhaps victim — of the Packers’ versatility-as-ultimate-goal approach to the offensive line. The Packers haven’t been shy about moving Belton around from tackle to guard and back again over the course of his NFL career to date, and I think there’s reason to believe it’s hurting Belton more than it’s helping the team. The thinking seems clear: they want Belton to at the very least be their swing tackle in 2026. That would be fine if that’s all they were doing, but they also seem to want him to be their starting right guard. Or rather, they did, right up until the constant moving around seems to have rattled him badly enough to make playing both guard and tackle an adventure. Now, having Belton at guard or tackle seems like a liability, and his development seems to have been slowed by not really having a job or a home — which is more or less exactly what happened with Jordan Morgan. To be clear, it’s certainly possible that Belton is just not very good. The Packers are good at drafting offensive lineman, but that doesn’t mean every lineman they pick is an All-Pro in the making. The Packers have missed on offensive linemen before. It happens! Even accounting for that, it’s hard to give up on Belton at this point. It’s still early, and he’s still a marvel of size and power. Even if there are bumps in the road now, he’s still an enormous and intriguing ball of clay. But that intriguing ball is never going to shape itself into anything if the Packers can’t find a job for Belton and let him stick with it. They already spent two years making that mistake with Jordan Morgan, but appear to have finally pulled out of the skid. Let’s hope it doesn’t take that long to figure something out with Belton.
author: Jon Meerdink

title: Texans sign two veteran wide receivers
summary: The vacancy in the wide receiver room has been addressed and addressed immediately. Reports are that the Texans have agreed to sign veteran wide receivers Sterling Shepard and Zay Jones. Both have had past success in their careers and served as starting receivers in recent seasons. The two wide receivers impressed in a workout and […]
full_text: The vacancy in the wide receiver room has been addressed and addressed immediately. Reports are that the Texans have agreed to sign veteran wide receivers Sterling Shepard and Zay Jones. Both have had past success in their careers and served as starting receivers in recent seasons. The two wide receivers impressed in a workout and Nick Caserio immediately acted to make the move. Texans Signing WRs Sterling Shepard & Zay Jones https://t.co/FW7VAlBNO5 #Texans — NFLTradeRumors.co (@nfltrade_rumors) August 21, 2026 For his part, Shepard most recently played for the Tampa Bay Bucs where he caught 39 balls and 371 yards and a touchdown. Shepard’s first five seasons in the league were very impressive as he topped 100 targets in two seasons and never caught fewer than 57 balls. However, The last five have seen him serve as a complimentary piece with the New York Giants and Bucs. He has a grand total of 443 receptions and 4800 yards. At five foot ten, he is on the smaller side and could end up fitting in the slot position. Even with Jayden Higgins, it was unclear as to who was going to take that slot position. Jaylin Noel and Tank Dell have both been recovering from injuries and have been in and out of practice all camp. The rest of the receiving core were either larger border targets like Xavier Hutchinson and Justin Watson and umproven receivers like Lewis Bond. Shepard gives the Texans a veterans they can plausibly put in that slot position. Jones fits the border category at six foot two. He caught just 12 balls a season ago for a Cardinals team that struggled all season. He also went down with a major knee injury in November. Like Shepard, he also has two seasons with more than 100 targets and two seasons with 50 or more catches. His best season was in 2022 when he had 82 catches and 823 yards with the Jacksonville Jaguars. This will be an interesting situation to keep an eye on because the Texans brought in both wide receivers. It could be that they expect only one to stick and just want to give both some time to figure out which one will stick. It also could be that they are not satisfied with their receiver room even independent of the Higgins injury. It could mean that Noel and Dell can’t be counted on when week one rolls around. Obviously, this also complicates the depth chart and final cut down day with only one preseason game to see them in live action.

title: SI.com shares interesting anecdote about football brain bond between Daniel Jones and Shane Steichen
summary: According to SI.com’s Albert Breer, the football brain bond between Indianapolis Colts starting quarterback Daniel Jones and his head coach Shane Steichen was already on full display during Week 1 of last season as part of their initial pairing: “And Jones was already getting there in certain ways, maybe best illustrated through a Week 1 […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, INDIANA - OCTOBER 17: Daniel Jones and Head coach Shane Steichen of the Indianapolis Colts watch the game between the Notre Dame Fighting Irish and the Butler Bulldogs at Hinkle Fieldhouse on October 17, 2025 in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Photo by Justin Casterline/Getty Images) | Getty Images According to SI.com’s Albert Breer, the football brain bond between Indianapolis Colts starting quarterback Daniel Jones and his head coach Shane Steichen was already on full display during Week 1 of last season as part of their initial pairing: “And Jones was already getting there in certain ways, maybe best illustrated through a Week 1 example from last year that Steichen brought up,” writes Breer. “On Fridays and Saturdays, Steichen and Jones would have a one-on-one meeting on how Steichen would call the game, and what Jones was most comfortable with that week. So they got to the fourth-down, gotta-have-it part of Steichen’s playsheet, and a run/pass/run option play came up. Steichen said if the Dolphins were in a soft Cover Zero look, the play would be really tight, and probably wouldn’t work. “He’s like, Well, I can get this protection, and then I got a one-on-one in zero on the outside, and I’m going to check this and throw it to [Josh] Downs ,” Steichen recalled. “Sure enough, he goes over that with the guys in the Saturday night meeting. And it comes up in the game. But we just talked about it. I didn’t put kill on it. I said, ‘If you see it, get to it.’ And he got to it, checked the protection and threw a quick out to Downs for a first down.” Of course, it’s now history, but the reason that Jones won the Colts starting quarterback job last training camp and preseason wasn’t necessarily solely because of his on-field play. Rather, it was a lot of the things that Colts fans didn’t get to see firsthand off of it: being the first one in and the last one to leave the team facility, his understanding of the offense and its intricacies, the extra film study, the bonding with teammates, etc. Both Steichen and him showed great initial chemistry, even being seen attending a Butler game courtside together in the early goings of last season—meaning they were spent time together even outside the complex. In his first season under Steichen, Jones was well on his way to a breakout season before critical later season injuries derailed his career year—eventually succumbing to a season-ending torn Achilles suffered in Week 14. That being said, the quarterback-and-head coach pairing showed a lot of initial production and promise together, and the Colts will be looking to continue that momentum offensively from where it left off around midseason.
author: Luke Schultheis

title: Aziz’s 53-man depth chart prediction
summary: Offense (25) Quarterback (3) – Daniel Jones | Anthony Richardson | Riley Leonard Running Back (3) – Jonathan Taylor | DJ Giddens | Seth McGowan Receivers (6) – Alec Pierce | Josh Downs | Keenan Allen | Ashton Dulin | Nick Westbrook-Ikhine | Anthony Gould Tight Ends (4) – Tyler Warrren | Mo Alie-Cox | […]
full_text: WESTFIELD, INDIANA - AUGUST 19: Head coach Shane Steichen of the Indianapolis Colts looks on during the joint practice with the Atlanta Falcons at Grand Park Sports Campus on August 19, 2026 in Westfield, Indiana. (Photo by Justin Casterline/Getty Images) | Getty Images Offense (25) Quarterback (3) – Daniel Jones | Anthony Richardson | Riley Leonard Running Back (3) – Jonathan Taylor | DJ Giddens | Seth McGowan Receivers (6) – Alec Pierce | Josh Downs | Keenan Allen | Ashton Dulin | Nick Westbrook-Ikhine | Anthony Gould Tight Ends (4) – Tyler Warrren | Mo Alie-Cox | Drew Ogletree | Will Mallory Offensive Line (9) – Bernhard Raimann | Quenton Nelson | Tanor Bortolini | Matt Goncalves | Jalen Travis | Blake Freeland | Jalen Farmer | Josh Sills | Dalton Tucker The offense is fairly straightforward, with the biggest decision already made by the Colts themselves. Indianapolis has said it plans to keep three quarterbacks, and after the way Ed Dodds has publicly vouched for Anthony Richardson, it does not sound like he is going anywhere. Daniel Jones is the starter, Richardson remains on the roster, and Riley Leonard sticks as the developmental option. At running back, Jonathan Taylor is obviously locked in as RB1, while DJ Giddens and Seth McGowan have both done enough in camp to make the roster and potentially split the backup work. That battle should continue into the season, especially if the Colts are serious about taking some of the load off Taylor. Receiver also feels like a six-man group. Alec Pierce, Josh Downs and Keenan Allen should all have significant offensive roles, while Ashton Dulin and Anthony Gould bring clear special teams impact. Nick Westbrook-Ikhine gets the final spot because of his veteran presence and ability to serve as the true WR4 if the offense needs him. Tight end is another spot where the Colts could go heavier than usual, especially with the expected increase in 12 personnel. Tyler Warren, Mo Alie-Cox, Drew Ogletree and Will Mallory all bring enough value to justify keeping four. On the offensive line, nine feels like the right number. Bernhard Raimann, Quenton Nelson, Tanor Bortolini, Matt Goncalves and Jalen Travis are the projected starters, while Blake Freeland gives them an experienced swing tackle, Jalen Farmer is the young rookie guard, and Josh Sills and Dalton Tucker round out the interior depth after working with the second-team group against the Patriots. Defense (25) Defensive Line (10) – Laiatu Latu | DeForest Buckner | Grover Stewart | Arden Key | JT Tuimoloau | Colby Wooden | Adetomiwa Adebawore | Michael Clemons | Caden Curry | George Gumbs Jr Linebackers (5) – CJ Allen | Akeem Davies Gaither | Austin Ajiake | Bryce Boettcher | Jaylon Carlies Cornerbacks (6) – Sauce Gardner | Charvarius Ward | Justin Walley | Mekhi Blackmon | Jonathan Edwards | Jaylon Jones (Cam Taylor Britt suspended for week 1) Safeties (4) – Cam Bynum | AJ Haulcy | Jonathan Owens | Hunter Woehler Ten defensive linemen may sound like a lot, but this is one of the deepest and most talented groups on the roster, so it makes sense for the Colts to go heavy here. Laiatu Latu, DeForest Buckner and Grover Stewart are returning impact players, while Arden Key, Colby Wooden and Michael Clemons give the front several new veteran additions. Adetomiwa Adebawore and JT Tuimoloau have played well enough to feel safe, and Caden Curry has helped himself with a strong camp and preseason. George Gumbs Jr. is probably the one closest to the cut line, but for now, the depth and upside along the defensive line make him worth keeping. Linebacker is thinner but still fairly clear. CJ Allen and Akeem Davis-Gaither look like the probable starters, while Austin Ajiake has played a lot with the second-team defense and appears to be in good position. Bryce Boettcher helped himself with a strong showing against New England and could work his way toward a starting role at some point this season, while Jaylon Carlies gets the final spot because he played well in the preseason opener and brings special teams value. At cornerback, Cam Taylor-Britt’s Week 1 suspension changes the math because he will not count toward the initial roster, meaning someone else can stick for now before a later decision has to be made. Sauce Gardner, Charvarius Ward and Justin Walley are the starters and obvious locks, Mekhi Blackmon is safe because of his veteran experience, and Jaylon Jones’ experience with the Colts bring a lot of value. Jonathan Edwards is right on the cut line after struggling at corner in the first preseason game, but his special teams value keeps him in for now, with Taylor-Britt’s return likely putting him in the most danger. At safety, the Colts keep four true safeties with Cam Bynum, AJ Haulcy, Jonathan Owens and Hunter Woehler, and this seems to be the position that might get a real chop so that others can thrive. Special Teams (3) Kicker – Blake Grupe Punter – Rigoberto Sanchez Long Snapper – Luke Rhodes The specialist group is simple outside of kicker. Rigoberto Sanchez and Luke Rhodes are locks, while the kicking battle remains extremely close. I lean toward Blake Grupe for now because of his consistency in training camp and because he may be the harder player to sneak through waivers if the Colts want to keep both kickers in the building. Spencer Shrader still has a legitimate case, and this feels close to a true 50/50 battle, but Grupe gets the slight edge in this projection. If the Colts can keep Shrader on the practice squad, that would be the ideal outcome, although there is always some risk when exposing a kicker with NFL ability. title: Reacts Survey Results: Hype builds for Jaguars LG Emmanuel Pregnon
summary: This week, we asked Jacksonville Jaguars fans which player impressed them most in this year’s first preseason game. A third of the respondants went with rookie left guard Emmanuel Pregnon. With the caveat of it not being a true NFL game against the league’s top players and schemes… Pregnon looked really good! It sounded like […]
full_text: NEW ORLEANS, LOUISIANA - AUGUST 15: Emmanuel Pregnon #75 of the Jacksonville Jaguars against the New Orleans Saints at Caesars Superdome on August 15, 2026 in New Orleans, Louisiana. (Photo by Chris Graythen/Getty Images) | Getty Images This week, we asked Jacksonville Jaguars fans which player impressed them most in this year’s first preseason game . A third of the respondants went with rookie left guard Emmanuel Pregnon. With the caveat of it not being a true NFL game against the league’s top players and schemes… Pregnon looked really good! . @Jaguars @Saints @PregnonEmmanuel had a fine debut playing the entire first half. Showed the same skills that we saw @oregonfootball last year..Very high on this prospect becoming a starter. #duval #BaldysBreakdowns pic.twitter.com/TrlLsRQRD7 — Brian Baldinger (@BaldyNFL) August 17, 2026 It sounded like head coach Liam Coen was trying to slow down the hype train. “Did some nice things,” he said on Monday of Pregnon’s performance. “Did some really nice things. Moved people in one-on-one situations, de-cleated a guy on a pull … He flashed. That was for sure. He flashed. He flashed in the joint as well when he got some opportunities with the ones, and he’s just continuing. It’s a process. It’s not something that we’re obviously trying to push. It’s just, hey, when the time comes, he’ll be ready. He’s trying to work through that and the continuity with the group. And you’re not seeing as much as he’s going to see, obviously, when we get going. So, pumping the brakes a little on it, but just for what he was able to do and the ops that he had, we were pleased with him.” The Jaguars seemingly planned for Pregnon to “redshirt” this season before seizing a starting job as a second-year pro. With a slew of injuries hitting Jacksonville’s O-line, though, Pregnon has taken the bulk of first-team reps in practice this week — and continues to impress in such opportunities. “Coach [Brian] Picucci, Coach [Shaun] Sarrett do a great job preparing him,” offensive coordinator Grant Udinski said Tuesday. “And he puts in a lot of extra work on his own time. I see him in here at the facility. I’ll take a stroll downstairs and it’s 10 o’clock at night and I’m expecting it’s only the cleaning crews around, but it’s Emmanuel rolling around through the locker room, just finishing up his recovery work. So, I probably don’t have enough good things to say about a guy like that.” Safe to say that Pregnon is trending up! Hopefully, he’ll continue to flash in Week 2 of the preseason when the Jaguars host the Carolina Panthers at 7:30 p.m. on Friday. The good guys are 1.5-point underdogs, per FanDuel Sportsbook . Let us know your thoughts in the comments below!

title: Chiefs-Buccaneers: 5 things to watch in NFL Preseason Week 2
summary: The Kansas City Chiefs will take on the Tampa Bay Buccaneers in Week 2 of the NFL preseason on Saturday in Tampa Bay. The game will kick off at 6:30 P.M. Arrowhead time and be broadcast on KSHB 41 for local viewers. The Chiefs lost the first preseason game against the Los Angeles Rams 20-12, […]
full_text: TAMPA, FLORIDA - OCTOBER 02: A general view of the line of scrimmage between the Tampa Bay Buccaneers and the Kansas City Chiefs at Raymond James Stadium on October 02, 2022 in Tampa, Florida. (Photo by Mike Ehrmann/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Kansas City Chiefs will take on the Tampa Bay Buccaneers in Week 2 of the NFL preseason on Saturday in Tampa Bay. The game will kick off at 6:30 P.M. Arrowhead time and be broadcast on KSHB 41 for local viewers. The Chiefs lost the first preseason game against the Los Angeles Rams 20-12, but the team showed tremendous glimpses of how the 2026 roster could shape up. There will be plenty to watch this week as the Chiefs break from training camp in St. Joseph, Missouri, and begin to prepare for the regular season. Here are five things to watch: 1. Cyrus Allen targets In the Chiefs’ first preseason game, Allen tallied two receptions for 20 yards, but he has picked up steam in training camp. It will be worth watching if he will gain more targets in Week 2 of the preseason. Justin Fields will once again be the Chiefs starter against the Buccaneers, but it should be expected that he and the Chiefs’ projected starters will play more snaps in preparation for the season. Allen has shown a variety of skills in camp and the preseason so far, and many have him pegged for a breakout rookie season. This week could tell us a lot about how the Chiefs fully view Allen, and if he does end up with a large share of targets, then he should be on everyone’s radar come week one. 2. Emmett Johnson : RB2? The Chiefs running back room has been crowded so far during camp and the preseason, but last week, fifth-round rookie Emmett Johnson flashed with his 12 carries and 59 yards. Brashard Smith and Emari Demercado were both in the mix during camp and into preseason Week 1, but Johnson stole the show, showing vision and quickness the Chiefs haven’t seen at the position in some time. The room obviously belongs to Kenneth Walker, but when Johnson came out as the first back behind him this week at camp, it likely signified that he is on his way to becoming the backup running back this season, and could have a larger role within the offense. 3. Backup Tight Ends One of the more intriguing roster battles for the team is how depth at tight end will end up, and all of the challenges to be tight end two received targets and recorded receptions in week one of the preseason. Noah Gray, Jake Briningstool, Jared Wiley, and Tre Watson all caught passes last weekend, with Briningstool leading the way with three receptions for 29 yards. Due to his experience, Gray is still the leader of the pack to back up Travis Kelce this season, but the young trio is pushing for more playing time. Briningstool has impressed in camp and the preseason so far with his ability to catch the ball and flow within the offense. After missing most of the 2025 season with injury, Wylie has flashed in camp and had a terrific sideline catch in week one of the preseason. When mixed in, Watson has made plays, but he will have a long way to climb. This week all eyes will likely be on Briningstool and Wylie, who both seem to be competing for the third tight end spot. Neither has shown much prowess in run blocking — which likely boosts Gray — but with their height and size, either has a chance to become the Chiefs’ third tight end and compete for a spot on the active roster. 4. The offensive line without Josh Simmons Late in the week, the Chiefs offensive line got shaken up even more than it was with starting right guard Trey Smith (Hip) missing time. Josh Simmons was out of practice towards the end of the week with a back injury — yikes — and the Chiefs lineup was from left to right: Jaylon Moore, Kingsley Suamataia, Creed Humphrey, Mike Caliendo, and Kahlil Benson. This lineup stands out for multiple reasons, but the most notable is Benson sliding back out to right tackle, where he began training camp. When Smith went down, Benson slid inside to guard while Moore moved up to first-team tackle, but with multiple key starters down, Moore will now slide to the blindside while Benson bumps back out to right tackle and Caliendo slides into the starting rotation. Chiefs fans had scoffed at Moore for most of camp for being on the second team behind the undrafted rookie, but with the slew of injuries, he has displayed his value and versatility already. Regardless of what Chiefs Kingdom thinks of Caliendo, he has been a player the Chiefs have leaned on when the depth of the interior has crumbled, and he will once again be at the forefront of the offensive line. Time will only tell when the Chiefs’ full starting front five will be back, but in the meantime they will rely on the experience of their depth. 5. Mansoor Delane Mansoor Delane spent most of training camp in a yellow non-contact jersey, drawing angst from much of the Kingdom, but earlier this week he replaced the yellow with a white jersey and fully entered practice. The Chiefs traded up to get Delane with the sixth overall pick in the draft, but his inability to participate fully in practice has been a cause for concern for many. These concerns were dashed away this week, as Delane suited up and appeared to perform well during his practice repetitions. All eyes will be on the highly touted rookie corner on Saturday to see if he makes his professional debut in Tampa Bay; defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo said head coach Andy Reid needed to make that call earlier this week .

title: The hardest and easiest stretches on the Chiefs’ 2026 schedule
summary: Nine of the Kansas City Chiefs‘ games this year will be played against teams that made the playoffs in 2025. Still, the team has two separate three-game stretches against teams that missed the playoffs last season. But if you do the math, there are still more tough games on this schedule than tea parties. But […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - AUGUST 15: Head coach Sean McVay of the Los Angeles Rams speaks with head coach Andy Reid of the Kansas City Chiefs prior to an NFL preseason game at Arrowhead Stadium on August 15, 2026 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by David Eulitt/Getty Images) | Getty Images Nine of the Kansas City Chiefs ‘ games this year will be played against teams that made the playoffs in 2025. Still, the team has two separate three-game stretches against teams that missed the playoffs last season. But if you do the math, there are still more tough games on this schedule than tea parties. But the question is, which stretches of the schedule are the most murderous? And likewise, which games are easy enough that you’re not chasing shots of Mylanta with extra doses of your blood pressure medication at halftime? That’s what we’re trying to figure out today. And for the sake of arbitrary consistency, for this article, we’ll define a stretch as any span of three or more games that’s not interrupted by a cupcake. So without further ado, let’s take a look at the Chiefs schedule and see if we can distill the hardest and easiest stretches of the 2026 season. Hardest stretches There are really two contenders for the most difficult stretch of the season, and oddly enough, both of them involve a team that plays in Los Angeles. And if we were only looking at the minimum threshold of three-game spans, Week 6-8 of the Chiefs’ schedule is an intriguing pick for the toughest stretch. But if you can think objectively and not visualize the Cincinnati Bengals as the NFL equivalent of a bunch of hungover trainwrecks doing the walk of shame in the morning (and if you can, then you’re a better person than me), then the clear-cut winner for the hardest stretch of the season is Weeks 12-17. It starts with three games on the road, including two back-to-back Thursday nights against the Buffalo Bills and the Los Angeles Rams . Then, after a brief reprieve, the Chiefs get to play the Bengals at Paycor Stadium. It’s back home to play against a tough New England Patriots team. The stretch ends with another home game against the San Francisco 49ers , and another road game to the West Coast, only this time it’s against the Chiefs’ division rivals, the Los Angeles Chargers . The Chiefs play against three of the best quarterbacks in the league during this stretch (and Joe Burrow). The Chiefs also play the Chargers, which is like eating dry wheat toast in the morning. Toughest games in this stretch: 1.) Week 13: at Rams Quarterback Matt Stafford was the league MVP last season. To make matters worse, the Rams traded for Myles Garrett, and there are rumors that the Incredible Hulk, a.k.a Aaron Donald, is contemplating coming out of retirement. When you add the Chiefs’ two best cornerbacks from a year ago to this defense, it’s starting to look pretty daunting. 2.) Week 15: vs. Patriots New England is a well-coached team with a stud young quarterback in Drake Maye, who finished in the top four in both yards and touchdowns last season. The Patriots have an excellent running game with the one-two punch of Rhamondre Stevenson and TreVeyon Henderson. And then, when you figure in the offseason acquisition of No.1 receiver AJ Brown, the Patriots are primed to make another run in the AFC East. 3.) Week 16: vs. 49ers The 49ers and head coach Kyle Shanahan are like black mold, in that you can never really get rid of them. Luckily, San Francisco also seems to oscillate between a good season one year and double-digit losses the next. The fate of the 49ers rises and falls with the health of running back Christian McCaffrey. Easiest stretches Without a doubt, Weeks 9-11 are by far the easiest stretch of the season and serve as the calm before the storm of every. Coming off a late-game road game against the Denver Broncos the week before, the Chiefs have an opportunity to return home during this stretch and fortify themselves before hopefully making a push for the playoffs. And while there is no such thing as a gimme in the NFL, the Arizona Cardinals are about as close as it gets to being a team full of players who should be clamoring to try to return to play in the NCAA. On the other hand, I still expect the New York Jets to be, well, um—the Jets. But they are a sneaky candidate to be a trip-up game this season if they can stay healthy and get all their young offensive weapons on the field at the same time. Easiest games in this stretch: 1.) Week 9: vs. Jets The Jets tanked last season so they could load up on young talent on both sides of the ball. The result is a handful of players who could be legitimate stars in this league. Draft picks like edge rusher David Bailey and tight end Kenyon Sadiq. Along with some players who have already made a name for themselves, such as running back Breece Hall, wide receiver Garrett Wilson, defensive tackle T’Vondre Sweat, etc. But once you get past these players, the roster falls off a cliff, especially on the defensive side of the ball, with guys like Kiko Mauigoa and Andre Cisco expected to play big roles this season. 2.) Week 10: at Atlanta Falcons I mean, just copy-paste what I wrote above, and replace Love with Bijan Robinson, and McBride with Kyle Pitts Sr. The only difference is that Atlanta has two bad starting quarterbacks, instead of two good backups. 3) Week 11: vs. Cardinals On paper, there are things to like about this team. Like the fact that they have a pair of dynamic offensive weapons, including running back Jeremiyah Love and tight end Trey McBride. But this roster is top-heavy and lacks a starting quarterback. If the Chiefs don’t beat the Cadinals, then this is going to be a long season. Do you agree with our assessment of the easiest and hardest stretches of the season? You know the drill—tell us if we’re either geniuses or morons in the comments below.

title: What can the Chiefs realistically expect from Cyrus Allen this season?
summary: I’m done being a hater. Kansas City Chiefs rookie wide receiver Cyrus Allen looks real. The consistent drumbeat throughout training camp and his performance in the Chiefs’ first preseason game have convinced me the kid can play. Go ahead and include me among the Cyrus Allen truthers. But don’t include me among those getting out […]
full_text: I’m done being a hater. Kansas City Chiefs rookie wide receiver Cyrus Allen looks real. The consistent drumbeat throughout training camp and his performance in the Chiefs’ first preseason game have convinced me the kid can play. Go ahead and include me among the Cyrus Allen truthers. But don’t include me among those getting out over my skis on what that means for his production this season. That’s a different story entirely. And it’s less about Allen and more about the situation he’s walking into. There’s a non-zero chance Cyrus Allen is just the Chiefs WR1 — SleeperNFL (@SleeperNFL) August 19, 2026 It’s true that the Chiefs’ wide receiver room is not exactly full of known commodities, but let’s not pretend it lacks for talent. Rashee Rice can be a top-20 receiver in the league when he’s both healthy and has his head on straight. Unfortunately, neither of those factors has proven to be reliable over the past two seasons. Xavier Worthy has shown promise, but his second season was plagued by injuries. Tyquan Thornton was encouraging when utilized last season, but his utilization waned as the season progressed. That’s to say nothing of Travis Kelce, one of the greatest tight ends in the history of the league. He’ll also command his fair share of targets in what could be the final season of his illustrious career. That’s a lot of mouths to feed, and a lot of targets to project. This is where the math comes in for 17-game sample sizes. Rice has averaged roughly 125 targets per 17 games in his NFL career. That would have ranked 15th among NFL pass-catchers last season. Feels about right. Travis Kelce is probably good for at least 100 targets, even at this stage of his career. Worthy has been around that 100-target threshold when healthy. Thornton is tougher to project, but a serious threat like him typically earns 50-75 targets. That’s roughly what Marquez Valdes-Scantling finished with annually in his Chiefs tenure, for example. Add it all up, and that’s approximately 400 targets to the top three wide receivers, plus Kelce. Add in approximately 75-80 targets for the running backs and another 40 for Noah Gray, and we’re already projecting more than 500 targets without including any of the other ancillary pieces of the offense. Is now a good time to mention that Patrick Mahomes has averaged approximately 600 pass attempts per season in recent years? Long story short, we’re left with roughly 80 targets to play with for Cyrus Allen and the rest of the receivers and tight ends. This assumes everyone stays healthy. Only six wide receivers last season with fewer than 60 targets finished with more than 500 receiving yards . It’s hard to put up significant volume without bulk targets. Thus is life for a third or fourth wide receiver, and the likely fifth or sixth option in the offense. It goes beyond just what we’ve seen from the Chiefs in recent years, though. Allen will also have to beat the odds as a late-round selection. There have been 75 wide receivers selected on day 3 of the NFL Draft over the past five years, according to Pro Football Reference . Among those 75 players, 15 had more than 200 receiving yards in their rookie year. Only eight eclipsed the 400-yard plateau. Only two — Amon Ra St. Brown of the Detroit Lions and Puka Nacua of the Los Angeles Rams — finished their rookie year with more than 600 receiving yards. It’s hard to earn a role as a young player. It’s even harder when you enter the league with little to no draft pedigree. The track record is slightly more encouraging for rookie wide receivers under head coach Andy Reid, but with a strong caveat we’ll get to. The Chiefs have drafted nine wide receivers in the Andy Reid era, according to Pro Football Reference . Among those nine, more than half (5) finished their rookie campaign with at least 200 yards. A sixth (Chris Conley) finished with 199 receiving yards. Mecole Hardman (538), Tyreek Hill (593), Xavier Worthy (638) and Rashee Rice (938) each had at least 500 receiving yards as a rookie for the Chiefs. Impressive list. The Eagles drafted 13 wide receivers while Andy Reid was at the helm between 1999 and 2012, according to Pro Football Reference . Only four of those 13 finished their rookie campaign with at least 200 receiving yards; Reggie Brown (571), Jeremy Maclin (773), and DeSean Jackson (912) recorded 500+ receiving yards. Now for the caveat. The vast majority of those big rookie seasons were from wide receivers selected in the first two rounds. Jeremy Maclin (19th), Freddie Mitchell (25th), Xavier Worthy (28th), Reggie Brown (35th), DeSean Jackson (49th), Skyy Moore (54th), Rashee Rice (55th), and Mecole Hardman (56th) were all top-60 selections. Draft status matters. It leads to early opportunity, and most of those players took advantage of the opportunity granted to them as premium draft picks. The one outlier in Reid’s tenure as a head coach was Tyreek Hill. He was the 165th overall selection, but we all know he’s a unique case for a million different reasons. He’s a special talent, and his production reflected as much as a rookie. Allen was selected in the fifth round with the 176th overall selection. Players selected at that point in the draft aren’t even a lock to make the roster, much less to contribute in a meaningful way as a rookie. Allen already looks like a home run selection, regardless of what the production states as a rookie. My personal projection for Allen this season? 30 receptions for 350 yards. Those are approximately the numbers JuJu Smith-Schuster produced a year ago. Replicating that kind of production as a rookie is a heck of a starting point for a fifth-round pick. The hype is real. The excitement is hard to contain. Let’s just keep on-field expectations realistic so we don’t walk away from Allen’s rookie season feeling disappointed with what would otherwise be a heck of a debut campaign. What is your statistical projection for Allen this season?

title: Chiefs Injuries: Analyzing Ashton Gillotte’s ruptured plantar fascia
summary: As Kansas City Chiefs training camp comes to a close, a major injury update was shared with the media regarding second-year defensive end Ashton Gillotte. Gillotte was diagnosed with a ruptured plantar fascia after being injured during Tuesday’s practice. The injury affects an already thin defensive line group. Gillotte did not play in the preseason […]
full_text: ST. JOSEPH, MO - JULY 29: Ashton Gillotte #97 walks to the field during the Kansas City Chiefs training camp on Aug 11, 2026 at Missouri Western State University in St. Joseph, MO. (Photo by Scott Winters/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images As Kansas City Chiefs training camp comes to a close, a major injury update was shared with the media regarding second-year defensive end Ashton Gillotte. Gillotte was diagnosed with a ruptured plantar fascia after being injured during Tuesday’s practice. Per Andy Reid, #Chiefs DE Ashton Gillotte suffered a ruptured plantar fascia on this play two days ago. pic.twitter.com/r82yk6a3To — Matt Foster (@MattFosterTV) August 20, 2026 The injury affects an already thin defensive line group. Gillotte did not play in the preseason opener due to a prior hamstring injury. Fortunately, Reid downplayed the severity of the second-year pro’s injury during his media availability. How serious is a ruptured plantar fascia, and when can we expect Gillotte to return to the lineup? The injury The plantar fascia is a thick band of connective tissue that connects the calcaneus (heel bone) to all five toes. The plantar fascia absorbs shock and supports the arch of the foot. It also acts as a “spring” of sorts, assisting to propel the foot forward with each step. Plantar fascia strain is very common in athletes and non-athletes alike and can result in plantar fasciitis , an inflammatory condition. As with all soft tissue injuries, strains and tears are graded on a scale to determine severity of injury. A rupture of the plantar fascia indicates a complete tearing of the soft tissue. A ruptured plantar fascia initially results in sudden and intense sharp pain, difficulty weight-bearing, bruising, and swelling. Fortunately for Gillotte, a complete rupture offers a better prognosis and quicker return to play than a partial tear. Once past the acute phase of higher pain, the pain does subside, and normal weight bearing can be restored. Any injury involving the plantar fascia is painful, but it can be managed, allowing professional athletes to return to the field quickly. A defensive end obviously requires a great deal of power to get off the line quickly and fight off blocks. Once Gillotte’s pain has decreased, restoring power and get-off will be essential to returning to his prior level of play and returning to the field. The bottom line In their initial evaluation, the Chiefs are optimistic that Ashton Gillotte, who ruptured his plantar fascia, could return in about 3 weeks. If his rehab goes well, Gillotte would have a chance to be available Sept. 14 to play on opening night against the Broncos. — Nate Taylor (@ByNateTaylor) August 20, 2026 It is certainly realistic for Gillotte to be available for the Chiefs in Week 1. The second-year pro is looking to build upon a slow start to his professional career. Gillotte appeared in all 17 games and had 1.5 sacks along with an interception during his rookie year. It shouldn’t be shocking to expect Gillotte to miss the rest of the preseason and likely be a limited participant in most practices. As long as Gillotte’s rehab goes according to plan, however, this should not be an injury that sidelines him for a significant portion of the beginning of the regular season. The Chiefs open their 2026 season at home on “Monday Night Football” against their division rival, the Denver Broncos .

title: Emmanuel Ogbah always planned to return to the Chiefs
summary: On Saturday, the Kansas City Chiefs will travel to face the Tampa Bay Buccaneers for their second of three preseason contests. Fans of the team will likely see a familiar face on the field. Last week, Kansas City signed veteran defensive end Emmanuel Ogbah. Ogbah previously played for the Chiefs in 2019 and delivered 5.5 […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MO - NOVEMBER 03: Defensive end Emmanuel Ogbah #90 of the Kansas City Chiefs gets set on defense against the Minnesota Vikings during the first half at Arrowhead Stadium on November 3, 2019 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by Peter G. Aiken/Getty Images) | Getty Images On Saturday, the Kansas City Chiefs will travel to face the Tampa Bay Buccaneers for their second of three preseason contests. Fans of the team will likely see a familiar face on the field. Last week, Kansas City signed veteran defensive end Emmanuel Ogbah. Ogbah previously played for the Chiefs in 2019 and delivered 5.5 sacks over 10 games. Unfortunately, a torn pectoral muscle ended his season early, even as the Chiefs went on to win Super Bowl LIV. Speaking from the team’s training camp at Missouri Western State University in St. Joseph on Monday, Ogbah appeared to have been waiting seven years for his return to red and gold. Even as he returned to the dorms at Missouri Western, he was happy to be back in Kansas City. “It’s been a long time,” Ogbah remarked. “I always knew I was going to come back eventually; I just didn’t know when. But it feels good being back. I did not miss the dorms, but you know it feels good being back here.” Even with more than a half-decade away from the Chiefs, Ogbah remains close to defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo. “I definitely kept in touch with Spags,” he recalled, “but at the same time, I just knew there was something for me still in Kansas City. When you have that in the back of your head, whenever there’s an opportunity, you try to come back. That was my goal, and I’m glad I was able to make it work.” Ogbah is also thrilled to be back with the only defensive player remaining from his first Chiefs tenure: star defensive tackle Chris Jones. “I know Chris,” the veteran declared. “I’ve been knowing Chris since draft prep. Big character guy, [I] love Chris. He’s a worker, an All-Pro; just being back with him brings a different energy.” This time around, two rookies are carrying heavy expectations for the Chiefs’ front seven. Ogbah is high on what he has seen from defensive tackle Peter Woods and edge rusher R Mason Thomas in their short time together. “Talented,” he observed of the pair. “I loved watching them out there in the game last week. It was good to see them get after the quarterback and play the run well. They’re young cats, but they’re definitely talented.” Understanding that the team will want to develop the younger talent, Ogbah is ready for whatever his past and now current team chooses to do with him. “Just whatever they need me to play,” he remarked. “Just attack whenever my name is called, and I’ll be ready to go.” Many Chiefs fans — hoping for a higher profile signing at the position — were underwhelmed by Ogbah’s return to the team. Expect to see a motivated player added to the defensive end rotation. “I can still play,” Ogbah declared. “Keep going and keep getting better. You learn every year. You try to push yourself as much as you can. I still have a lot of football left in me, so I just want to keep going out there and just keep balling.”

Kansas City Chiefs Win Total Projection for 2026 Season (Is the Chiefs Era Over?) | Sports Illustrated In my NFL betting preview article, 32 Bets for 32 Teams, I made the case for betting on the UNDER 10.5 wins for the Chiefs: I don’t think this is automatically going to be a bounce-back season for the Kansas City Chiefs. title: What does Sean McVay have in store for preseason Week 2?
summary: As the Los Angeles Rams enter Week 2 of the NFL preseason, there are still roster questions to be answered. On offense, QB#2, RB#3, WR#5&6, and T#3 appear to be open to interpretation. Defensively, the picture is somewhat clearer. The battles don’t seem positional, so much, but rather those final 3-4 overall spots. Although special […]
full_text: Stetson Bennett and Jarquez Hunter are embroiled in position battles (Photo by David Eulitt/Getty Images) | Getty Images As the Los Angeles Rams enter Week 2 of the NFL preseason, there are still roster questions to be answered. On offense, QB#2, RB#3, WR#5&6, and T#3 appear to be open to interpretation. Defensively, the picture is somewhat clearer. The battles don’t seem positional, so much, but rather those final 3-4 overall spots. Although special teams could make the difference, it may boil down to who the Rams want to protect from final cut waiver claims, stashing them on the roster and using them as a weekly inactive. It’s hard to get a grip on what to expect from New Orleans, they use preseason games similarly to the Rams, sitting their major contributors. In a 20-24 Week 1 loss to the Jacksonville Jags, they sat 37 players. They also participated in two controlled scrimmages this week. Considering this, Rams fans should hope the L.A. braintrust doesn’t go down the buddy/buddy path and take their foot off the gas. Fans deserve more and the bottom half of the L.A. roster deserves the chance to work out depth. Here’s what I’ll be watching for in Week 2 of the preseason. Quarterback No matter who you want to see at QB#2 , it’s the same thing for both Stetson Bennett and Ty Simpson. Just keep stacking solid work. That may sound overly simplistic, but show control and command of the offense. That’s the job as a backup, manage the game in the starter’s stead. That said, most fans want the passing offense stretched out to see who can put the ball into tight windows and create downfield plays.. Running back Do we have a real, live roster battle for RB#3 and possibly #4? Or is it one of those preseason mirages? I didn’t think Jarquez Hunter played bad enough to lose any ground. He ran hard between the tackles and showed off his burst/speed, breaking a stuffed inside run out around the corner. Dean Conners was able to show off all facets of his game and is on the rise. Be nice to see him on kickoff returns. Jordan Waters played hard, but lost ground. Wide receiver Watching for a spirited four-man battle concerning the two likely remaining roster jobs in this year’s receiver room. Xavier Smith made a fair case for one slot last week and has the power of incumbency. Would the Rams consider rostering two “small” receivers? At the very least, Brennan Presley continues to show he can perform against preseason competition. His burst really stands out, as does his versatility. CJ Daniels and Tyler Scott close out the realistic competition, both need to show separation and run after catch skills to catch an eye. Too bad for Mario Williams, released with an injury settlement. Reports were that he had a strong camp and a couple of kickoff return touches against the Chiefs. Tru Edwards has to make something happen in limited opportunities. Alex Bachman is the camp body in for Williams. Ty Simpson zips it to Brennan Presley for a 23-yard pick up. LARvsKC on @NFLnetwork Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/NomnCI9rqT — NFL (@NFL) August 15, 2026 Tight end In today’s NFL, receiving tight ends get the most run. Sean McVay has consistently acquired theses types, preferring to coach up their blocking skills over time. Max Klare is the latest. Mark Redman showed very well in his action, but is clearly going back to the practice squad barring injuries. Investment in the growth of Klare and Redman is obviously at the expense of Dan Villari and Rohan Jones. The Rams ran so many three receiver sets in Week 1, there wasn’t much spare work. Would like to see them both get more action. How about this rep by Rams TE Mark Redman (#83)! pic.twitter.com/ARrUDOuDJW — JP Acosta (@acosta32_jp) August 16, 2026 Offensive line With Keagan Trost’s injury , a new set of questions need to be answered. For fans, it’s difficult to really put a finger on how long he will be out. “Weeks” is a fairly ambiguous term and with the opener a little over three weeks away, is it even possible to realistically expect Trost to be of service in Week 1? Time to put a spotlight on the Week 2 tackle play. Austin Blaske acquitted himself quite well vs, the Chiefs. By stacking another solid day’s work, in theory, he could work himself into position for a roster spot. I don’t think anyone would have predicted that when he was signed as a UDFA. An interior addition at that. To my eye, Blake Hance had rough outing last week. He’s been around quite awhile, eight teams in eight seasons. Just doesn’t inspire confidence. Bryce Henderson played the last two drives, both ending in scores, and deserves more this week. Where was AJ Arcuri? The interior seemed pretty solid against K.C., but there are lingering questions here as well. How soon will Justin Dedich return to action? Although Beaux Limmer should be locked in, it will be interesting to see if he gets some/any work at center. If not, Dylan McMahon could have a path as C#2. For the remaining linemen, barring any more injuries, the cupboard is pretty full and battling for a practice squad berth is their future. Special teams The good: Obviously the three L.A. specialists are of high caliber. I thought the double-teaming of opposing gunners was successful and welcome news for whoever returns punts. Although Xavier Smith has good long speed, he is not a twitchy runner, his return strength is vision and ability to make cuts at speed. He can make the first guy miss but needs a bit of space/runway to get into high gear. The bad: Kick coverage was still cringe-worthy. A fair number of “starting” special teamer’s aren’t out there for preseason, but after last year’s performance, it’s hard not have rattled nerves. As an aside, I would have liked to have seen the Rams send out Meevis to try a 60-yard field goal at the end of last week’s first half. Ty Simpson did well to get the team into that position and those kinds of conversions set up emotional carryover to the second half. Defensive interior Searching for consistency. DL#5 and #6 are not a major roles, maybe 10 snaps per game and mostly insurance against major injury. Still, it would nice to see one of the candidates step up and stake a claim, not be the best of the rest. No real movement from Week 1, Ty Hamilton still maintains at the top of the heap. He goes from powerfully controlling the line on one play to being pushed aside on others. Tim Keenan has the typical rookie ups and downs, having trouble holding his ground. You could argue that Bill Norton had the best Week 1, he doesn’t really offer the versatility to line up other than the nose, but is tough to move off his spot in the middle. Larrell Murchison fades back after a lackluster game. Payton Zdroik and Jaxson Moi are seeing plenty of reps, looking for incremental improvement. Edge There’s a need to see Desjuan Johnson and Keir Thomas to show more dominance against lesser competition. While Johnson is a likely lock at E#4, Thomas is standing on shaky ground. Although he may not be pressed by the lower rungs of the edge room, he’s in a battle with a half-dozen others for those last few roster spots. Tomon Fox missed last week’s game due to “family problems”, so fans will get to see what he has. Undrafted Darryl Peterson and Wesley Bailey got their feet wet with plenty of reps and both could find a place on the practice squad. Off-ball linebacker Hard to make a case for an LB#5 making the opening roster. I’m still rooting for Nikhai Hill-Green, he played every snap last week and called the defense on the field. He didn’t play bad, but he’s really going to have to show out on both defense and special teams. To a lesser extent, Daniel Rickert and Monty Rice are in the same boat. All three are prohibitive long shots to slip in at the very end of the roster. Safety There’s still a possible roster spot for S#5 to watch for. That battle appears to have boiled down to undrafteds, Nick Anderson and Nate Valcarcel. Although both are green, they are good tacklers…
