title: Treydan Stukes has much-needed strong performance in Las Vegas Raiders’ preseason game against Houston Texans
summary: Two-thirds of the Las Vegas Raiders’ preseason is over after the 22-20 win against the Houston Texans on Thursday night, which means training camp is winding down and the position battles are nearing an end. With that in mind, let’s dive into this week’s winners and losers. WINNER: Treydan Stukes A lot was made about […]
full_text: HOUSTON, TX - AUGUST 20: Wide receiver Daniel Sobkowicz #17 of the Houston Texans is hit hard by free safety Treydan Stukes #31 of the Las Vegas Raiders and linebacker Tommy Eichenberg #44 of the Las Vegas Raiders during the NFL preseason game between the Houston Texans and the Las Vegas Raiders on August 20, 2026, at Reliant Stadium in Houston, TX. (Photo by David Buono/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Two-thirds of the Las Vegas Raiders’ preseason is over after the 22-20 win against the Houston Texans on Thursday night, which means training camp is winding down and the position battles are nearing an end. With that in mind, let’s dive into this week’s winners and losers. WINNER: Treydan Stukes A lot was made about Stukes getting off to a slow start in training camp, and he was pretty quiet in the Raiders’ first preseason game, too. However, the second-round pick had a much-needed strong performance against the Texans. He only played in the first half and managed to record four tackles, with three of them being impactful stops. According to Pro Football Focus , Stukes only allowed 13 yards on three catches in coverage, and one of those was an eight-yard grab. Even the rep he lost, he was at least in a position to contest the catch. More importantly, the versatile defensive back was sharp at both the free safety and nickelback spots. The coaching staff has mentioned that they threw a lot at him to begin camp and that it seemed like everything was starting to click for him more recently, which showed up on Thursday night. LOSER: Malik Benson While Benson technically only had one drop, he also had a pass ripped out of his hands that should have been hauled in for a completion. To make matters worse, those two failed catch attempts came on third downs, and he hauled in just one of five targets on the evening. The sixth-rounder has put together a strong training camp to have a bigger role than expected in year one, but he likely ended any hopes of beating out Jack Bech for the third wide receiver spot on the depth chart. WINNER: Dylan Laube On the opposite end, there wasn’t much competition for the third running back role in Las Vegas, but the team was looking for someone to take command of the battle. Laube answered the call with a handful of impressive runs, toting the rock six times for 37 yards (6.2 ypc) and a touchdown, while adding a 14-yard catch to his stat line. That likely cemented his roster spot. LOSER: Kansei Matsuzawa There’s some hyperbole in this statement, but I think you’d be hard-pressed to find a kicker with a worse preseason than Matsuzawa in NFL history. He had a disastrous kickoff and missed a chip shot field goal last week, and then missed two PATs against the Texans. At this point, it’s safe to say Matt Gay won the kicker job, and one has to wonder if it’s even worth keeping the Tokoyo Toe on the practice squad as the IPP exemption. WINNER: Patrick Johnson I have no idea how Johnson is going to make the Raiders’ 53-man roster with how deep edge is, but the guy has done his job by forcing the coaching staff to make a tough decision. Per PFF , Las Vegas has 18 total pressures during the preseason, and he accounts for five or about 28 percent of them. The strip sack in Houston was icing on the cake, and the 28-year-old has been playing well against the run too, earning a 71.3 PFF run defense grade and recording three defensive stops as a run defender over the two games. Johnson could be a prime candidate to occupy one of the four veteran spots on Las Vegas’ practice squad, unless another team picks him up after camp. LOSER: Run Defense To the defense’s credit, they did buckle down once the Texans brought their backups into the game and only gave up 78 total rushing yards . However, Woody Marks averaged over nine yards per carry on the first drive, capping it off by breaking a few tackles for a 20-yard touchdown run. Sure, it was against the Raiders’ second-team defense, but many of the players on the field for that drive are expected to contribute this season. Also, this is the second week in a row that an opponent has had no issues running the ball right down the middle of the Silver and Black’s defense to begin the game. The unit is still looking for a defensive tackle to step up and be a run-stuffer, but their best option right now is Foley Fatukasi, who was signed earlier this week. Granted, if you’re looking for optimism, the positive spin is that Fatukasi looked good and had a strong showing against the run. WINNER: Aidan O’Connell At this point, O’Connell is auditioning for another team, and putting together a game-winning drive certainly helps his cause. He finished 15 of 24 for 166 yards and no interceptions while engineering three touchdown drives, and he was the Raiders’ best quarterback of the night. Whether that’s at the end of camp this year or during the offseason, that should be enough for AOC to get another opportunity elsewhere. To address the elephant in the room, Fernando Mendoza definitely had an off-night, ‘lowlighted’ by the pick-six. He also looked jittery and had a slow start during his first couple of drives. But there’s some shared blame/a miscomunication with Mike Washington Jr. on the interception, and I liked how he settled in to make a handful of quality throws and somewhat salvage the performance. Also, Benson’s issues made the No. 1 pick’s stat line look worse. In my opinion, that’s what keeps Mendoza from being a ‘loser’, but there’s no denying that he needs to play better moving forward. LOSER: Caleb Rogers With Jackson Powers-Johnson sidelined, Rogers had an opportunity to take command of the right guard competition. He didn’t play poorly in pass protection with just one pressure on 17 opportunities, per PFF , but a 46.9 run blocking grade against the Texans’ second-team defense isn’t going to get the job done. The second-year pro could still win the starting battle next week, but he certainly didn’t take advantage of the situation on Thursday night. WINNER: Hezekiah Masses After a tough NFL debut where the Cardinals completed every pass they threw at him, Masses had a bounce-back performance in Houston. He was targeted four times and only surrendered one catch for one yard, per PFF . That’s the type of game the fifth-round pick needed to justify the training camp hype. LOSER: Team Discipline Mistakes are expected in the preseason, but Klint Kubiak talked about how frustrating last week’s eight penalties for 75 yards were, and the team responded by getting flagged nine times for 83 yards . If the Raiders are going to pull off any upsets this season, they can’t beat themselves. Giving up over 150 free yards to the other team in two preseason games isn’t exactly encouraging in that department.

title: Raiders roster 2026: Tre Tucker, Jalen Nailor, and Hezekiah Masses are underrated
summary: The Las Vegas Raiders are no strangers to internal restructuring. Since the franchise moved from Oakland in time for the 2020 season, there have been six different head coaches, both intentionally hired and interim — Jon Gruden, Rich Bisaccia, Josh McDaniels, Antonio Pierce, Pete Carroll, and now, Klint Kubiak. Kubiak is coming off the high […]
full_text: LAS VEGAS, NEVADA - AUGUST 13: Jalen Nailor #9, Michael Mayer #87, and Tyler Linderbaum #65 of the Las Vegas Raiders in the first quarter of the preseason game at Allegiant Stadium on August 13, 2026 in Las Vegas, Nevada. (Photo by Ian Maule/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Las Vegas Raiders are no strangers to internal restructuring. Since the franchise moved from Oakland in time for the 2020 season, there have been six different head coaches, both intentionally hired and interim — Jon Gruden, Rich Bisaccia, Josh McDaniels, Antonio Pierce, Pete Carroll, and now, Klint Kubiak. Kubiak is coming off the high of winning Super Bowl LX as the Seattle Seahawks’ offensive coordinator, which is nice, but McDaniels has several Super Bowl rings as an OC with the New England Patriots, so… you never know how a guy is going to be as a head coach until he’s a head coach. “The main thing is, this is no ordinary job,” Kubiak said in his introductory presser on February 10. “This is the Silver and Black. This is the Raiders. This is a historic franchise. So, when the opportunity came up to stay in Seattle and continue there or to have a chance to come here and compete with this organization, it was a no brainer. I grew up, obviously, watching a lot of Broncos football (Kubiak’s father Gary was John Elway’s backup from 1983-1991, Denver’s offensive coordinator from 1995-2005, and the head coach in 2015-2016) , going against the Raiders twice a year, and the grit of this franchise sticks out. “When you hear ‘ The Autumn Wind is a Raider ,’ I can hear that in my mind growing up watching NFL Films, and seeing these guys next to me play. Seeing Howie Long and Jim Plunkett, it’s pretty powerful to be sitting up here with you guys, and I just want you to know that those values that you guys played with, that’s what we’re going to play with. It’s really important to me that we’re a gritty team the way that they were back in the old days. And how do we do that? Well, it’s our silent tape. It’s nothing that we say. It’s what we do on the field, and it’s what the silent tape speaks about our team, how physical we are, our effort, all the little things that win that have nothing to do with scheme. “So, really excited to get to work with your players, go turn your tape on, see what you guys are about right now, and then go see how we can get better together.” Well, the new guy appears to get it. Kubiak has what looks to be a future franchise quarterback in Fernando Mendoza, and a coaching staff that seems miles ahead of what Pete Carroll put together in 2025. Now, it’s about getting these Raiders past last season’s 3-14 embarrassment, and finding the right path forward. Grit and history are cool and all, but talent will win out. These Raiders need a new version of this: The Autumn Wind is a Raider, Pillaging just for fun. He’ll knock you ’round and upside down, And laugh when he’s conquered and won.” Guys who will growl as they storm the country. Villains big and bold. The trees should shake and quiver and quake, as these new Raiders rob opponents of their gold. To that end, I’ve identified three Hidden Gems for Kubiak’s 2026 team — one underrated veteran, one underrated free-agent signing, and one underrated draft pick. Underrated veteran: WR Tre Tucker Whatever it was that alleged offensive coordinators Chip Kelly and Greg Olson put on the field in 2025, it wasn’t exactly conducive to a high-energy passing game. So, it was all the more impressive that Tre Tucker, the 2023 third-round pick out of Cincinnati, had his best season to date in all that mess. Somehow, Tucker caught 57 passes on 90 targets for 696 yards and five touchdowns, and he did so in some unconventional ways for a player his size. You don’t expect 5’9”, 185-pound receivers to have the toughness and route acumen to excel on the outside, but Tucker took 505 of his 618 offensive snaps on the outside last season, and that’s where most of his explosive plays came from. Tre Tucker scorching dudes outside at 5'9", 185. Klint Kubiak has to be excited about this. pic.twitter.com/sPLZSTxuOI — Doug Farrar ✍ (@NFL_DougFarrar) August 18, 2026 “Really no surprise there from what you’ve seen previously,” Kubiak said of Tucker on May 20. “He can run all day. He’s a quiet leader, a guy that we’re going to put in a leadership role. He’s got to be a playmaker for us, and he has been. And now, let’s go see what else we can get out of him. “When you’ve got a guy who’s that size, and that competitive, and works that hard, there’s not a whole lot of humans on the planet who can put as many yards on the field at that high of a speed, so he’s been really impressive.” Last season, Tucker was running posts, overs, digs, and corner routes as you’d expect from a guy about four inches taller and 20 pounds heavier. Now, it’s about getting some targets around him, so it’s not just the Brock Bowers Show With Special Guest Tre Tucker. Which is where we go next. Underrated free agent: WR Jalen Nailor The Raiders didn’t take any receivers in the draft until Oregon’s Malik Benson heard his name called with the 195th pick in the sixth round, but they had already made an estimable (albeit underrated) move by signing former Minnesota Vikings receiver Jalen Nailor to a three-year, $35.03 million contract with $18 million guaranteed. The 2022 sixth-round pick out of Michigan State never became a featured part of the Vikings’ passing game, but his 2025 season was worth watching, and clearly, the Raiders were paying attention. Last season, Nailor caught just 29 passes on 49 targets for 444 yards and four touchdowns, but the ratio of big plays to catches should be a precursor to future possibilities — especially since J.J. McCarthy made every receiver on the roster (including and especially Justin Jefferson) struggle to match their usual productivity. Jalen Nailor in 2025: 29 catches, eight explosive plays. The @Raiders could certainly use some of this. pic.twitter.com/MIQ30bJW8G — Doug Farrar ✍ (@NFL_DougFarrar) July 14, 2026 The Raiders’ new mentor for Fernando Mendoza, who played with Nailor in Minnesota in 2022 and 2023, couldn’t be happier about the addition. “I’m really excited about Jalen, because I was with him in Minnesota, and I could see his ability,” Kirk Cousins said in April. “When you have Justin Jefferson and Adam Thielen, it’s hard to get the ball as a receiver, because you’re going to target Justin Jefferson and Adam Thielen, and yet, every time Jalen got opportunities, he showed what he could do. And I think that showed even more there once I left Minnesota. But I think to have him here, and now in a bigger role, I think that’s really exciting, because it allows the player to really fulfill his potential. “He knows that, I know that, and I’m excited to get on the grass with him, and routes on air and in team drills, and just start to build that rapport and really allow him to have a much bigger role moving forward, because I think he’s capable of carrying a bigger role.” We’ll see how Jack Bech, Dont’e Thornton Jr., and the rest of the Raiders’ receivers do behind Tucker as the main man, but there is certainly an open lane for Nailor to show what he can do. Underrated draft pick: CB Hezekiah Masses With Rob Leonard as the team’s new defensive coordinator, the Raiders made it clear in the draft that the secondary was about to get a lot of new faces in the draft. Arizona safety Treydan Stukes went in the second round, Tennessee cornerback Jermod McCoy went at the top of the fourth round (obviously, a healthy McCoy would have gone in the top of the first round, based on his 2024 tape ), and Dalton Johnson, another Arizona safety, went in the fifth round. Then, with the 175th overall pick in the fifth round, the Raiders took Cal cornerback Hezekiah Masses. And that, friends, could be a spicy meatball. Last season for Cal after three seasons at Florida International, the 6’1”, 185-pound Masses allowed 30 catches on 61 targets for 413…

New York took it to the Dolphins throughout the practice, repeatedly sacking quarterback Malik Willis and dominating all around throughout the day. Miami’s players got frustrated as the heat, humidity, and Giants pressure boiled over, including leading to right tackle Austin Jackson being removed from the workout after throwing a punch. It was not a great way to end public practices for Miami this year. The Miami Herald’s Omar Kelly wrote about the practice, and the skirmishes that seemed to break out as soon as the teams started their joint work, stating: Thursday’s session was the first time the Hafley-coached Dolphins lost their composure during training camp. But they seemingly didn’t back down from the Giants, unlike last year’s joint practice against the Chicago Bears, who were hitting the Dolphins in a practice that was supposed to only be thudding (wrapping up, but nobody gets taken to the ground). “We tried to hold our composure as much as we can, but when you are out there playing football things get chippy. summary: The Minnesota Vikings dominated all eight situational drills against the Baltimore Ravens in joint practices, and Dallas Turner is primed for a massive breakout. Vikings training camp, joint practices, preseason, Brian Flores defense, J.J. McCarthy — that define this episode of The Real Forno Show, where Tyler Forness and Dave Stefano broke down every takeaway […]
full_text: EAGAN, MINNESOTA - AUGUST 19: Dallas Turner #15 of the Minnesota Vikings and John Simpson #76 of the Baltimore Ravens participate in a drill during a joint practice between the Baltimore Ravens and Minnesota Vikings at Twin Cities Orthopedics Performance Center on August 19, 2026 in Eagan, Minnesota. (Photo by David Berding/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Minnesota Vikings dominated all eight situational drills against the Baltimore Ravens in joint practices, and Dallas Turner is primed for a massive breakout. Vikings training camp, joint practices, preseason, Brian Flores defense, J.J. McCarthy — that define this episode of The Real Forno Show, where Tyler Forness and Dave Stefano broke down every takeaway from two days of work in Eagan. If the Vikings’ defense is a “house,” as Forness described it, then the Ravens just walked through the wrong front door. Tyler Forness didn’t mince words about what he saw: “This defense is a house. It’s an incredible unit.” The Vikings won all eight situational drills across both days — four on offense, four on defense — sweeping the Ravens in two-minute scenarios. Both quarterbacks improved from a shaky day one, with J.J. McCarthy and Kyler Murray each leading scoring drives in the two-minute drill. But the story was the defense, starting with Dallas Turner, who Forness declared is “primed to break out in a huge way this year.” Turner’s fluid coverage drops, consistent pressure, and a viral rep where a guard’s block accidentally redirected him into a sack highlighted his versatility. Eric Wilson, meanwhile, may be the surprise of camp: “Eric Wilson just might be the best linebacker on the team,” Forness said, praising his blitzing, run defense, and coverage. Jay Ward made the strongest case yet that Harrison Smith’s return isn’t needed, with an interception and pass breakup. Rookie Charles Demmings drew a caution flag of a different kind — Forness noting he’s “way too physical” and could face regular-season penalty issues. Dave Stefano offered context: “I love his attitude,” but agreed the rookie must dial it in. Key Points from the Episode: Vikings swept all 8 situational drills against the Ravens across two joint practices Dallas Turner consistently generated pressure and dropped fluidly into coverage; Forness: “He looks really fluid dropping into coverage” Eric Wilson called “the best linebacker on the team” after a dominant practice showing Jay Ward had an interception and pass breakup, strengthening the case to start over a potential Harrison Smith return Charles Demmings flagged for overly physical play — “He is way too physical. That’s not gonna fly in the regular season” Da’Veawn Armstead, a UDFA corner from North Texas, is “showing that he belongs” with the twos Jacob Thomas, an undrafted safety, is making a real roster case: “It’s a non-zero proposition that Jacob Thomas could be a really impactful player” J.J. McCarthy rated a “six out of 10” but improved from day one; Kevin O’Connell confirmed McCarthy will start the preseason game Forness reframed KOC’s QB reputation: “I think KOC’s a quarterback elevator,” not a whisperer — yet Max Bredeson excitement tempered with realism: “If he plays more than 300 snaps, I’ll be a little bit surprised” Ravens WR Jacoby Lane (6th round, USC) was the most impressive Ravens player in practices Listen: Or on your favorite podcast aggregator. title: Patriots 2026 scouting report for ED Elijah Ponder
summary: The New England Patriots entered the 2025 NFL Draft facing significant questions at multiple positions, including the defensive edge. However, their investments were relatively minimal. In fact, their best contributions from a rookie edge last season came not from a draft pick but an undrafted free agent. Heading into his second season in the league, […]
full_text: DENVER, CO - JANUARY 25: Elijah Ponder #91 of the New England Patriots rushes the passer during the AFC Championship NFL football game against the Denver Broncos at Empower Field At Mile High on January 25, 2026 in Denver, Colorado. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images The New England Patriots entered the 2025 NFL Draft facing significant questions at multiple positions, including the defensive edge. However, their investments were relatively minimal. In fact, their best contributions from a rookie edge last season came not from a draft pick but an undrafted free agent. Heading into his second season in the league, Elijah Ponder now is looking ready to play an even more prominent role. Hard facts Name: Elijah Ponder Position: Defensive edge/Outside linebacker Jersey number: 91 Opening day age: 24 (8/24/2002) Measurements : 6’2 7/8”, 261 lbs, 10 1/8” hand size, 33 1/8” arm length, 80” wingspan, 4.63s 40-yard dash, 6.99s 3-cone drill, 4.28s short shuttle, 41” vertical jump, 11’0” broad jump, 22 bench press reps, 9.87 Relative Athletic Score Experience NFL: New England Patriots (2025-) | College: Cal Poly (2020-24) A multi-sport athlete at Bishop Amat High School in La Puente, CA, Ponder received some FCS interest as a two-star outside linebacker recruit. Ultimately, however, he decided to head for the FBS and joined Cal Poly. In five seasons with the Mustangs, he saw action in 47 games with 42 starts. He also registered 26.5 sacks and 43.5 tackles for loss, and was named All-Big Sky in all four of his non-redshirt campaigns (first team 2023, 2024; honorable mention 2021, 2022). Despite his college success, Ponder did not hear his name called in the 2025 NFL Draft. He joined the Patriots as an undrafted free agent afterwards and appeared in 19 games as a rookie with four sacks and three fumble recoveries. Scouting report Strengths: Checking in at 6-foot-3 and 261 pounds, Ponder offers good size on the defensive edge. He combines it with an intriguing athletic skillset; his explosivity, agility and speed are rare, and he looks the part on the field as well. He is quick to attack the pocket and has the burst to challenge blockers’ leverage and balance early into a rep, plays with active hands, and can properly bend the corner around the edge. He also has good spatial awareness, which in turn allows him to locate the football effectively even in traffic, and the range to be a factor in pursuit. Weaknesses: Ponder moves as well as any outside linebacker in football, but he fails to consistently look the part on the field. His game speed and timed speed do not always align, in parts because he is still a developing player from a technical and processing perspective. He also lacks ideal length and is not the most powerful player at the point of attack. He furthermore is a pass-first player whose contributions against the run have been limited so far. When he has been asked to play the run, he has failed to consistently set the edge and contain runs to the inside. 2025 review Stats : 19 games (0 starts) | 314 defensive snaps (24.5%), 287 special teams snaps (52.4%) | 17 tackles, 1 missed tackle (5.6%), 4 TFLs, 2 FRs | 24 QB pressures (4 sacks, 3 hits, 17 hurries) | 11 special teams tackles, 3 missed tackles (21.4%), 1 FR | 3 penalties (incl. 0 declined/offsetting) Season recap: Despite his small-school status, Ponder was invited to both the Hula Bowl and the East-West Shrine Bowl heading toward the draft. As noted above, however, he was not selected in any of the seven rounds and had to navigate the free agency waters before finding a home in the NFL. The journey, however, was a rather short one: he joined the Patriots as one of their first-wave UDFA signings. While that meant he started out buried on the depth chart, Ponder steadily climbed his way up the ranks. Strong showings in training camp and preseason ultimately allowed him to join wide receiver Efton Chism as the only two undrafted rookies to make New England’s initial 53-man roster. Even though he lacked pedigree, he remained there throughout the sesaon. Early on, Ponder was mostly a special teamer. Even as his defensive role evolved, he kept seeing regular action as a four-unit contributor in the kicking game to eventually finish sixth among his teammates in snaps and third in tackles. On defense, meanwhile, he saw a handful of snaps over the first half of the season. However, with starting edge Harold Landry starting to deal with nagging injury woes, he managed to grow his role: from Week 12 on, when Landry’s issues started impacting his availability, Ponder was on the field for roughly 36.8% of snaps. Those snaps came predominately in the passing game, with early-down duties falling on fellow edge Anfernee Jennings. In that relatively specialized role, Ponder delivered some good performances. In fact, his affinity for finding the football and recovering fumbles — his three FRs were tied for the team lead in 2025 — turned out crucial: he helped set up the only touchdown of the Patriots’ AFC Championship win in Denver (and in fact would have scored himself on the play if not for a bad call by the officials). BALL WAS OUT – GOING THE OTHER WAY‼️ 📺 CBS pic.twitter.com/swmdTx0TYV — New England Patriots (@Patriots) January 25, 2026 All in all, Ponder had a very good first season in the NFL. It may not have started as he had hoped by not hearing his name called in the draft, but his effort and playmaking abilities earned him his way onto the Patriots’ roster. Once there, he showed that he belonged. 2026 preview Position: Outside linebacker | Ability: Depth player/Role player | Contract: Signed through 2027 (2028 RFA) What will be his role? Ponder has worked as an outside linebacker throughout training camp so far, and in fact has been a regular as the starter opposite Dre’Mont Jones. While Harold Landry’s eventual return from the physically unable to perform list will shake things up, Ponder currently projects as a rotational third or fourth option at the position as well as a key special teamer. What is his growth potential? From an athletic perspective, Ponder’s ceiling is sky-high. There are, however, questions about how far he can actually still climb and whether he can become more than a depth piece. If he can clean up his own personal operation, there is no reason to believe that he can’t be a serviceable third or fourth member in an edge room. Does he have positional versatility? Defensively, Ponder’s versatility is somewhat limited; he is mostly a pass rusher at this point in his development. However, the game’s third phase is a different story. On special teams, he played at least 45 snaps on each of the core four units (kickoff return, kickoff coverage, punt return, punt coverage) and there is no reason to believe he can’t play a similar role in 2026. What is his salary cap situation? Arriving via a standard three-year UDFA deal last offseason, Ponder is carrying a $1.01 million cap number into the coming season. That number consists almost entirely of his $1.005 million base salary as well as a $5,000 signing bonus proration. That bonus is the only part of the deal guaranteed, which means that it also is currently his only trace in New England’s books under the NFL’s Top 51 role. How safe is his roster spot? Heading into the second preseason game, anything but Ponder making the 53-man roster would be a surprise. He has been the top option to replace Harold Landry in the lineup, after all, and has had some positive moments throughout training camp. Add his special teams role and he should be expected on the active team come the fall. Summary: Ponder is one of those players who won’t be able to make the game-changing plays or demand special attention on a weekly basis. That said, he is still immensely valuable to the operation but defensively and in the kicking game. What do you think about Elijah Ponder heading into the 2026 season? Will he increase his role? Or will he cede…

title: The Patriots have found their commander in the secondary
summary: Had it not been for Drake Maye and A.J. Brown, the biggest story coming out of their first joint practice with the Philadelphia Eagles on Wednesday would have been the New England Patriots’ ability to create turnovers on defense. No player was better in that regard than Craig Woodson. The second-year safety ended the session […]
full_text: Jul 25, 2026; Foxborough, MA, USA; New England Patriots safety Craig Woodson (4) walks to the practice field at training camp at Gillette Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Eric Canha-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Had it not been for Drake Maye and A.J. Brown, the biggest story coming out of their first joint practice with the Philadelphia Eagles on Wednesday would have been the New England Patriots’ ability to create turnovers on defense. No player was better in that regard than Craig Woodson. The second-year safety ended the session with two interceptions of Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts; he also added a sack to his big-play production. While he was quiet on Thursday’s before eventually departing for unknown reasons — allowing cornerback Marcus Jones to steal the show that day — Woodson can feel good looking back at the joint practices with Philadelphia. In fact, he can feel good about his entire summer so far if you ask his teammates. “He’s been having a phenomenal camp, in my opinion. Two takeaways [Wednesday], can’t get any better than that,” said fellow safety Kevin Byard. His development coming off an already promising rookie season has allowed Woodson to solidify himself as a stater in the Patriots secondary, and more. According to Jones, the 25-year-old has become a “commander” in the team’s defensive backfield and somebody the entire group is gravitating toward. “He’s a commander back there in the backend. We listen to him and we trust him,” Jones said on Thursday. “When he came in last year, he was a rookie, but when it comes to the calls, knowing what to do and everything. And now, you can definitely tell that he feels way more comfortable being in the same scheme. … You can definitely tell the comfortability. When it comes down to it, you know what to do, you can run fast and make plays, and that’s what he’s been doing.” Woodson arrived in Foxborough as the 106th overall selection in the fourth round of the 2025 NFL Draft. Despite joining a room headed by veterans Kyle Dugger, Jabrill Peppers and Jaylinn Hawkins, he managed to quickly climb the depth chart and toward the end of summer secure a starting spot. He went on to start 19 of 21 games during his rookie season, leading New England’s defense with a playing time share of 93.7% and effectively rendering both Dugger and Peppers expendable. Now in Year 2, he is locked into a starting role at safety. Outside of his own natural development, the biggest change is that Kevin Byard is now his running mate instead of Hawkins. The All-Pro has also been impressed by Woodson in their first camp together. “He’s a very mature guy. He’s 25, so he’s not a young 21-year-old second-year player. He’s very mature,” Byard said. “He obviously played in this defense all last year, started every single game. So, it’s not like this is his first time learning everything. We’ve been helping out each other, honestly; me just bringing my experience and things I’ve seen around the league, but also as far as this defense it’s good for me to have him because this isn’t the same defense that I was in in Tennessee. We’ve been helping each other a lot and it’s been fun just getting our chemistry together.” Woodson’s maturity and playmaking ability are also not lost to players at other positions, such as linebacker K.J. Britt or the aforementioned Marcus Jones. “Craig is a baller, man,” the free agency signing said. “You don’t see too many Year 2 players act like a 10-year vet. How poised he is, the game is not too big for him. He just plays his game and he’s comfortable in the scheme. Knows what to do. He’s very smart. He’s just a very good player.” He showed that against the Eagles, and the Patriots are optimistic he will also do so once the regular season begins. And, if so, the team might indeed have found a player worthy of being described as the secondary’s “commander” for years to come.
author: Bernd Buchmasser

title: Aggressive Patriots defense stacking interceptions in Eagles joint practices
summary: On Thursday, the commencement of the New England Patriots’ joint practice marked the end of a two-day session with the Philadelphia Eagles, where New England’s defense secured seven interceptions across both workouts. With only one turnover through the first six practices of training camp, veteran safety Kevin Byard challenged the safeties to secure more takeaways, […]
full_text: FOXBOROUGH, MASSACHUSETTS - AUGUST 20: Marcus Jones #25 of the New England Patriots runs during a joint practice with the Philadelphia Eagles at Gillette Stadium on August 20, 2026 in Foxborough, Massachusetts. (Photo by Billie Weiss/Getty Images) | Getty Images On Thursday, the commencement of the New England Patriots’ joint practice marked the end of a two-day session with the Philadelphia Eagles, where New England’s defense secured seven interceptions across both workouts. With only one turnover through the first six practices of training camp, veteran safety Kevin Byard challenged the safeties to secure more takeaways, Dell Pettus shared earlier this summer. Just hours later, Pettus came away with the defense’s second interception of the summer. But now, the cornerbacks are getting involved. Nickel cornerback Marcus Jones secured three turnovers throughout the joint sessions, with two on Thursday. “I feel like we’re always trying to get turnovers,” Jones said after Thursday’s practice. “I’m a hard critic of the [defensive back] room, so I feel like there’s always room for improvement, for sure.“ During the 11-on-11 period, Philadelphia quarterback Jalen Hurts targeted wide receiver Dontayvion Wicks toward the sideline, but Jones leapt in front to jump the route, getting his feet down before falling out of bounds. “I was in front of [Wicks]. [He’s a] great route-runner and everything like that. I kind of felt the pressure of him trying to get back to the sideline and everything, and I made sure to drive toward him a little bit,” Jones said. “And then next, I was like, ‘When the ball is in the air, you have to make a play.’” The Houston product’s first pick of the day also came against Hurts, plucking a pass out of the air that hit the hands of the opposing running back. He also jumped another Hurts sideline throw on Wednesday in seven-on-seven drills, returning the turnover for a hypothetical pick-six. A common session in both practices was a series of two- and one-minute drills under pressure. Cornerback Kindle Vildor prematurely ended a Tanner McKee two-minute drive on Wednesday, intercepting a sideline pass intended for a comeback route. “I feel like every time we get on the field, we’re trying to be aggressive,” Jones added. “[The] only way you can make turnovers is by being aggressive and violent, which we always talk about. And then always make the plays that you need to make.” Competition has been a common theme for improvement this offseason with this Patriots roster, a culture instilled by head coach Mike Vrabel. Jones described the team as competitive, and because they know the Eagles carry themselves the same way, their “big thing” is bringing energy to the turf. Additionally, that same on-field intensity is channeled toward the group’s goal for 2026 to become the No.1 scoring defense in the NFL. “Oh, man, [confidence] is at an all-time high,” Jones continued. “We know when it comes down to it, we want to be the number one scoring defense. And when it comes down to that, you know, it’s everyone on the back end making plays. So us as [defensive backs], we understand that. And whenever we do make turnovers, man, as you can tell, we’re trying to score with the ball. We don’t get too many opportunities like that, so we have to take advantage of it.” Following the seven-interception performance, Jones believes it heavily impacts the unit’s confidence approaching 2026. He explained that as a defensive back, you need to have the confidence to know when to break on the ball and how to go get it. They’ll have another chance on Saturday to continue generating turnovers in New England’s preseason game against Philadelphia at Gillette Stadium at 7 p.m. ET.

title: Contract details for Patriots free agency signing Greg Van Roten
summary: After losing both Ben Brown and Andrew Rupcich to injury in their preseason opener against the Indianapolis Colts, the New England Patriots explored the free agency market to further bolster their depth along the interior offensive line. They ended up signing three players in the days after the game. But while Darrian Dalcourt and Joseph […]
full_text: Greg Van Roten, a guard with the NY Giants, speaks to the press after a practice at Quest Diagnostics Training Center, East Rutherford, NJ, May 28, 2025. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co After losing both Ben Brown and Andrew Rupcich to injury in their preseason opener against the Indianapolis Colts, the New England Patriots explored the free agency market to further bolster their depth along the interior offensive line. They ended up signing three players in the days after the game. But while Darrian Dalcourt and Joseph Michalski were low-cost investments, the team decided to spend quite a bit of money to bring in Greg Van Roten . What this shows is that the 36-year-old appears to be in the team’s plans for 2026. OL Greg Van Roten: Contract details Base value: $3,000,000 Maximum value: $4,500,000 Guarantees: $1,000,000 Base salary: $500,000 Signing bonus: $500,000 2026 (age 36): Base salary: $1,480,000 Signing bonus: $500,000 Roster bonus: $1,020,000 Incentives (LTBE): $1,500,000 Salary cap hit: $4,500,000 Van Roten had remained unsigned since his prior contract with the Giants expired in January. He nonetheless ended up receiving a deal from the Patriots that clearly is above the $1.3 million that would have been the veteran minimum for a player of his experience. Besides getting a partially-guaranteed $1.48 million salary, the team also added a $500,000 signing bonus as well as $2.52 million dependent on availability and performance. He has $1.02 million in roster bonuses on the line as well as up to $1.5 million in playing time incentives, both of which considered likely to be earned and therefore part of New England’s salary cap calculations. At $4.5 million, his cap number is only slightly below that of starting left guard Alijah Vera-Tucker ($4.78M), one of the players Van Roten will be backing up this year. And what the relatively high guarantees in particular show is that the Patriots very well might be counting on that. Even though Ben Brown is a strong candidate to resume his spot as the top interior backup once he returns from his injury, Van Roten looks like the frontrunner to fill that role until then. This also means he might just sneak his way onto the 53-man roster despite only joining the team in mid-August.

title: Defensive head-to-head preview: Rams vs. Saints
summary: Heading into the second preseason game, the Saints will face off against the Rams, who featured a very good defense last season. They took that good defense and then went out and made it even better. They sent young star edge rusher Jared Verse, along with three first-round picks, for Myles Garrett, and they are […]
full_text: NEW ORLEANS, LOUISIANA - AUGUST 17: Jaylan Ford #53 of the New Orleans Saints celebrates with teammates after a interception against the Jacksonville Jaguars during the second half of a preseason game at the Caesars Superdome on August 17, 2025 in New Orleans, Louisiana. (Photo by Derick E. Hingle/Getty Images) | Getty Images Heading into the second preseason game, the Saints will face off against the Rams, who featured a very good defense last season. They took that good defense and then went out and made it even better. They sent young star edge rusher Jared Verse, along with three first-round picks, for Myles Garrett, and they are still currently flirting with the possibility of getting Aaron Donald out of retirement. The Rams finished last season ranked 17th in total defense. The Saints finished ninth. Since this is a preseason game, several starters are not expected to make an appearance. But last week against the Chiefs, the Rams’ defense held Kansas City without a touchdown, forcing four field goals to serve as the Chiefs’ only points of the game. They also allowed 314 total yards, with 189 coming through the air and 125 on the ground. They were also able to record two sacks. Considering who the starters will be for the defensive unit, getting a consistent pass rush throughout the roster shows just how talented this defense can be because of the depth of the entire unit. The Saints, on the other hand, had a better overall performance statistically but gave up touchdowns instead of field goals. The Saints’ defense allowed only 275 total yards last week against the Jaguars, with 157 yards through the air and 118 yards on the ground. However, they gave up two touchdowns. Had those been field goals, the Saints would have been able to walk out of the Caesars Superdome as winners. The Saints’ defense was also able to force two turnovers and record four sacks. The defense literally checked every box. If they are able to improve on the 2-for-5 red-zone number just a little more, the defense could be the unit that leads the team through the final two games of the preseason. This will be a very intriguing matchup to watch as these defenses go after the preseason offensive units they will face on Saturday. Who do you think will have the better defense on Saturday? Share your thoughts in the comments.

title: Key matchups: Saints vs. Rams
summary: The New Orleans Saints are traveling to California to take on the Los Angeles Rams. New Orleans had a busy week, participating in two joint practices, making starters unlikely to appear in the team’s second preseason matchup. Despite a lack of starters, there are still plenty of matchups to keep an eye on for Saturday. […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - SEPTEMBER 28: Kendre Miller #5 of the New Orleans Saints celebrates after scoring a touchdown during the first quarter of the NFL 2025 game against the Buffalo Bills at Highmark Stadium on September 28, 2025 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Lauren Leigh Bacho/Getty Images) | Getty Images The New Orleans Saints are traveling to California to take on the Los Angeles Rams. New Orleans had a busy week, participating in two joint practices, making starters unlikely to appear in the team’s second preseason matchup. Despite a lack of starters, there are still plenty of matchups to keep an eye on for Saturday. Saints run game vs. Rams run defense One of my biggest keys to the game is getting the run game going. While an obvious feature of a good offense, it will be a bit more important for the Saints as they look for a potential RB2 while Alvin Kamara is out with an injury. The two feature backs for Saturday will be Kendre Miller and Devin Neal, each former draftees who have promising upsides. Both Neal and Miller also missed significant time last season with injuries. The two young running backs won’t have it easy, however. They’ll be facing one of the better run defenses in the NFL that features plenty of talent. While I doubt Myles Garrett makes an appearance, other stars such as defensive tackle Braden Fiske have found early success in the league and could be a problem for the two young backs. Despite a tough matchup, Los Angeles allowed 125 rushing yards on 4.5 yards per carry in their preseason opener to the Kansas City Chiefs. While the Saints were on the opposite end of the spectrum, rushing for just 56 yards on 13 attempts. If New Orleans wants to sneak out with a win on Saturday, it would likely come from a strong game from either of their young running backs. Saints wide receivers vs. Rams secondary The Saints wide receivers make consecutive appearances in key matchups, this time against the Rams’ rebuilt secondary. With news that Jordyn Tyson will be out for at least the first month of the regular season, an opening for WR3 has become more pivotal. New Orleans has plenty of prospects hoping to earn that role when the regular season starts. Bub Means and Barion Brown each had strong showings in the team’s first matchup with the Jacksonville Jaguars, and Bryce Lance has continued to make plays throughout training camp and joint practices. While we might not see Trent McDuffie for the Rams, we still may see their other big-money corner in Jaylen Watson and the surging Emmanuel Forbes Jr, who has revived his career a bit with Los Angeles. Facing a strong cornerback room, it will be important to see which wideouts stand out the most. DE Michael Heldman and DE Garrett Nelson vs. Rams quarterbacks While this could’ve been the Saints pass rush vs the Rams pass protection, I really wanted to highlight Michael Heldman and Garrett Nelson, each of whom had outstanding games against the Jaguars. Heldman ended the day with 2 sacks and 3 tackles for loss, while Nelson had a strong game, logging a sack and tackle for loss himself. Heldman and Nelson were an unstoppable pass rush duo in the team’s preseason opener and look to continue that success as they work towards making the final 53-man roster. It won’t be easy, however, as the Rams didn’t allow a single sack in their last preseason matchup. While the offensive line certainly did their jobs, it was quarterback Ty Simpson who made quick and decisive decisions, making it impossible for the pass rush to reach him. Heldman and Nelson need to follow up their big games with another strong outing, and will have the chance to do it against a young quarterback.

title: Our offense vs. their defense: Los Angeles Rams
summary: The New Orleans Saints are set to play the Los Angeles Rams this Saturday in a week two preseason contest. The Rams are coming off of a 20-12 win over the Kansas City Chiefs while New Orleans suffered a 24-20 defeat to the Jaguars in dramatic fashion. Offensively, the Saints managed to put up 221 […]
full_text: The New Orleans Saints are set to play the Los Angeles Rams this Saturday in a week two preseason contest. The Rams are coming off of a 20-12 win over the Kansas City Chiefs while New Orleans suffered a 24-20 defeat to the Jaguars in dramatic fashion. Offensively, the Saints managed to put up 221 yards through the air which ranked 10th in the NFL over last week’s schedule. Meanwhile, the Chiefs put up 189 against the Rams’ defense. On the ground, New Orleans unfortunately could not muster any sort of momentum finishing with just 56 rushing yards against the Jags. That number put them dead last in the league. Los Angeles gave up 125 ground yards to Kansas City last weekend. New Orleans and Los Angeles recently held a joint practice with one another ahead of Saturday’s preseason matchup. During the workout period, both teams’ expected starters received majority of the action leaving the expectation that the backups and reserves will once again get increased opportunities in the actual game this weekend. With a second preseason game upon us and we continue to inch towards the start of the 2026 regular season, teams will really begin to dial in their final roster moves ahead of the new 53-man cut deadline which is scheduled for Sunday, August 30 this year.
author: Jason Watson Jr

title: Interview with the Enemy: Los Angeles Rams
summary: The New Orleans Saints will head to Inglewood to face the Los Angeles Rams at SoFi Stadium in Week 2 of the 2026 NFL preseason. To break it down, Evan Craig of Turf Show Times joins us to preview this weekend’s matchup. NJ: With Ty Simpson’s strong debut in the books, what stood out most about his performance, […]
full_text: NEW ORLEANS, LOUISIANA - AUGUST 17: Tyler Shough #6 of the New Orleans Saints is sacked by Travon Walker #44 of the Jacksonville Jaguars during the first quarter of the NFL Preseason 2025 at Caesars Superdome on August 17, 2025 in New Orleans, Louisiana. (Photo by Sean Gardner/Getty Images) | Getty Images The New Orleans Saints will head to Inglewood to face the Los Angeles Rams at SoFi Stadium in Week 2 of the 2026 NFL preseason. To break it down, Evan Craig of Turf Show Times joins us to preview this weekend’s matchup. NJ: With Ty Simpson’s strong debut in the books, what stood out most about his performance, and what are you hoping to see from him against the Saints? EC: Ty Simpson had quite a special debut, even if he was mainly going against third- and fourth-stringers. He was incredibly efficient, with only four incompletions and a pair of touchdown passes against the Chiefs. Simpson demonstrated quite a bit of poise and command of the offense, more so than many fans had expected to see from him. It was everything you could’ve wanted in a rookie quarterback’s debut. Ahead of the game, I mentioned that Simpson might be under pressure, considering that fellow high-profile QBs from this year’s draft class like Fernando Mendoza, Carson Beck and Drew Allar had been performing well so far this preseason. We’ll definitely have to see more from him, but it was a heck of a way for him to kick things off. All I’m hoping to see from Simpson is whether he can build on his debut. He doesn’t have to play as well as he did in KC, but it would be nice to see him maintain a level of consistency, even if the games are ultimately meaningless. Also, not that you ever want to see your quarterback make mistakes, yet I’m curious to see how he bounces back from mistakes or a tough series of plays. That will give fans a better understanding of his mental makeup, especially when looking ahead to whenever he takes over for Matthew Stafford long-term. NJ: Which Rams position battle or group of players has the most to gain from the additional preseason reps against New Orleans? EC: Wide receiver is one of the most glaring question marks on the roster, given it’s very top-heavy. The Rams have a clear hole at the WR3 spot behind Puka Nacua and Davante Adams, so many of the younger players on the roster have as good a chance as any to join them on the field this season. It was a good sign when Brennan Presley led LA with 58 receiving yards on four receptions, including a 23-yard catch in the first quarter against the Chiefs. Jordan Whittington and rookie CJ Daniels are two other options at the No. 3 position. The Rams don’t have a shortage of talent at that spot; there’s just a shortage of experience there, combined with too many mouths to feed, which has forced LA to lessen its emphasis on addressing wideout compared to other positions on the offense. NJ: What are you hoping to learn about the Rams from Saturday’s matchup against the Saints, and what did you learn from training camp and the preseason opener that you’d like to see the team build on? EC: From the preseason opener at least, we learned that the Rams have a quality defense from top to bottom. Myles Garrett (and potentially Aaron Donald) shouldn’t be the only headlines the defense grabs ahead of the season. Even if the Rams and Chiefs were engaged in a backup battle, Los Angeles managed to hold Kansas City without a touchdown. Additionally, they held KC’s three quarterbacks under 200 passing yards. Defensive issues have contributed to the Rams falling short in the playoffs each of the last two years. They need all the depth they can get, and Saturday proved they’ve got enough, which will be needed if their season goes as long as they hope. Also, the opener showed Rams fans that the team has plenty of young talent to work with. Rookie tight end Max Klare is an excellent example of that, as the Ohio State product led the team in receptions and demonstrated that he can be a quality pass catching option in an already crowded TE room. General manager Les Snead has done such a phenomenal job in stocking the roster with a promising array of youngsters. NJ: Who is one Rams player you think Saints fans should keep an eye on Saturday—someone who may not be receiving much national attention but could make a strong impression? EC: Keep an eye on undrafted running back Dean Connors, who caught both of Simpson’s two touchdown passes and added 22 yards on the ground Saturday. He is vying for a spot in a crowded Rams running back room, and will certainly be a difficult player to keep off the roster when final cutdowns happen. Expect to see him in the backfield a lot this weekend. NJ: According to FanDuel Sportsbook , the Saints (-132) are currently 1.5-point favorites over the Rams (+112) in Sunday’s matchup; what is your final score prediction? EC: I expect this to be a pretty competitive game throughout. Simpson should receive many of the reps at quarterback in this one. This one will be defined by whether the Saints’ depth can outlast the Rams’ and I think they have a good chance to do so. I’m expecting Simpson to still play well, but he’ll have one or two hiccups that power New Orleans to a close win. Saints 23. Rams 22. Thank you again to Evan Craig for joining us to preview this week’s matchup! You can check out the rest of his work here .

title: Fantasy Football 2026: Green Light! Players I’m targeting in my drafts
summary: The NFL season starts in less than three weeks, and the big wave of drafts in redraft leagues is upon us. What a time to be alive! Two of my favorite columns to write each season are this one, and its sister, Red Light: Players to Avoid (coming next).  Here’s a link to where you […]
full_text: Still the ONE | Getty Images The NFL season starts in less than three weeks, and the big wave of drafts in redraft leagues is upon us. What a time to be alive! Two of my favorite columns to write each season are this one, and its sister, Red Light: Players to Avoid (coming next). Here’s a link to where you can find my other preseason fantasy football content here at Big Blue View, including my July rankings, sleepers, a Giants fantasy preview and much more: Fantasy Football Hub. This column lists some of the players I’m most interested in targeting. I’m looking to take these guys at or around their current Average Draft Position (ADP), or even a little earlier. You’ll notice that my rankings on almost every player listed in this column are either equal to or ahead of market. That’s the idea. This isn’t a breakouts or sleepers column, but rather a list of players who I think offer solid value at current pricing. If a player isn’t listed, that doesn’t mean I’m out on him. I can’t list everyone. I’m not going to discuss first-rounders. I’m mainly focusing on players going AFTER the first 15 or so picks, but still inside the first 130. Rounds 2-10 of a draft are critical, as that’s where you’ll build the foundation of your starting lineup and top reserves. These rounds are all about finding good values and upside, while avoiding landmines. After Round 10 or 11, you’re getting deeper into your bench, and sleeper territory. For those who play in auction leagues, (a) bravo, and (b) I’m interested in the same players, if I can get them at a fair price. Make sure to see my Sleepers column for players I like who are ranked outside the Top-130 ADPs listed are as of August 21, 2026, are a consensus of several sites, and are for Half PPR scoring. Rankings reflect Half PPR scoring, on a points per game basis, with Week 18 excluded. ADPs are a little all over the place right now – your mileage may vary. GREEN LIGHT PLAYERS, 2026: Quarterback Jayden Daniels (ADP 64, my rank 58) and Jalen Hurts (ADP 70, my rank 60). QB is insanely deep this year, and in one-QB leagues, there’s really no reason to take one early. You’re passing up on too much value elsewhere. But several rounds after Josh Allen and Lamar Jackson are long gone, if I can get one of the two remaining elite dual-threats in Round 6, I’m certainly thinking about it. The opportunity cost is manageable at that juncture, considering the QB points you could be getting on a weekly basis. I like the addition of Stefon Diggs for Daniels, who was the QB4 in his rookie season (22.5 FPPG) before injuries derailed his 2025 campaign. Washington’s defense is still bad and Daniels and the offense are going to need to keep pace. Hurts gets a lot of criticism as a thrower and that helps to make him underrated for fantasy. Bottom line: He hasn’t finished outside the Top-8 QBs in any of the last five seasons, and while the rushing TDs dipped last year to just eight, he’s still a good bet for double digit scores with the tush push in play. I’m not overly worried about the departure of A.J. Brown. Hurts is cash money for fantasy, and he hasn’t been this cheap in years. Others: QB is so deep with quality this season, you can absolutely wait and then take one or two guys in the QB12-22 range and you’ll probably do just fine at the position. Streaming options will abound. In Superflex leagues, very good second QBs should be fairly easy to nab. I like any of high-upside Justin Herbert (ADP 88, my rank 82), Trevor Lawrence (ADP 89, my rank 83), Dak Prescott (ADP 91, my rank 85) , and Jaxson Dart (ADP 92, my rank 93) in the Round 8-9 range, or if you want to wait even further while you continue to load up at other positions, Brock Purdy , Bo Nix , and Jared Goff (ADP range 113-125) are great choices in Round 10-11 (or later if they fall further). Goff in particular is a terrific value at his ADP (125), if you want to wait until the final QB1s are being taken. He doesn’t run and isn’t an exciting pick. When you take him, your leaguemates will barely notice. But he’s been a very consistent (and healthy) low-end QB1 for fantasy since his arrival in Detroit. On top of that, the Lions have one of the league’s easiest schedules, their defense is perennially banged up and undermanned, and new OC Drew Petzing is a nice upgrade. Running Back I had some solid extra-base hits with my green light RBs last season, including Travis Etienne, Jr., Chase Brown, and D’Andre Swift. Here are some green lighters for 2026: Kenneth Walker III (ADP 18, my rank 15) and Derrick Henry (ADP 19, my rank 11) are big name players who are in play for me starting around the 1-2 turn and certainly early in Round 2. Walker has a great opportunity to finally secure a workhorse role in Kansas City, with a QB in Patrick Mahomes who is coming off a torn ACL and figures to scramble less and dump it off more. Walker has never gotten much credit as a pass-catcher and I think he’ll outproduce expectations in that area. The key with him is health. In two seasons in Baltimore, Henry has done nothing to make anyone think he’s slowing down. He’s averaged 5.9 and 5.2 yards per carry in his two seasons with the Ravens. Fine, he doesn’t catch passes. So what? When you top 3,700 rushing yards with 32 rushing TDs across two seasons, you’re fantasy gold. At his Round 2 cost, he’s a great choice as your RB1, or second stud RB in a back-heavy build. Father Time can keep waiting. King Henry owns him. Chase Brown (ADP 15, my rank 16). No notes. Rinse and repeat for a back who does everything well and has minimal competition in a potent offense. Omarion Hampton (ADP 16, my rank 18) is a player I like a lot this year too, in a Mike McDaniel offense and with his size and skillset. He’s going to visit the end zone quite a bit. But the bandwagon is full, the ADP is very high, and I don’t think I’ll get much of him given that I’m a little behind consensus, and have Waker, Henry, and Brown ahead of him. In late Round 3, I’m in on Javonte Williams (ADP 31, my rank 27). He’s expensive for a player who was a late bloomer. But I like the situation, with an excellent offense and not that much competition for high-leverage touches. Let’s also run back Travis Etienne, Jr. (ADP 41, my rank 38). He’s in a great situation to produce in Kellen Moore’s fast-paced offense, and I’m not worried about Alvin Kamara (who is already banged up) siphoning off the high value touches. They paid Etienne a lot to go there and Kamara’s excellent career is at or near its end. Further down, I’m green lighting David Montgomery (ADP 48, my rank 44), D’Andre Swift (ADP 50, my rank 45), Rhamondre Stevenson (ADP 74, my rank 66), Jonathon Brooks (ADP 88, my rank 80), and Jordan Mason (ADP 100, my rank 91). All are attractively priced RB2s/Flexes, in my view. Montgomery should be the workhorse on a team with a stellar defense and limited receiving weapons. Their O-line isn’t great, but the opportunity is. Just look at what Joe Mixon did in this offense two seasons ago. The Bears figure to get into plenty of shootouts and Swift is positioned to repeat what he did last season. Stevenson isn’t going away, and is criminally underpriced. Brooks is a flier given that he’s never been healthy, but the price is attractive for someone who might get lots of work and showed a ton of talent in college. Chuba Hubbard is already banged up. Mason is very cheap for a player who has a good chance to be the top RB in what should be an improved offense. Wide Receiver The injury bug strikes again. Damn. Three receivers who I planned on highlighting in this column have gotten hurt in the preseason ( Emeka Egbuka , Jordyn Tyson , and Jayden Higgins ). Higgins is done for the year (ACL), unfortunately. I’ll reevaluate the other two as we get closer to the season, but if they’re good to go Week 1, they’re likely still going to be green light plays for me, at cost. I think a lot of receivers in the first 4-5 rounds are pretty fairly priced. Here are…

title: Do Jake Kubas, Evan Neal have a chance with NY Giants? Let’s look at the film
summary: The New York Giants shook up their offensive line depth chart when they traded guard Daniel Faalele to the Jacksonville Jaguars after their preseason opener against the Minnesota Vikings. It had been widely believed that Faalele was set to be one of the Giants’ primary interior depth pieces considering his familiarity with both John Harbaugh […]
full_text: ﻿New York Giants guard Evan Neal against the Minnesota Vikings. | Getty Images The New York Giants shook up their offensive line depth chart when they traded guard Daniel Faalele to the Jacksonville Jaguars after their preseason opener against the Minnesota Vikings. It had been widely believed that Faalele was set to be one of the Giants’ primary interior depth pieces considering his familiarity with both John Harbaugh and Greg Roman. Suddenly, however, that piece is elsewhere and there’s a void on the Giants’ depth chart. That, in turn, creates an opportunity for young interior linemen to step up and potentially put themselves in position to be a primary backup and perhaps establish themselves in the teams’ long-term plans on the offensive interior. But how good is the Giants’ young depth at guard? The fact that they traded Faalele is encouraging, but it’s always best to go to the tape and see for yourself. Joshua Ezeudu was the first player up at guard once Faalele was traded, however he played tackle against the Vikings. We’ll give him a close look if he plays guard against the Miami Dolphins this week — assuming he plays at all after reportedly being “banged up” at the end of Thursday’s joint practice. So with that in mind we’ll take a look at 26-year-old Jake Kubas and 25-year-old Evan Neal . Jake Kubas Kubas was on the field for 21 snaps against the Minnesota Vikings, spending his first 10 snaps at center and the final 11 at left guard. We’ll start with the later snaps and Kubas’ work at guard, as that’s where the trade of Faalele has created the opportunity for movement. Kubas doesn’t have anywhere near the size of Faalele, or Neal. He’s listed at 6-foot-4, 308 pounds, but has a definite advantage over Faalele in terms of athleticism. Kubas has quick, smooth feet that allow him to easily mirror interior rushers, work up to the second level, execute zone blocks, or pull. He isn’t the type to drive defenders off the ball, but understands angles and how to position himself to seal off defenders. Here we see Kubas at left guard, executing the guard-center double team on the nose tackle. Kubas does a great job of playing with a wide base and good pad level, allowing him to anchor against the nose tackle. He’s able to run his feet just enough to turn the tackle out of the hole with half-man leverage. His mobility also makes him a capable pass protector. Here we see him in pass protection at left guard on a third-and-5. As we should expect, the Vikings are showing a heavy pressure look with seven defenders on the line of scrimmage, though they ultimately send just four rushers. Kubas isn’t initially engaged and he does a good job of splitting his attention between helping rookie left tackle JC Davis with the defensive end before sliding back to his right to help Jaimes with the blitzing linebackers. The ball is out long before the rush would have been able to get home, however the two linebackers execute a well-schemed twist that would have gotten No. 48 free had Kubas not redirected to pick up the blitzers. It’s a forgettable play on a quick-hitting third-down completion, but it shows solid awareness as well as lateral agility on the part of Kubas. Moving to center, we see both the good and bad in Kubas’ game. He has the requisite athleticism to play the position and is able to get out of his stance and into position to make his block. Likewise, he understands how to execute the center part of a guard/center double-team, as well as work off the double team to the second level. But thanks to the athletic demands of the center position, we also see what happens when he isn’t quite able to establish leverage. Kubas does a good job of getting the snap off and establishing the double-team withNeal before working to the second level. However, he isn’t quite able to establish the block on the linebacker. Kubas isn’t able to establish leverage, nor is he able to really disrupt the linebacker without good positioning, and the linebacker goes on to trip up Dante Miller as he runs through the gap. Likewise, we also saw at center that Kubas can struggle to hold his ground if his stance narrows or hips rise. It typically wasn’t disastrous, but still more noticeable than when he was better able to establish a wide base and run his feet through half-man leverage at guard. Overall, he did a good job playing center in his first 10 snaps against the Vikings. He wasn’t a revelation, but he also didn’t hold the offense back and he played like a viable reserve at both center and guard. Kubas’ versatility has to be an asset when it comes to making the roster. Teams typically keep eight offensive linemen, and being able to back up three spots is a big advantage. In fact, my question is whether he can play well enough at center to unseat veteran Lucas Patrick as the backup center as well as guard depth. Evan Neal Neal came on the field with the third team, playing 20 snaps all at right guard. Guard seems to agree with Neal when it comes to pass protection. His feet are much more controlled, which translates to improved hand usage. Neal tended to let his hands drift high and wide as he used them for balance while mirroring speed at tackle. He’s able to keep his punch loaded without as much ground to cover, which allows him to fire his punch into defenders’ chest plates and win inside leverage. Here we see Neal handle a stunt on the right side extremely well. He engages the defensive tackle with good hand placement and leverage, passing him off to Josh Ezeudu at right tackle. Neal doesn’t stay stuck on the tackle after passing him off, smoothly anchoring to pick up the looping edge defender and bouncing him well around the pocket. Neal’s power and play strength leap off the screen in both run blocking and pass protection. His height demands that he plays with good hip and pad level, but he’s the type of blocker who can take a defender out of the play once he latches on. Here, Neal does a good job of picking up the 1-technique, engaging with great hand placement. He latches onto the defensive tackles’ chest plate with tight elbows and thumbs up, allowing him to control the defender. Neal gets great extension, using his length to keep the defender from accessing his chest, while using a wide base and good knee bend to maintain his leverage. He stays latched on and simply rides him around the pocket. Despite concerns among fans regarding his pass protection, his worst plays came when run blocking. Neal missed a pair of blocks, both coming when he lunged at defenders. Neal’s height will always mean that he needs to play with good hip and pad level. It’s a bit too easy for defenders to get around him when he gets out over his skis, letting his knees straighten and hips rise. Neal has to make the reach block on the nose tackle with the center and left guard doubling the defensive end. Unfortunately, he gets his chest way out over his toes, and whiffs badly on the tackle. That allows the defender into the backfield to help make the tackle for a loss. The good news is that this and another similar play later in the quarter were isolated incidents when Neal’s game is taken as a whole. Lunging seems less a consistent pattern and more something that can be worked on and cleaned up with continued reps. We know he’s capable of driving defenders off the ball and distorting the line of scrimmage when he plays with good leverage. And while Neal might not have the feet to be a tackle at the NFL level, he does have good feet for a massive guard. It remains to be seen how the Giants’ coaches view Neal. He’ll need to have another good game against the Miami Dolphins, with an emphasis on not allowing himself to lunge when trying to blow up blockers. If he does that, the absence of Faalele could provide an opportunity.
author: Chris Pflum

title: NY Giants vs. Miami Dolphins: 5 things to watch
summary: Opportunities are dwindling for New York Giants players to impress the coaching staff in the competitions for playing time and roster spots. With that in mind, here are some of the potential storylines for Saturday’s preseason game agains the Miami Dolphins. Will any starters play? The answer is probably few, if any. Head coach John […]
full_text: Deonte Banks is one of the Giants in a competition for playing time. | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Opportunities are dwindling for New York Giants players to impress the coaching staff in the competitions for playing time and roster spots. With that in mind, here are some of the potential storylines for Saturday’s preseason game agains the Miami Dolphins. Will any starters play? The answer is probably few, if any. Head coach John Harbaugh would only go so far on Thursday as to hint that some players would sit after Thursday’s joint practice with the Dolphins. “Certain guys, I’m sure, got enough work,” Harbaugh said. “Certain guys, we’ll have to talk about what we want to do.” Best guess — and it is just a guess — is that the only front-line players we will see are some of the rookies and a few of the players competing for starting jobs. Will we see Najee Harris? The veteran running back practiced for the first time on Tuesday. Perhaps surprisingly, he had a few carries on Thursday. Could we see Harris at least a little bit on Saturday? I don’t know, but I would personally like to see him get a couple of carries. Backup offensive line competition There were some interesting developments in the competition for backup offensive line spots over the past week. Daniel Faalele was traded to the Jacksonville Jaguars. Josh Ezeudu emerged as a second-team guard, and took reps with the first team when Francis Mauigoa left Thursday’s practice with a stinger. Ezeudu apparently limped off the field himself on Thursday. Will we see him Saturday? What is going on at backup center? Veteran Lucas Patrick has been considered the likely backup to John Michael Schmitz, and that is probably still the case. Patrick, however, has missed some time during camp with knee issues. That has opened the door for Bryan Hudson and Jake Kubas. Kubas, a former undrafted free agent now in his third season, was excellent at both center and guard in the preseason opener against the Minnesota Vikings. Could he push for a spot? What about Evan Neal? He has still been working with the third team. If neither Mauigoa or Ezuedu play Saturday, though, that should provide Neal an opportunity to play a ton of snaps to make a case for a roster. Let’s not forget rookie tackle J.C. Davis. The sixth-round pick has moved up the tackle depth chart with Ezeudu practicing at guard recently, but his path to a roster spot is not clear. Can he impress vs. the Dolphins. Cornerback competition Who the starters are at cornerback remains unclear. Paulson Adebo had an interception on Thursday, but he has still been taking a lot of second-team reps. If he plays Saturday, that could be a sign that he isn’t guaranteed a starting role. Colton Hood, Deonte Banks, Greg Newsome, Art Green, and maybe even Korie Black are all battling for roles. Who will impress on Saturday? QB3 After Brandon Allen’s disastrous two-interception performance in the second half against the Vikings, the Giants signed quarterback Jake Haener. The Giants probably are not keeping a third quarterback on the active roster, but will need one on the practice squad. Has Haener had enough time digest the playbook well enough that he could get into Saturday’s game and perhaps leapfrog Allen in an effort to earn that spot?

John Harbaugh Attempting To Make the Giants ‘ Special’ Again | SI.com The new head coach spent decades coaching special teams before becoming a head coach, and he’s already reshaping the Giants’ punter, kicker, and long snapper competitions to match. title: Final Score: Jets Beat Steelers As Geno Shines
summary: In the New York Jets’ second preseason game of 2026 in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, the Jets shut out the Pittsburgh Steelers, 17 – 0. The Jets opened on offense with Omar Cooper in with the starters this week. Geno Smith looked sharp as he led the Jets on a long drive culminating in a touchdown pass […]
full_text: PITTSBURGH, PA - AUGUST 21: Jelani Woods #86 of the New York Jets celebrates with teammates after catching a 13-yard touchdown pass in the first half against the Pittsburgh Steelers at Acrisure Stadium on August 21, 2026 in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Justin K. Aller/Getty Images) | Getty Images In the New York Jets’ second preseason game of 2026 in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, the Jets shut out the Pittsburgh Steelers, 17 – 0. The Jets opened on offense with Omar Cooper in with the starters this week. Geno Smith looked sharp as he led the Jets on a long drive culminating in a touchdown pass to Jelani Woods. Smith was a perfect 7 for 7 on the drive. The Jets defense then held the Steelers to a three and out. This is how you hoped the Jets starters would look, dominating the early action. The Jets starting offense called it a night after their impressive game opening touchdown drive. Cade Klubnik and a bunch of backups came in on offense and were immediately shut down by the Steelers defense. The first quarter ended with neither team putting additional points on the board. As the second quarter opened the Steelers had the ball in their own territory. The Steelers drive ended with something we haven’t seen in a very long time – an interception of a Will Howard pass by Andre Cisco. Late in the second quarter the Jets defense did it again. Samuel Womack picked off Will Howard to shut down a promising Steelers drive in Jets territory. That preserved a 7 – 0 Jets lead as the first half wound down. Cade Klubnik overcame a couple of sacks to get the Jets into position for a very long 59 yard field goal attempt as time expired. Cade York had plenty of length but pushed his kick wide as the Jets went into the locker room with a 7 – 0 lead. The Jets opened the third quarter with a bunch of scrubs and Cade Klubnik. The offense couldn’t get anything going. Midway through the third quarter Drew Allar led a Steelers drive deep into Jets territory before the drive bogged down on a Chase Wilson sack. The ensuing 44 yard field goal attempt was missed by the Steelers and the Jets continued to lead the game 7 – 0. The third quarter ended with the score still Jets 7, Steelers 0 as neither offense had much success moving the ball. Bailey Zappe replaced Cade Klubnik late in the quarter as Klubnik was shut out in roughly two quarters running the Jets offense. Midway through the fourth quarter the Jets got their first first down of the second half when Junior Bergen found a crease on a short pass and scooted downfield for a 44 yard gain. The drive bogged down from there and the Jets settled for a field goal and a 10 – 0 lead with seven minutes left in the game. With two minutes left Brady Cook connected with Quincy Skinner on fourth and three for a 31 yard touchdown pass and a 17 – 0 Jets lead. The Steelers could not get the ball in the end zone as time expired and the Jets defense finished off a shutout. Final score: Jets 17, Steelers 0. The victory brought the Jets’ preseason record to 1-1. The Jets had a bit of everything in this win. The front seven put pressure on the quarterback and racked up four sacks, including one by #2 overall draft pick David Bailey. The secondary got a couple of interceptions. And the first team offense, led by Geno Smith, dominated the Steelers in their one drive of the night. It’s just preseason, but it was a promising follow up to last week’s loss. Now the Jets move on to their final preseason game of 2026 next Friday. They will be facing the New York Giants at MetLife Stadium to wrap up the preseason.
