title: Scouting Jets wide receiver/return specialist Junior Bergen
summary: The Jets recently signed wide receiver and return specialist Junior Bergen. Today, we break Bergen down in detail. The 23-year old Bergen is listed at 5’9” and 184 pounds and was a seventh round pick out of Montana in the 2025 draft. He received FCS all-American and all-Big Sky Conference recognition multiple times during his […]
full_text: Aug 3, 2026; San Francisco, CA, USA; San Francisco 49ers wide receiver Junior Bergen (86) during training camp at Levi's Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Sergio Estrada-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The Jets recently signed wide receiver and return specialist Junior Bergen. Today, we break Bergen down in detail. The 23-year old Bergen is listed at 5’9” and 184 pounds and was a seventh round pick out of Montana in the 2025 draft. He received FCS all-American and all-Big Sky Conference recognition multiple times during his college career. Background Bergen was just a two-star prospect out of high school and headed to Montana, where he was originally going to be a receiver but ended up getting moved to running back in the spring due to injuries. His freshman season in 2021 saw him rush for almost 500 yards and four touchdowns with 21 catches for 230 yards and a touchdown. He also got a chance to return some punts and averaged 17.5 yards per return. In 2022, Bergen moved back to wide receiver and generated 256 yards from scrimmage and four touchdowns on offense. However, he really made his mark in the return game as he averaged almost 15 yards per punt return with two more touchdowns to earn all-Big Sky third team recognition. 2023 was his most productive season as he caught a career high 59 passes for 791 yards and five touchdowns, and he was a second team FCS all-American as a return man with four touchdown returns, including the first kickoff return of his career. 2024 again saw Bergen gain all-Big Sky recognition as a receiver and return man as he caught 48 passes for 542 yards and three touchdowns, and added three more punt return touchdowns. He was an honorable mention FCS all-American as a return man. After an impressive college career, Bergen heard his name called in the seventh round of the draft as the 49ers brought him in to be their return specialist. However, he muffed a punt in preseason and ultimately did not make their roster. Although he spent all year on the practice squad, Bergen never did get to make his NFL debut and was then cut right before preseason this year. The Jets signed him last week following an injury to DT Sheffield. Let’s move onto some more in-depth analysis of what Bergen brings to the table, based on in-depth research and film study. Measurables/Athleticism Bergen is small for a wide receiver, but there are plenty of return specialists who are even smaller than he is in the league right now. He shows some good burst and agility on film, but his pro day numbers across the board were about average. He ran a 4.52 in the 40-yard dash with decent explosiveness and agility numbers and 17 bench press reps which is pretty good for his size. Usage On offense, Bergen has primarily played in the slot, which would almost certainly be the main way he’d be used in the Jets’ offense. He could also be used on jet sweeps. Even after moving back to wide receiver, Bergen carried 21 times over the next three years for 84 yards. In addition, he played as a dual threat quarterback in his senior year of high school and put these skills to good use in college with a 27-yard touchdown pass as well as throwing a game winning two-point conversion. Deep threat Bergen had the speed to get behind the defense at the FCS level with some decent success on deep passes, especially in his last two seasons. Hands Bergen had a reasonable 65 percent catch rate at Montana. He dropped just eight passes in four seasons, with four in 2023 but only two in his final season. He had one in preseason last year, though, as he caught just one of three targets for one yard. He doesn’t have too many highlight reel catches in his film but shows an ability to make catches outside his frame and good body control on sideline catches. Routes Bergen developed his route running skills over the course of his college career and shows some ability to lose his defender with double moves and quick changes of direction. He also breaks down well at the top of his route on quick hitches, which can be effective when his downfield threat gets defenders backing off too much. Red zone Bergen is no stranger to the end zone with 26 career touchdowns, although only 13 of them were touchdown catches and he never had more than five offensive touchdowns in a season. Here’s one play where he did well to get open in close quarters for a red zone score. After the catch With his experience as a running back and return man, Bergen is adept at maximising yardage however you get the ball into his hands. He is elusive, with good open field speed and vision. He has only fumbled after the catch once during his career, but did fumble four times as a rusher. However, he didn’t have any fumbles on offense in his final two seasons. Blocking Blocking wasn’t something Bergen was asked to do much of, and you wouldn’t expect it to be a primary role at the NFL level if he gets any offensive reps. His performance grades on analysis sites such as Pro Football Focus were neutral, which for a player like him often just means he was primarily used as a decoy. Physicality Bergen’s lack of size means he doesn’t employ much physicality when running routes, carrying the ball or blocking. He did have a decent record on contested catches though. Special Teams Clearly Bergen’s primary role at the NFL level is going to be as a return man, although he did also see time as a gunner in college, albeit with just one special teams tackle in limited work. Interestingly, Bergen had no return experience ahead of his freshman year but clearly took to it like a natural. He returned four kickoffs in his sophomore year and then started doing that full time as well. His kickoff return numbers are solid but unspectacular as he had 24 yards per return and one touchdown. However, his punt return numbers are sensational, as he averaged 17 yards per return with eight career touchdowns in college. One concern is muffed punts. He muffed three during his college career and this one during preseason action. Instincts and Intelligence As noted, Bergen took to returning punts like a duck to water as he obviously had a natural affinity for it. His vision and patience are outstanding, especially once he breaks into the open field. Attitude Bergen is a hard worker who wasn’t vocal but led by example in college. He had a team-first attitude with his willingness to try new roles and was humble, grounded and determined. He once said he used to pretend to be ill so he could skip school and watch path to the draft, which showcases his passion for the game, but is also the closest thing he has to a discipline concern. On-field discipline was good, though, with just one offensive penalty in his career. Injuries Injuries weren’t a major issue for Bergen as he played 51 games in four seasons at Montana. However, anyone with his lack of size was always going to create a durability concern and he was banged up at times. In 2022, he was bothered by a hand injury that affected his production. Then in 2023 he missed a couple of weeks with an AC joint sprain in his shoulder. A minor knee injury bothered him in 2024 but he didn’t miss any time. Scheme Fit Bergen replaces Sheffield who didn’t get any offensive reps in the first preseason game but had all the return reps in the second half, so we can probably expect Bergen’s role in the rest of preseason to be similar. He was a teammate of current Jets cornerback Tre Brown while with the 49ers last year. Conclusions After last season, the Jets’ punt return role obviously belongs to Isaiah Williams. However, if Williams continues to ascend on offense, the Jets might opt to take those duties away from him and an opportunity for someone like Bergen could arise. His body of work as a return man is much better than that of Sheffield – and Jamaal Pritchett, his other main competition. This makes a spot on the practice squad and the hope of a call-up at some point this season a realistic possibility. He doesn’t…

full_text: NEW ORLEANS, LOUISIANA - FEBRUARY 09: Johnny Wilson #89 of the Philadelphia Eagles celebrates after beating the Kansas City Chiefs 40-22 to win Super Bowl LIX at Caesars Superdome on February 09, 2025 in New Orleans, Louisiana. (Photo by Emilee Chinn/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Eagles continue to tinker with the roster as they approach their final 53 guys, and are adding some depth at center by signing Zeke Correll, and also brought back WR Brandon Hayes, who has bounced on and off the roster since late-Spring. We signed C Zeke Correll and WR Brandon Hayes. We also placed Tariq Castro-Fields on the Injured Reserve List and waived/injured WR Johnny Wilson. pic.twitter.com/LgpZqKM4Uj — Philadelphia Eagles (@Eagles) August 21, 2026 Zeke Correll is a 6-foot-3, 307-pound center who spent the 2025 offseason with the Minnesota Vikings. Ultimately, he was waived due to injury as they approached final roster cuts, and eventually landed on the team’s injury reserve list for the season. Correll spent last year with new Eagles OL coach Chris Kuper in Minnesota, so there’s so familiarity with what they’re trying to do in Philly. Right now, the depth at center starts with Cam Jurgens, followed by Willie Lampkin, who has impressed this training camp, and now Correll with get into the mix. Wide receiver Brandon Hayes has signed and been waived several times over the past few months by the Eagles, and this time, it took less than a week for him to return to the roster. The WR room is pretty crowded, even with the team waiving Johnny Wilson due to a lingering knee injury. Hayes could make a good practice squad candidate, and someone who can take extra reps as other receivers, like DeVonta Smith and Makai Lemon, come back from injuries of their own. Wilson being waived is a shame, and also removes the biggest WR on the team. Head coach Nick Sirianni and OC Sean Mannion have both lauded the variety of skill-sets by the receiver room, and losing Wilson will affect their overall abilities. Still, the former Eagles draft pick missed the 2025 season due to injuries, and was trending in that direction for 2026. Now, he will revert to injured reserve if/when he goes unclaimed through waivers.

title: The Eagles need to win back the fourth quarter in 2026
summary: This is the time of year when everything new is being installed, and training camp darlings are created. There will be a ton of things to look at this Saturday night when the Eagles face the Baltimore Ravens, and Sean Mannion’s offense, or what small portion of it is shown, will get scrutinized. But the […]
full_text: BALTIMORE, MD - AUGUST 15: Head coach Nick Sirianni of the Philadelphia Eagles looks on during the first half of the preseason game against the Baltimore Ravens at M&T Bank Stadium on August 15, 2026 in Baltimore, Maryland. (Photo by Scott Taetsch/Getty Images) | Getty Images This is the time of year when everything new is being installed, and training camp darlings are created. There will be a ton of things to look at this Saturday night when the Eagles face the Baltimore Ravens, and Sean Mannion’s offense, or what small portion of it is shown, will get scrutinized. But the real reality of the Eagles’ 2026 season will not arrive until around 6:30 p.m. Sunday, September 13 at Lincoln Financial Field. It’s about the time when the Eagles will be in the throes of their first fourth quarter of the season, in the season opener against the Washington Commanders. Winning the fourth quarter will be a big key to the Eagles’ 2026 success. In 2025, the Eagles did not win the fourth quarter. Last season, the Eagles wilted offensively and defensively. In the fourth quarter, the Eagles gave up an average of 7.6 points in the fourth quarter, which was ranked 24th overall, and gave up an average of 13.0 points a game in the fourth quarter of their last three games, granted, games played with backups. What is more disturbing is the Eagles’ offense averaged 5.1 points in the fourth quarter, which was ranked 30th overall. Only Tampa Bay (4.8) and Cleveland (4.1) averaged less. The Eagles’ fourth-quarter production was a precipitous drop from their Super Bowl-winning 2024 season, when they averaged 9.1 points in the fourth quarter, which was No. 1 in the NFL, and 13 points in their last three games. Maybe it was the Kevin Patullo factor, being an offensive coordinator who was learning on the job last season and sometimes falling into over-conservative traps. Whatever the reason, on both sides of the ball, the Eagles better address it in 2026. Was it conditioning? Was it scheme? And no one was immune. It goes beyond Patullo. Vic Fangio’s vaunted defense gave up 1,439 yards in the fourth quarter last season, more than any other quarter and were on the field for 296 plays, which may partially explain why the Eagles struggled in the fourth quarter in 2025. In 2024, opposing teams ran off 267 plays in the fourth quarter. This is where the offense and defense intertwine. In 2024, the Eagles’ offense kept the defense off the field in the fourth quarter, gouging opposing defenses. In 2025, the Eagles ran off 249 plays in the fourth quarter, in the Super Bowl 2024 season, the Eagles ran off an even 300 plays, 51 plays more. They scored 16 touchdowns and gained 1,605 yards in the fourth quarter in 2024; they scored 11 TDs in 2025 and gained 1,325 yards. The biggest difference came in running the ball, where in 2024, Saquon Barkley and his bulldozing offensive line smashed defenses for 832 yards rushing, averaging 4.3 yards a carry, whereas the running game collapsed in the fourth in 2025, falling 456 yards to 376 in 2025, averaging more than a yard less (3.2). That was the result of a creaky, banged up offensive line, Barkley recovering from a career-best 345 carries and 2,005 yards rushing in 2024, and Patullo running basic stuff, which lacked motion and a passing presence down the middle of the field. If the Eagles, favorites to threepeat as NFC East champions, are going to get beyond the defending Super Bowl champion Seattle Seahawks, Los Angeles Rams or Chicago Bears in the NFC, they will need to win the fourth quarter. Hopefully, Mannion will find a cure to the Eagles’ 2025 fourth quarter woes.

Patriots-Eagles joint practice recap: Defenses fight back on Day 2 – Pats Pulpit Red zone woes: Improving in the red zone is an area of focus for the Patriots this season after struggling as a unit last year. On Thursday, the inconsistencies continued even though Drake Maye and Co. started strong with touchdowns to Mack Hollins and A.J. Brown on a contested catch over Quinyon Mitchell. From there, pressure became more of an issue and Maye was late targeting Brown along the goal line which led to a long pick-six by Riq Woolen. Maye’s end-of-game drive then ended on one play as a slant to Brown was broken up with the ball popping up into the air and Jalyx Hunt recording an interception. The unit was given a second chance which ended better with a touchdown to Romeo Doubs. “Felt like we could have done more in the red zone,” Maye said after practice. “That’s something for us to learn. It’s one of our focuses this year… so we got some work to do.” […] Will Campbell and Caleb Lomu each split their 1-on-1 reps. Campbell continued to have some issues in pass pro against Jalyx Hunt, who is a breakout candidate for the Eagles this year, but did have a nice stunt pickup with Alijah Vera-Tucker to lead to Romeo Doubs’ touchdown. Eagles-Patriots Practice Notes: Jalen Hurts finishes strong, defense bounces back – BGN Speaking of Jalyx Hunt, he produced two takeaways today. In addition to the pick, there was a rep where he simply stole the ball away from Rhamondre Stevenson’s hands for an instant forced fumble and recovery. I love the aesthetic of that kind of play where the ball doesn’t even touch the ground. Hunt is a beast. He’s had an awesome summer. Welcome to the NFC East Mixtape Feed! – SB Nation As the 2026 NFL season draws near, SB Nation is launching a new discussion community focused on the sport’s most historic division. The NFC East Mixtape Feed will be a spot for fans of the Commanders, Giants, Cowboys and Eagles to discuss the latest divisional news, share their takes about their favorite team and, of course, talk a little smack. Eagles-Patriots 2026 training camp joint practice notes, Day 14: Birds defense finishes strongly – PhillyVoice Jeremiah Trotter has continued to have a very good camp. Just generally, he was physical against the run today, and he had good coverage on an incomplete pass to the end zone against the speedy TreVeyon Henderson. Trotter can play. Jalen Carter didn’t practice today, but I thought that Moro Ojomo and Jordan Davis owned to the interior of the line against the Pats’ run game for the better part of the day. They each had multiple tackles for loss, and Davis had a batted pass, as he often does. Even when they weren’t making the stops themselves, Ojomo and Davis were messing up Pats run plays. For example, Ojomo got a great jump on one snap and instantly got into the backfield with an impressive swim move, forcing the back to stop dead in his tracks and try the backside, which wasn’t blocked up. Eagles-Patriots observations: Jalen Hurts’ clutch TD drive, skirmishes stall running game – The Athletic That last period overshadowed what had been an inconsistent day for the passing offense. Hurts threw two interceptions to Marcus Jones, including one on a deflected pass to Brown. He was also under duress from the Patriots’ pass rush, with multiple would-be sacks. The interceptions are uncustomary for Hurts but were more frequent this week. This offense will target the middle of the field, so there might be more “interceptable” passes this year. It’s a number worth monitoring for Hurts; he had 11 total interceptions over the last two seasons, down from 15 in 2023. His interception rate has been 1.4 percent or lower in three of the past four years. There were some good moments, including two touchdowns in a red zone period (one to Goedert, one to Wicks), but it wasn’t as smooth a performance as you would like to see from the passing offense. It sounds repetitive, but I expect it to look more efficient when the top receivers return. Both Smith and Lemon can help with quick completions that move the chains. Eagles-Patriots joint practice observations: Jalen Hurts and offense struggle until the end; Riq Woolen and pass defense strike back – Inquirer Even without Carter and Young, the Eagles’ interior defensive line won the run battle. Every time I glanced over to the other field, defensive tackles Jordan Davis and Moro Ojomo disrupted the Patriots’ ground assault. Vic Fangio can get away with the highest percentage of light boxes in the NFL because he has the horses up front. I didn’t catch all of the one-on-ones between the Eagles’ pass rushers and the Patriots offensive line, but of the matchups I watched, they fared well. Hunt split his two reps vs. tackle Will Campbell, but edge Nolan Smith Jr. had victories over tackle Marcus Bryant. Defensive tackle Ty Robinson used his trusty old club/swim move to win his first turn, but guard Alijah Vera-Tucker took the rematch. Linebacker Zack Baun took a rare pass rush and dusted tackle Caleb Lomu. Edge Arnold Ebiketie had a win and draw vs. tackle Dametrious Crownover. The education of rookie defensive tackle Uar Bernard continued. Guard JonDarius Morgan handled him with relative ease. The Five Archetypes of the Modern NFL Cornerback – The Ringer Quinyon Mitchell, Philadelphia Eagles. Philadelphia does not play a man-heavy defense—its 24 percent man coverage rate last season was just above the league average of 22 percent—but Mitchell thrives when he does get the chance to be left alone on the perimeter. Mitchell spent a large part of last season following elite receivers like George Pickens, Davante Adams, and Justin Jefferson wherever they lined up—and Denver’s Courtland Sutton was the only one who tallied more than 15 receiving yards against Mitchell. The Eagles’ young star had multiple weeks without allowing a single completion on his coverage targets. He’s yet to intercept a pass in his 32 regular-season games (but has picked off four passes in the postseason). That lack of ball production makes it hard to draw 1:1 comparisons across eras, but his closest comp is Stephon Gilmore, who played for six teams from 2012 to 2024 and won NFL Defensive Player of the Year in 2019. Like Gilmore, Mitchell doesn’t bait quarterbacks into risky throws; instead, he wants to take away space and erase receivers from the offense’s game plan entirely. Like Gilmore, Mitchell is surprisingly physical at the line of scrimmage, despite weighing under 200 pounds, and he is fluid enough to get in and out of his breaks without losing speed. And like Gilmore, Mitchell is a good tackler on the perimeter. He isn’t the type of player an offense will want to challenge in the run game. 2026 NFL running back unit rankings: Falcons top the list – PFF 3: Philadelphia Eagles. title: Stock report after the Steelers’ 17-0 preseason loss to the New York Jets
summary: The Pittsburgh Steelers fell to the New York Jets, 17-0, on Friday night at Acrisure Stadium. Strangely enough, it was the first time the Steelers were shut out in a preseason game since 2016, when they lost to the Philadelphia Eagles by an identical score. Although Pittsburgh didn’t put up a single point, there is […]
full_text: PITTSBURGH, PENNSYLVANIA - AUGUST 21: Will Howard #18 of the Pittsburgh Steelers looks to pass during the second quarter of a preseason game against the New York Jets at Acrisure Stadium on August 21, 2026 in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Joe Sargent/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Pittsburgh Steelers fell to the New York Jets, 17-0, on Friday night at Acrisure Stadium. Strangely enough, it was the first time the Steelers were shut out in a preseason game since 2016, when they lost to the Philadelphia Eagles by an identical score. Although Pittsburgh didn’t put up a single point, there is still plenty to talk about. Let’s have a look at who helped their stock and who hurt themselves in the Steelers embarrassing preseason shutout loss. Stock up: LB Elandon Roberts The Steelers could shut Elandon Roberts down for the rest of the preseason, and it would be justified. The linebacker seemed to be on a different level than anyone else in this game. Roberts made his presence known from the moment he stepped on the field, stopping a run at the line of scrimmage. His most impressive play came on a fourth-and-two where he made a phenomenal open-field tackle to prevent a New York first down. Roberts played with his hair on fire, and is going to bring that same energy and production into the regular season. S Rayshawn Jenkins Safety is one of the Steelers’ thinnest positions on the roster, and Jenkins’ performance in this game gave his chances of making the roster a serious bump. Defensive coordinator Patrick Graham made it a point to blitz Jenkins early and often, and it worked like a charm as Jenkins recorded a TFL early in the contest. Jenkins has proven that he is a solid veteran presence that can change the game in the blink of an eye while chasing the quarterback. He has a real shot to make the 53-man roster. P Cameron Johnston If the punter is one of your biggest winners, your team likely didn’t have a great week. All jokes aside, Johnston averaged 50.5 yards on his 6 punts in the contest. The Steelers defense will be thanking Johnston for giving them more room to work with if he keeps this going into the regular season. Stock down: QB Will Howard There really isn’t a nice way to talk about Will Howard’s performance in his first career start. The young quarterback finished 10/15 for 74 yards and two interceptions. Both of the turnovers were pretty easy snags for the defense, in which Howard simply didn’t recognize that a defender was waiting to jump the route — though Roman Wilson failing to flatten his routes and drifting downfield didn’t do the young passer any favors. For someone who is competing for a backup quarterback job, a performance like tonight’s will make it hard for the Steelers to trust Howard in that role. Mason Rudolph may be one of the biggest winners from tonight, and he didn’t take a single snap. The offensive line I hate to have negative takeaways on the offensive line for a second straight week, but this game was arguably worse than their effort in Week 1 of the preseason. One of the lone bright spots on the line last week was Broderick Jones, but he was unable to replicate his performance. However, my main concerns come from starting right tackle Dylan Cook. Cook gave up a sack early in the game, one of the four that the line gave up overall on the night. Rookie Max Iheanachor remains sidelined with a neck/shoulder injury, which is unfortunate because he could have had a serious shot to earn the starting right tackle job as early as Week 1 based on his performances in training camp. There are a lot of moving pieces and new starters on this offensive line. Hopefully it all sorts itself out for the better, but there are plenty of reasons to be concerned after this week. title: Will Howard struggles, throws two INTs in Steelers’ loss to Jets
summary: After a preseason opener featuring a duo of fantastic debuts at quarterback, the Pittsburgh Steelers saw their offense tumble back down to Earth in a 17-0 loss to the New York Jets in Week 2 of exhibition play. The leadup to the game was highlighted by the announcement that Will Howard would get the start, […]
full_text: PITTSBURGH, PENNSYLVANIA - AUGUST 21: Will Howard #18 of the Pittsburgh Steelers reacts during the second quarter against the New York Jets at Acrisure Stadium on August 21, 2026 in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Joe Sargent/Getty Images) | Getty Images After a preseason opener featuring a duo of fantastic debuts at quarterback, the Pittsburgh Steelers saw their offense tumble back down to Earth in a 17-0 loss to the New York Jets in Week 2 of exhibition play. The leadup to the game was highlighted by the announcement that Will Howard would get the start, as head coach Mike McCarthy said he saw all he needed to see from Mason Rudolph and gave him the night off. Unfortunately, the Ohio State product did anything but impress. After a three and out and a four-play drive that ended with a punt, Howard tossed an interception directly to Jets safety Andre Cisco in the red zone. The interception killed what had been a 12-play drive. The next drive ended in similar fashion with Howard under-throwing a pass to Roman Wilson that was picked off by Samuel Womack. The former sixth-round pick’s day was done after the first half, finishing with 74 yards and a pair of interceptions on 10-of-15 passing. With a chance to potentially show he was worthy of being the backup to Aaron Rodgers, Howard, instead, may have played himself off the 53-man roster all together. Unfortunately, it wasn’t a picturesque night for Drew Allar, either, but for different reasons. The Steelers’ offensive line gave up constant pressure, allowing the third-round pick to get sacked three times. Allar did, however, avoid pressure and broke out to the left before launching a 38-yard pass down the sideline to Lake McRee for the longest play of the game for the Steelers. However, seven dropped passes and a lack of separation from the likes of Cornell Powell, Levi Wentz, Jaheim Bell, and Joaqin Davis led to an 11-of-23, 110-yard outing for Allar. Defensively, the first-team unit looked less than prepared. The Jets marched down the field to begin the game, driving 69 yards in 10 plays and ending the drive with a touchdown pass from Smith to Jelani Woods. On the pass, both Alex Highsmith and Patrick Queen crashed on Smith, leaving Woods wide open in the flat. Pittsburgh kept the Jets from reaching the end zone again until late in the fourth quarter when Quincy Skinner caught a 31-yard touchdown. Of course, in preseason, the final score isn’t important, it’s how individual players look that matters most, and Pittsburgh did have a few performances that stood out in a positive light. Defensive tackle Yahya Black got a big mit on a Geno Smith throw, batting it down at the line of scrimmage. DeShon Elliott forced a fumble on third down. And while it wasn’t recovered by the Steelers, it was good to see a healthy Elliott making plays. Carson Bruener had a tremendous sequence of plays, as well, batting down a Cade Klubnik pass and then sacking Klubnik with under a minute left in the first half. The return of No. 50 Elandon Roberts was also a highlight of the night for the defense, as he led the team with five tackles, one of which was for loss and other that came on fourth down and ended a Jets drive. Second-year edge rusher Jack Sawyer had a nice night, as well, picking up a sack and a pass deflection while rookie Robert-Spears Jennings and veteran Rayshawn Jenkins both looked good in pass coverage and crashing down in the run game, respectively. Offensively, both Howard and Allar had a few nice rips downfield. Howard connected with Ben Skowronek on a third-and-eight for a 16-yard gain and had a nice 12 yard completion to Robert Tonyan. Allar had the deep connection to McRee, as well as 15 and 17-yard shots to Isaiah Winstead. That’s about all the good to come from the offense, though. The pair of interceptions from Howard far outweigh the few completions that moved the chains, he offensive line was putrid in all four quarters, and none of the skill position players who were on the field for the majority of the second half are NFL-caliber players. Pittsburgh will close out its preseason next Thursday night in Buffalo against the Bills. Then comes the cut down to 53 players ahead of Week 1 against the Atlanta Falcons. title: Seahawks receiver Tory Horton will be ‘out for a period of time’
summary: The Seattle Seahawks were delighted to get second-year receiver Tory Horton back in time for the start of training camp, having recovered from a season-ending cracked tibia. Horton has been available and a full-go for the majority of practices, but he wasn’t there for the Seahawks’ preseason opener against the Dallas Cowboys, and he won’t […]
full_text: Sep 14, 2025; Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, USA; Seattle Seahawks wide receiver Tory Horton (15) runs into the end-zone to score on a twenty-one yard touchdown catch against the Pittsburgh Steelers during the first quarter at Acrisure Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Charles LeClaire-Imagn Images | Charles LeClaire-Imagn Images The Seattle Seahawks were delighted to get second-year receiver Tory Horton back in time for the start of training camp, having recovered from a season-ending cracked tibia . Horton has been available and a full-go for the majority of practices, but he wasn’t there for the Seahawks’ preseason opener against the Dallas Cowboys, and he won’t be back for Sunday’s game at the Tennessee Titans. With Horton absent for Friday’s joint scrimmage with the Titans in Nashville, Seahawks head coach Mike Macdonald provided the vaguest of timelines and straight-up did not disclose why he’s not practiced over the past several days. “He’s still working through his stuff,” Macdonald said. “He’s going to be out for a period of time.” Macdonald also said, with a wry smile, “Sorry, I just don’t want to tell you.” He did not indicate whether it was an injury or if it’s a personal matter. Of course, “a period of time” can mean anything from a few days to a month to five minutes. For as long as teams aren’t required to release an injury report, this ambiguity will continue. The last notable thing involving Horton was a training camp scuffle back on Aug. 11, which Tacoma News Tribune’s Gregg Bell documented in his report : Camp’s biggest fight yet happened one play after a sideline official flagged wide receiver Tory Horton for offensive pass interference pushing into cornerback Nathaniel Pritchett with a two-arm shiver. That was with Horton coming out of his break on a deep out route in an 11-on-11 scrimmage. The pass fell to the grass incomplete. The defensive players yelled at Horton for the penalty. On his way back to his offense’s huddle, Horton went into the defensive huddle and talked smack at all 11 players there. Horton lined up flanked outside left again for the next snap. He caught a quick pass outside, in front of arriving safety Ty Okada. Okada hit Horton hard in his back from behind after the play was over. Then he hit him again. Then Okada hit Horton a third time in the back, along the sideline where all the defensive players were massed. Horton, the team’s fifth-round pick last year from Colorado State in his first weeks back from a cracked shin that ended his rookie season in November, went at Okada following the third late hit. Okada threw Horton to the ground, and into the mass of about three-dozen defensive players. With the players’ and coaches’ significant others and kids watching from across the way, a giant pile of defensive players went at the fallen Horton. He was almost the lone offensive player on the sideline opposite his offensive teammates. When an offensive lineman ran over from the middle of the field to try to assist Horton, linebacker Derick Hall stood in front of him and stopped him. With Horton currently unavailable and Jake Bobo likely out for the season after his knee injury in the Titans scrimmage, Seattle’s wide receiver depth is stretched a bit at the midway point of preseason. For the likes of Montorie Foster Jr, Ricky White III, Cody White, and Emmanuel Henderson Jr, it’ll be an opportunity to stake their claim for a roster spot.

Seattle’s star receiver was named one of the final 10 players on the NFL Top 100 Players of […]
full_text: After a historic season in which he led the league with an astounding 1,793 receiving yards and earned the NFL Offensive Player of the Year award , Seattle Seahawks wide receiver Jaxon Smith-Njigba continues to earn his flowers. Seattle’s star receiver was named one of the final 10 players on the NFL Top 100 Players of 2026 list, meaning he’ll join linebacker Ernest Jones IV (No.97) and quarterback Sam Darnold (No. 21) as the lone Seahawks on the ranking. In addition to Jones, Smith-Njigba’s appearance marks the first of his career, and unlikely the last. The final stretch of the ranking will kick off on August 24, unveiling one player per week day. The remaining 10 players on the NFL Top 100 listed in alphabetical order. See where they are ranked next week. 👀 pic.twitter.com/aSAoUCVnCB — NFL (@NFL) August 21, 2026 It should surely come as a surprise the reigning Super Bowl champions have just three players on the list, especially considering their division rival Los Angeles Rams, who the Seahawks defeated 31-27 in the NFC Championship last season , have the same number in the top 10 alone. Albeit, defensive end Myles Garrett hasn’t played a snap for the franchise yet. But, perhaps the most noteworthy part of the ranking from Seattle’s perspective isn’t who made it, but who was left off. Pro Bowl cornerback Devon Witherspoon, now the highest paid player at his position , narrowly missed (No. 107), and was placed behind Jalen Ramsey (No. 82), Jaycee Horn (No. 76) and Cooper DeJean (No. 38). While Witherspoon’s absence is notable, defensive lineman Leonard Williams, who helped anchor one of the most dominant defenses of the modern era, was arguably a far bigger snub. Williams had another incredibly productive year in 2025 under head coach Mike Macdonald, racking up seven sacks and 58 pressures, while remaining an elite force in stopping the run. Yet, he didn’t even earn a mention, unlike Derrick Brown (No. 90), Zach Allen (No. 73), and Jalen Carter (No. 29), who all soared through the ranking. Although Smith-Njigba, Darnold, and Jones earned the respect the deserved, several members of the Seahawks (including Byron Murphy II and Nick Emmanwori, by the way) did not.

title: Jake Bobo injury update: Seahawks receiver has ‘long-term’ knee injury
summary: It looks as if Jake Bobo’s fourth season with the Seattle Seahawks is already over. The fan favorite wide receiver and special teams contributor suffered what was described as a “bad-looking leg injury” during Friday’s joint practice with the Tennessee Titans in Nashville. He was carted off after awkwardly landing on a catch attempt, and […]
full_text: SEATTLE, WASHINGTON - JANUARY 25: Jake Bobo #19 of the Seattle Seahawks lines up during an NFC Championship NFL football game against the Los Angeles Rams at Lumen Field on January 25, 2026 in Seattle, Washington. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images It looks as if Jake Bobo’s fourth season with the Seattle Seahawks is already over. The fan favorite wide receiver and special teams contributor suffered what was described as a “ bad-looking leg injury ” during Friday’s joint practice with the Tennessee Titans in Nashville. He was carted off after awkwardly landing on a catch attempt, and barring some very favorable imaging, that will be his last action on the field this year. “Our heart goes out to Jake Bobo,” Mike Macdonald said after practice. “Seems like it’s going to be a serious knee, we’re going to get it imaged, but early returns—looks like it’s a long-term injury. So that’s unfortunate.” Bobo re-signed with the Seahawks on a two-year deal after matching the Jacksonville Jaguars’ restricted free agent offer sheet. He’s functioned as the fourth or fifth option at wide receiver, doing a lot of the dirty work as a blocker and in kick and punt return coverage. His NFC Championship touchdown against the Los Angeles Rams was his only score all season and it helped Seattle get to the Super Bowl. In all likelihood, Bobo would’ve played the Sunday preseason game against the Titans, having played the first half of last week’s game against the Dallas Cowboys. Unfortunately, it appears as if the next time we see Bobo will be 2027. For any semblance of good news, Macdonald indicated that other Seahawks injuries (which included Montorie Foster and Abe Lucas) were heat-related/cramps, so there’s nothing to worry about on that front. But this is ultimately a devastating injury for Bobo and a blow to both Seattle’s offense and special teams.

title: Member of Seahawks’ Super Bowl team retires
summary: While DeMarcus Lawrence opted to continue his NFL career even after winning that elusive Super Bowl with the Seattle Seahawks, one member of Seattle’s 2025 squad has played his last down. Myles Gaskin, born and raised in the Seattle area and a standout running back on the Washington Huskies, has announced his retirement after seven […]
full_text: SEATTLE, WASHINGTON - NOVEMBER 30: Myles Gaskin #33 of the Seattle Seahawks looks on prior to the game against the Minnesota Vikings at Lumen Field on November 30, 2025 in Seattle, Washington. (Photo by Jane Gershovich/Getty Images) | Getty Images While DeMarcus Lawrence opted to continue his NFL career even after winning that elusive Super Bowl with the Seattle Seahawks, one member of Seattle’s 2025 squad has played his last down. Myles Gaskin, born and raised in the Seattle area and a standout running back on the Washington Huskies, has announced his retirement after seven seasons in the pros. The 29-year-old wrote his farewell to the gridiron in an Instagram post . View this post on Instagram Thank you, God; you have allowed me to live my childhood’s greatest dream, which was to play the game I loved at the highest level. You have allowed it for seven years as a professional, four years in the greatest setting in college football as a Dawg at the University of Washington. Before that, at O’Dea High School… and before that as a Richmond Bulldog. Thank you to all those who showed love and support both on and off the field. To the Miami Dolphins, boy was that fun. To the Seattle Seahawks, thank you for letting me play my last snaps back at the crib. To the fans, you make this game special every Friday, Saturday, Sunday… Monday, Thursday -really, every day, eight months out of the year. To the staff, the organizations, my teammates, and coaches at every level, there are too many laughs, stories, and lessons to name, but every snap helped me grow into the man always wanted to become. Tracy Ford, thank you for taking a chance on a random kid who just showed up at your gym. Salvon Ahmed.. what a ride. Thank you, Ivan Gaskin, for being the first person who ever believed in me. Scott and Robbie Gaskin- you gave me the green light to chase a dream and the work ethic to get there, while never adding any pressure to the journey. Thank you. couldn’t have asked for better parents. Football… there will never be enough words to explain how I feel about you, so I won’t even try. What I will do is give all the game you gave me to the next generation of young players who dare to be great. Thank you. It’s been real. Myles Gaskin was signed to the Seahawks practice squad last October, and was off-and-on before eventually getting a game day call-up versus the Minnesota Vikings. In garbage time, Gaskin carried the ball three times for six yards to help run the clock out in a 26-0 shutout win. Gaskin was released from the practice squad on Dec. 13 and did not sign with another team. Gaskin rushed for over 1,000 yards in all four seasons with Washington, making him the school’s all-time leading rusher and the first back in Pac-12 history to clear 1k on the ground in four seasons. He netted first-team All-Pac-12 honors in 2016 when the Huskies reached the College Football Playoff. The Miami Dolphins took Gaskin in the seventh round of the 2017 NFL Draft, and he led the team in rushing in 2020 and 2021. Gaskin largely bounced around the league after Miami let him go in 2023, and his six rushing yards in Seattle were his only ones not with the Dolphins. Happy retirement to Myles, a Huskies legend whose final NFL chapter was playing for his hometown, Super Bowl-winning team!

title: 49ers Snap Counts and Grades: Is there a new RB2 in town?
summary: Following the joint practice with the Los Angeles Chargers, the San Francisco 49ers throttled the Jim Harbaugh-led Chargers on Thursday night and dropped a 40-burger in SoFi Stadium. Brock Purdy and the “starters” played a single drive and gave way to the backups and players fighting for a roster spot, but the dominance continued across […]
full_text: INGLEWOOD, CA - AUGUST 20: San Francisco 49ers running back Kaelon Black (26) rushes with the ball up the middle during the game between the Los Angeles Chargers and the San Francisco 49ers on August 20, 2026 at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood. (Photo by David Dennis/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Following the joint practice with the Los Angeles Chargers, the San Francisco 49ers throttled the Jim Harbaugh-led Chargers on Thursday night and dropped a 40-burger in SoFi Stadium. Brock Purdy and the “starters” played a single drive and gave way to the backups and players fighting for a roster spot, but the dominance continued across the board. Let’s take a look at the snap counts and grades from the 49ers’ 41-17 win over Los Angeles. Quarterbacks Brock Purdy 12 (64.1), Mac Jones 25 (51.3), Adrian Martinez 38 (26.3) The goal was to get Purdy in and get him out. Mission accomplished. Jones had some great throws and misfires in his first action of the preseason, but Martinez received the bulk of the reps with Kurtis Rourke dealing with a rib injury. It was a mixed bag for Martinez, but he did finish with a very nice rushing TD and ripped a TD to Jordan Watkins down the seam. Running backs Zamir White 24 (48.7), Sincere McCormick 20 (61.6), Kaelon Black 16 (73.1), Khalil Herbert 15 (76.0) The focus was on Black, who flashed in just about every way on Thursday night. The former Indiana Hoosier ran hard and forced three missed tackles, but his work in pass protection shouldn’t go unnoticed. The quickest way to find yourself in Kyle Shanahan’s doghouse is to miss a blocking assignment, and Black showed that his reputation as a pass blocker is well earned. Black is likely the RB2 with Jordan James still dealing with an injury. McCormick has been an unsung hero for the 49ers with injuries mounting at the position. Being able to take reps isn’t exactly glamorous, but McCormick was rewarded following a long 37-yard run with a rushing touchdown. Depending on how the injuries shake out, his performance might have earned him a roster spot in the running back room. Wide receivers Jordan Watkins 53 (66.4), Trenton Irwin 30 (40.7), Jacob Cowing 28 (58.5), KhaDarel Hodge 26 (78.8), Demarcus Robinson 19 (53.5), De’Zhaun Stribling 14 (90.5), Will Pauling 11 (56.0), Deebo Samuel 10 (55.5) Well, Stribling is human after all. Of course, I’m joking, but the rookie continued his fine play and is proving who he is, regardless of which quarterback is on the field. Sure, it would have been nice to bring in the potential touchdown pass, but the hype train is flying down the track for Stribling. Samuel and Robinson “started” the game. Still, Watkinsins played the most on Thursday and hauled in a touchdown pass, with another potential touchdown from Jones, which fell incomplete between two Chargers defenders. Cowing clinched a roster spot with his punt return touchdown. Further proof that players are one or two plays away from success. Is Christian Kirk’s roster spot in jeopardy? We’ll have to find that out. Tight ends Brayden Willis 37 (43.6), Jake Tonges 18 (43.0), Josiah Deguara 12 (64.0), Luke Farrell 13 (78.9), Hayden Rucci 29 (58.8) Tonges and Farrell are locks, but Willis did some of the dirty work while taking snaps at the FB spot, and helped spring McCormick’s long run with a beautiful seal block to open the hole for the running back. The 49ers received an encouraging report about George Kittle, but may have to lean on Tonges in Week 1 if the All-Pro tight end doesn’t make the trip to Australia. Offensive Line Enrique Cruz, Jr. 48 (54.6), Isaac Alcaron 38 (62.5), Brandon Parker 25 (74.5), Colton McKivitz 12 (49.4), Connor Colby 45 (49.6), Austen Pleasants 52 (55.8), Carver Willis 42 (40.0), Nick Zakelj 38 (72.9), Drake Nugent 25 (72.2), Doug Kramer 38 (64.1), Jake Brendel 12 (59.9) The left guard position remains a mystery. Colby began as the right guard, Willis got some run, and Pleasants was getting a long look at the end of the night before his injury. Depending on the severity of the injury, Willis and Colby would be the two most likely to compete to start in Week 1. It would be nice to get some clarity on a frontrunner, but here we are. Anyone know what Kevin Zeitler is doing right now? Defense Defensive Line Ogbo Okoronkwo 27 (84.3), Bryson Eason 26 (80.5), James Thompson, Jr. 26 (90.3), Sebastian Valdez 23 (75.5), Quinton Bell 23 (68.7), Victor Dimukeje 19 (52.5), Sam Okuayinonu 17 (61.2), Alfred Collins 20 (56.1), Romello Height 13 (69.0), Evan Anderson 14 (59.8), Osa Odighizuwa 9 (66.6) Odighizuwa took six pass-rushing snaps and looked every bit the part in his limited action. Thompson, Jr finished with the highest pass-rushing grade at 80.8. Okuayinonu had a team-high two pressures, and Collins wasn’t credited with a pressure, but shed RG Cole Strange with a quick swipe and was bearing down on Justin Herbert, which is a great sign for the second-year DT. Eason batted down a pass and finished with a team-high 88.4 true pass rush grade. Linebackers Nick Martin 33 (66.1), Garret Wallow 32 (31.2), Jaden Dugger 32 (66.5), Tatum Bethune 27 (78.4) The 49ers’ linebacker depth is a strength for the defense. Martin contributed with a forced fumble on special teams, with Bethune recovering the fumble. Dugger recorded a PBU on an intended pass to Orande Gadsden while trailing in coverage. It was Wallow who seemed to be in the mix on nearly any play he was on the field for. The 49ers will have an interesting decision on cutdown day. Secondary Jalen Stroman 42 (37.5), Darrell Luter, Jr. 42 (57.2), Jack Jones 29 (88.4), Jakob Robinson 27 (60.0), Ashtyn Davis 25 (29.7), Larry Worth III 18 (71.6), Ji’Ayir Brown 17 (78.6), Marques Sigle 17 (64.1), Patrick McMorris 17 (29.8), Deommodore Lenoir 17 (80.2), Renardo Green 9 (46.2), Upton Stout 8 (68.1), The bummer is the news of Green’s hamstring injury, but if he is forced to miss time in the regular season, Jones made a statement on Thursday night. Cornerback is much better with depth, but the hope is Green will be ready to go in Australia. Robinson flashed in run defense and nearly notched an interception, which could have been a pick-six. The safety spot opposite Brown could still be in the air. Malik Mustapha is still dealing with an injury, but there’s still time before the Australia trip to find out who will start.

title: 8 Winners and 2 losers from the 49ers’ preseason win over the Chargers
summary: The San Francisco 49ers looked like all of the tweets we saw about the Los Angeles Chargers during Tuesday’s joint practice. They dominated in all facets of the game and controlled the line of scrimmage on both sides of the ball, for the most part. Best of all, we saw game-changing plays in all three […]
full_text: INGLEWOOD, CA - AUGUST 20: San Francisco 49ers offensive tackle Enrique Cruz Jr. (69) defends agains the rush of San Francisco 49ers defensive tackle Sam Okuayinonu (91) during the game between the Los Angeles Chargers and the San Francisco 49ers on August 20, 2026 at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood. (Photo by David Dennis/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers looked like all of the tweets we saw about the Los Angeles Chargers during Tuesday’s joint practice. They dominated in all facets of the game and controlled the line of scrimmage on both sides of the ball, for the most part. Best of all, we saw game-changing plays in all three phases, leading to a lopsided victory. Here are the winners and losers from the 49ers’ second preseason game. Sam Okuayinonu He doesn’t have the upside as Mykel Williams nor the pass rush versatility to kick inside, but Okuayinonu showed why the 49ers will be just fine on early downs against the Chargers. Last year, Sam O was stretched into a full-time player, which hurt his effectiveness. It’s like taking a key bullpen player — let’s say your seventh inning guy — and asking him to pitch four innings. He was never going to be the same. But in spurts, Okauyinonu can be effective. He played five run snaps, had two stops, and won on another rep that forced the running back to redirect right into his teammate for a tackle for loss. He also had two pressures on 12 pass rushes, including a quarterback hit. Okuayinonu is an ideal role player. Kaelon Black Black’s discipline as a runner is impressive. He has zero interest in bouncing runs to the outside, as tempting as it may be. He stays on a vertical path and will pinball off defenders for a positive gain. Another positive trait about Black — that Brian Robinson Jr. couldn’t stop doing — was his refusal to stop his feet in the backfield. Black was always gaining ground. One cut and go. Black could’ve been tackled in the backfield on two occasions. He didn’t lose a yard on either, despite the line missing multiple blocks on both plays. Black forced three missed tackles, had 21 of his 33 yards after contact, and picked up a pair of first downs on eight carries. Equally important, Black was a key part of pass protection. He picked up a blitz on both opportunities. He knew where to go and did not give ground. Black looked prepared. He was fantastic. Osa Odighizuwa My goodness. What an upgrade at the position. Odighizuwa has the kind of activity reminiscent of DeForest Buckner. Raheem Morris will have the defensive line moving in enough directions on run downs for Odighizuwa to fall into multiple plays based on his athleticism alone. The Chargers couldn’t stay in front of him. On one play, Odighizuwa slanted right, but still got back to the other side of the line of scrimmage to force the runner to redirect. Two plays before that, he came free for a pressure after beating the left guard. Odighizuwa changes directions like a linebacker in a defensive tackle’s body. Losers Left guard competition The three-man competition turned into a four-man competition, but that’s because Robert Jones will probably miss the rest of the preseason with an undisclosed injury . Carver Willis needs more reps. Those might have to come on the fly with live bullets flying in the regular season. Rookie mistakes, like pulling and failing to look inside for the first threat, were on full display Thursday night. Willis also got bowled over late in the game in pass protection. The other options aren’t any better. Austen Pleasants, who also has a knee injury, takes two seconds to get out of his stance. He’s too slow to make an impact. That was apparent on multiple occasions. The final choice is Connor Colby. He’s competent for the most part in pass protection, but whiffs too much in the running game. If Thursday night’s game is any indication, the starting left guard isn’t on the roster. Garret Wallow Wallow had three of the eight missed tackles on defense. He also allowed all five of his completions to be completed for 44 yards, including a long of 18 and an additional 17 after the catch. His role is far from easy, but we’re also seeing why he’s been a lifetime special-teamer. Football is fluid. Wallow opened the door for some of the linebackers to make the roster. Winners Nick Martin Turnovers are how you earn roles. Martin forced a fumble on a kickoff. While he missed a tackle himself, Martin made up for it with aggressive run fits and a pair of stops on his way to four tackles. He limited the damage in coverage. I’d argue one of his completions allowed should’ve never happened if Romello Height didn’t rush inside on play-action. Martin took a step forward, which is what you want to see. Jacob Cowing Welcome to the roster, Jake. After the game, Kyle Shanahan smirked when he was asked whether Cowing would be the punt returner and said, “Not yet, but I like that he’s making it easier.” Cowing’s 83-yard return sealed the deal on the competition. He had another big kickoff return that was negated. Cowing had enough speed to reverse field on two returns and beat the defense to the other side. There’s still some untapped potential as a wide receiver. His frame means the margin for error isn’t great, but Cowing could help with timing routes, screens, and vertical routes. Jack Jones The “boom” side of Jones surfaced on Thursday. He broke up both passes in his direction. He jumped a route on third down. Jones played with a level of confidence you need at the position. Ideally, Renardo Green is OK. But if he’s not, Jones looked like he could slide in without a drop-off. De’Zhaun Stribling Stribling played 70% of his snaps in the slot in Week 1. That dropped to 42% in Week 2. You could tell Stribling didn’t pick up the would-be touchdown pass from Mac Jones until the very last second. It ended up as a drop. He had another play where Stribling hesitated as a blocker, which resulted in a stuff from the defense. I think he could’ve picked up more yards after the catch on the slant he caught from Brock Purdy in hindsight Aside from that, Stribling had a clean outing. He won at every spot on different routes. Stribling caught both of his contested catches and also ran through a tackle after one catch. He’s as advertised. Deommodore Lenoir Lenoir didn’t get credit for any pass breakups, but he was in a perfect position on both of his targets. Lenoir was feisty, even on his non-targets. The quarterback had nowhere to go on either throw. Lenoir also had a run stop. If this version of Lenoir is the cornerback the Niners are getting in 2026, the defense can flirt with being a top-10 unit.
author: Kyle Posey

title: 3 stars from the 49ers’ preseason win: A cornerback emerges
summary: The San Francisco 49ers emphatically earned their first preseason win with a 41-17 (we can mention the final score this week since the 49ers won) thumping of the Los Angeles Chargers. It was a thorough beating from the 49ers, who dominated the Chargers in all three facets of the game. A win that will likely […]
full_text: Inglewood, CA - August 20, 2026: San Francisco 49ers cornerback Jack Jones (25) breaks up a pass in the end zone to Los Angeles Chargers wide receiver Keandre Lambert-Smith (84) at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, CA on Thursday, Aug. 20, 2026. (Robert Gauthier/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images) The San Francisco 49ers emphatically earned their first preseason win with a 41-17 (we can mention the final score this week since the 49ers won) thumping of the Los Angeles Chargers. It was a thorough beating from the 49ers, who dominated the Chargers in all three facets of the game. A win that will likely keep Jim Harbaugh up late on Thursday night, an attitude that 49ers fans are far too familiar with. But as upset as Harbaugh will be, Kyle Shanahan will be just as excited, as there wasn’t much to complain about – outside of that little left guard issue, which Austen Pleasants is apparently very involved in. But let’s focus on the positives. Three of them to be exact. Here are the three stars from Thursday’s preseason win: 3rd Star – CB Jack Jones Garret Wallow was in consideration for the honor, but Jones’s performance stood out just a smidge more. Jones is in an interesting spot because there are different scenarios that could play out over the next few weeks, with several resulting in Jones getting significant playing time come the regular season. He may have added a few more scenarios with his game on Thursday night. He finished with a pair of pass breakups, and both were timely. Facing a third-and-goal, a Jim Harbaugh offense opted for a fade route, with Trey Lance targeting KeAndre Lambert-Smith. Jones never got his body around, but Lance’s throw tracked short, and Jones’s positioning was perfect to prevent the score (while also getting away with some contact), forcing the Chargers to settle for a short field goal. Jones would follow up with his second pass breakup on the next drive. With the Chargers facing a second down, Lance looked to Devonte Ross, but Jones perfectly read the play and ran the route for Ross, nearly coming up with an interception but having to settle for the PBU. Two plays later, Los Angeles would turn the ball over on downs, giving the 49ers offense the ball near midfield. Raheem Morris should have plenty of options in what could be a versatile secondary, and Jones played like he’s planning to work his way into those plans. 2nd Star – WR De’Zhaun Stribling For a second week in a row, Stribling was the standout of the 49ers offense. Sure, some production was left on the table, but once again, Stribling passed the eye test. His game didn’t have the numbers on Thursday night as he did last week against Tennessee, catching just four passes on five targets for 46 yards, but there’s some reading between the lines that has to be done to fully define Stribling’s game. The most important development wasn’t Stribling’s play on the field but his rapport with Brock Purdy. Now, the 49ers were without Christian McCaffrey, George Kittle, and Mike Evans, so keep that in mind. But even with Deebo Samuel, a man who has seen plenty of targets from Purdy, Stribling was Purdy’s preferred target on his lone drive. Of Purdy’s six attempts on Thursday, three went to Stribling, and all three were caught, with two converting third downs (ato be the first to suggest the nickname “third-and-De’Zhaun definitelyDe’Zhaun”). Also, it’s the preseason, so we can just brush over that drop on a perfectly thrown pass from Mac Jones to deny us our first trip into the Strib Club. With Evans not practicing a ton, Stribling has stepped in to get those reps with Purdy. It’s just something to keep in mind with Evans and the rookie likely to share the field plenty over the regular season. 1st Star – WR Jacob Cowing It had to be. We watched in real-time a player earn a roster spot. Cowing felt like he was on the outside looking in with the traffic jam going at the receiver position. It felt like Cowing’s only chance to make the roster was by winning the punt returner job. He grabbed that brass ring against the Chargers. While Cowing has 28 more punt returns in his career, it was Deebo Samuel who got the first chance at punt return duties on Thursday. However, Samuel didn’t get a chance to showcase his return skills as he let his first chance bounce and then waved for a fair catch on his second. Kyle Shanahan decided that was enough for Samuel and gave Cowing his opportunity. He would then take that opportunity 83 yards for a touchdown, a play that should ensure Cowing’s spot on the 53-man roster. Had it been a regular season game, it would have been the first time since Ted Ginn was returning punts for the 49ers that they scored a touchdown via punt return. And nobody looked more excited for Cowing than Deebo, who might have just been showing some relief of one less responsibility on his plate. With Cowing’s struggle to find his spot with the 49ers since getting drafted in 2024, the return created one of the cooler preseason moments in recent memory.

title: Would you cut electric Robert Henry or physical Kaytron Allen?
summary: The hardest decisions belong to the best rosters A deep roster complicates the final roster cutdown to 53 players. In the early stages of a franchise rebuild, roster cuts are straightforward because the talent drop-off past the top 35 players is steep. However, when depth increases across the board, NFL front offices are forced to […]
full_text: The h ardest decisions belong to the best rosters A deep roster complicates the final roster cutdown to 53 players. In the early stages of a franchise rebuild, roster cuts are straightforward because the talent drop-off past the top 35 players is steep. However, when depth increases across the board, NFL front offices are forced to expose genuinely talented players to waivers. This dilemma is evident in the offensive backfield of the 2026 Commanders. Historically, most NFL teams carry either three or four running backs on their initial 53-man roster, depending in part on special teams value. Under general manager Adam Peters and head coach Dan Quinn, the Washington Commanders have aligned with this standard. In 2024 , the Commanders kept four running backs on the initial roster. In 2025 , the team did the same, starting out with Austin Ekeler, Jeremy McNichols, Jacory Croskey-Merritt, and Chris Rodriguez Jr. However, when Ekeler was lost for the season in Week 2, he was not replaced on the roster and the team went through most of the season with just three running backs. Entering the final weeks of the 2026 preseason, locking onto a hard cap of four running backs would have a direct, cascading effect on the rest of the offense. If Washington keeps a fourth running back, they cannot expand depth at other positions. For instance, carrying an extra back means deciding whether to risk a developmental sixth or seventh wide receiver on waivers, or to squeeze the tight-end room down to a strict trio. In effect, the decision to keep a player at one position represents a sacrificed depth piece at another like quarterback, receiver, or tight end. The Commanders may want to keep three QBs, seven WRs, four TEs and four RBs, but the math simply won’t work out, and that means that some NFL-quality skill players are going to find themselves missing out on the Commanders 53-man roster in 2026. In this week’s Reacts survey, we asked Hogs Haven readers to focus on the running back position and decide, based on the information available to date, which of the team’s top four running backs would miss out if Adam Peters and Dan Quinn chose to keep only three on the initial roster. The Power of Pedigree: draft capital vs. the undrafted tag Roster battles are often talked about as if they take place in a strict meritocracy, but, in reality, draft pedigree heavily influences both front-office security and fan perception. Bill Croskey-Merritt enters 2026 with a year of NFL experience under his belt after being selected in the seventh round. Rookie Kaytron “Fatman” Allen carries the shield of a sixth-round draft choice. Rookie Robert Henry Jr. faces the steeper climb of an undrafted college free agent. The recent Hogs Haven poll, which asked readers to choose one back to leave off the roster, reflects this reality: Visit our partners at FanDuel Henry, the UDFA rookie , at 60%, is the popular choice to miss out on a 3-man running back room, while Allen, drafted in the sixth-round back in April, would be the choice of 26% of survey respondents. This disparity may highlight a clear psychological bias toward draft investment, or it may reflect the relative skills and play style of the members of the running back room. The first preseason game vs the Miami Dolphins Both rookies had excellent NFL debuts last Friday night in Landover : Kaytron Allen handled a heavy workload, rushing 23 times for 85 yards and a touchdown. It was a productive but grinding debut that averaged a modest 3.7 yards per carry. Robert Henry Jr. had 12 carries for 75 yards and a touchdown, and delivered the game’s signature play, exploding past the defense for a 22-yard rushing touchdown. Despite Henry having been the rookie back who generated the most excitement and greatest efficiency against Miami, it is he, Henry, and not Allen whom most survey respondents would leave off the roster. Draft pedigree Consider a hypothetical scenario where these two players’ draft pedigrees were perfectly reversed—Henry selected in the sixth round and Allen signed as an undrafted free agent. It feels like fan expectations entering the offseason and training camp might well have been reversed, and that the Reacts poll results might have been quite different based on last week’s preseason production against the Miami Dolphins. Had Henry carried the sixth-round label, his explosive touchdown run would likely have been heralded as proof of a draft-day steal, and his spot on the 53-man roster might well be considered secure. Conversely, if Allen were undrafted, his 23-carry workload could have been viewed as the team simply burning camp reps on a disposable asset, with his 3.7 yards per carry being seen as the unsurprising pedestrian output of an undrafted player. We know that fans and evaluators instinctively give drafted players a longer leash, viewing their struggles as temporary adjustment periods while assuming undrafted players have a lower absolute ceiling. The ‘style’ argument While draft status undoubtedly influences fan perception, a more strategic explanation for these poll results lies in rational understanding of structural roster construction and stylistic synergy. Knowledgeable fans, as we know, look beyond raw efficiency metrics to evaluate how a player’s skill set complements the existing depth chart. The Commanders backfield is anchored by Rachaad White and Bill Croskey-Merritt, both of whom excel as explosive, one-cut slashers tailored for outside-zone concepts. Henry Jr.’s dynamic 22-yard touchdown run showcased that exact same explosive, perimeter-oriented profile. Voting to keep Henry in a three-man running back room would give Washington a trio of outside runners, creating a highly redundant skill set in the position group. While explosive, this would leave a massive hole in the skill set of the position for Washington. “Fatman” Allen offers a distinctly different, complementary identity. Despite his lower yards-per-carry average against Miami, Allen’s physical, low-center-of-gravity style is built for running between the tackles and grinding out tough yards against stacked boxes – something that every NFL team needs. With the majority of Hogs Haven readers voting to keep Allen over Henry, they demonstrated a rational understanding of role optimization. They recognize that Allen provides the essential short-yardage and goal-line versatility that the roster would otherwise lack, making him a more logical puzzle piece for the final 53 than his redundant, albeit electric, counterpart. The Mason-Brennan paradox The survey results with respect to Robert Henry Jr. present a stark contrast – a paradox if you will — in fan sentiment. In a separate Hogs Haven survey exploring which young player generated the most “hype” following the Dolphins game, Henry dominated the field with 68% of the total vote. The contrast between these two surveys illustrates the difference between rewarding an exciting moment and constructing a viable 53-man roster. A 22-yard touchdown run is a highly visible, electric highlight that generates organic fan excitement. It provides immediate optimism for a fan base looking for hidden gems. However, when forced to make tough roster decisions, those same knowledgeable fans recognize the baseline floor required for the regular season. They understand that a complete NFL running back must reliably pass-protect, contribute on special teams, and sustain tough yardage down to down. While 68% of fans enjoy the flashes of talent Henry brings to the field, 60% logically conclude that Allen is the better fit for the Commanders running back room. If the Commanders keep four running backs on the initial roster, chances are high that both rookies make the team and contribute to the ’26 season. On the other hand, if the demands of roster construction constrain the number of running backs to just 3 to open the season, a tough choice will need to be made, and Hogs Haven readers see Allen as the right choice…

title: Commanders preseason: Frankie Luvu among players to watch vs. Lions
summary: The Commanders will play their second preseason game on Saturday in Detroit. If there was ever a time to get frontline players some game reps, this is it.   Generally speaking, it didn’t happen in the preseason opener versus Miami.   That third exhibition game’s a bit too close to the regular season to create […]
full_text: The Commanders will play their second preseason game on Saturday in Detroit. If there was ever a time to get frontline players some game reps, this is it. Generally speaking, it didn’t happen in the preseason opener versus Miami. That third exhibition game’s a bit too close to the regular season to create injury risk. Plus, that game in Baltimore comes right after a joint practice. Starters will get work there and then look towards games that count. That leaves Saturday as the best (and likely last opportunity) to play some real football during the summer. Will that happen? Yes. Head coach Dan Quinn admitted as much before Thursday’s practice. Who will play, and how much? Quinn wasn’t ready to reveal that. “A good amount of starters will get some playing time,” Quinn said during that Thursday press conference . “I’ll finalize that list tonight, after practice, once I get the overall health of all the positions where we’re at, but a lot of the guys who sat out for Miami will get an opportunity to get some work in for this week, all obviously different amounts.” Quinn has been getting asked about quarterback Jayden Daniels’ availability all week. Washington simply can’t afford him hurt in the preseason. Quinn said he’ll evaluate the health of those around Daniels before making that call. If he plays, Daniels is obviously the most important player to watch in Saturday’s game. Since that’s up in the air, you won’t see him discussed in the list below, despite the fact we’re hedging bets on some of them. If news breaks that Daniels will play, you’ll see a whole story about it. For right now, let’s discuss these other 10 players (assuming they go) to watch on Saturday against the Lions. LB Frankie Luvu Frankie Luvu has received rave reviews for his leadership and on-field tenacity during training camp. The veteran’s often running the show during practice, making it seem possible, if not likely, that he plays alongside Sonny Styles on the interior. While it’s not absolutely certain, it’s likely that Luvu plays in this contest. Finding old form after a down year in 2025 will be key for him and the Commanders defense overall. If Luvu’s successfully playing his aggressive brand of football, Washington will be way better for it. DL Javon Kinlaw With Tim Settle dealing with a calf strain and Daron Payne a bit banged up, it’s likely Javon Kinlaw’s the only frontline defensive lineman available for this contest. The former first-round pick is built out of granite right now and is pumped about his role in Daronte Jones’ defense. He has all the talent to be a disruptive force up front, even if his body of work hasn’t lived up to his lofty draft status. Interior pressure is so key in this scheme (and every other). Kinlaw can provide that. This will be a solid scouting report of his progress and fit within the system. DB Jeremy Reaves Quan Martin played a decent amount in the preseason opener, in tandem with Will Harris, and fared well in that contest. He had an interception and made solid plays during his time in the game, boosting his status in a battle for free safety spot. Reaves is the other combatant. The veteran and core special teams player is battling for a larger defensive role in 2026 and will get his chance to shine on Saturday. Quinn said the safeties who didn’t play versus Miami should play the Lions. Seeing Reaves and every-down player Nick Cross work together will be key, as will Reaves’ performance playing deep. WR Stefon Diggs He’s buried in this list of players to watch because it’s truly uncertain whether Stefon Diggs plays. Health is more important than preseason snaps for an established veteran who knows how to get open, but…If Daniels plays, I’d bet Diggs plays. If JD5 doesn’t play, hard to see Diggs suiting up. (As an aside, I think the same goes for Terry McLaurin and Chig Okonkwo). Fans surely want to see Diggs perform, even if it’s a cameo, for a little taste of his expert play. Diggs took an instant leadership role in Washington, and getting some game reps in could energize the offense and the fan base. LT Brandon Coleman Brandon Coleman played 12 snaps at left tackle in the preseason opener, so it’s a safe bet Laremy Tunsil’s replacement will play a bit more Saturday as he prepares for a massive season in his NFL career. This rep from Brandon Coleman in the Commanders preseason opener against the Dolphins was so good, @nick_akridge and I had to spend 5 mins breaking it down pic.twitter.com/BZmBB4ovVN — Mark Bullock (@MarkBullockNFL) August 18, 2026 Coleman had a solid game, by all accounts, flashing athleticism and steadiness you want from a blindside protector. Can he do it again? Doing so would increase confidence that the Commanders made the right choice not going outside the organization to fill the void left by Laremy Tunsil’s injury. LB Sonny Styles Sonny Styles was honest about his preseason debut versus Miami. He “wasn’t a fan of it.” While this year’s No. 7 overall draft pick played but one series, he surely could’ve done better. It didn’t raise any red flags, however, considering his exemplary training camp performance. Styles should play a little longer at least, to find a flow he wasn’t around long enough to establish in the first exhibition. CB Amik Robertson I’m betting we see all prominent members of the cornerback corps in this game, at least for a little while. Amik Robertson has been the veteran leader to this point and provides energy with the way he plays and how he speaks to the group. Robertson’s an accomplished slot cornerback, but there’s also a need on the outside with Trey Amos still banged up . Keep a close eye on how the cornerbacks operate and where the line up, especially if they’re all working together. WR Antonio Williams Antonio Williams didn’t enter the Miami game until the second half, which was somewhat surprising to have several others in line to play before him. The third-round pick remains an important piece of the passing game expected to have a big role during the regular season, but competition’s tight with Diggs in camp, and Williams is battling veterans for playing time and targets. This is a moment where he’ll need to assert himself some and show he’s ready for work as the No. 3 receiver. C/G Matt Gulbin The Commanders will work without starting center Nick Allegretti, who suffered a setback with his calf strain. That leaves more work for Matt Gulbin, a sixth-round rookie who looked good in his preseason debut as a center and blocked well in open space. Julian Good-Jones has been the first option with Allegretti out. Will Gulbin get a shot at first-team work and a shot to supplant Good-Jones on the depth chart? Quinn also mentioned Gulbin playing guard to expand his reach as a reserve interior lineman. If he plays there Saturday, how does he look? The Michigan State product has a chance to shine in this spot and build on last week’s positive momentum. DT Byron Cowart Byron Cowart hasn’t been with Washington long, but the training-camp signing has already asserted himself and been praised by Quinn for his work versus Miami. That comes into play regarding a possible 53-man roster spot after Johnny Newton was lost with a torn pectoral muscle that required surgery. Cowart will battle Ricky Barber for it, but there’s an opening along the defensive-line rotation that wasn’t there before. The veteran must continue performing well to make his case to stick around after final cuts.
