Commanders links Articles ESPN Commanders till need to see their run game evolve All offseason, the two words heard most from those who know Daniels well were these: “Locked in.” The result has been a standout camp. He impressed Miami’s coaches in the joint practice, both during one-on-one drills and in full-team work, with his accuracy. It helps that Daniels has a full complement of receivers, unlike last summer, when Terry McLaurin was holding in. Another wideout expected to help, Noah Brown, was injured most of camp. The result: an offense that lacked any rhythm. Daniels’ season was then derailed by multiple injuries, limiting him to four full games. But the question will be whether the Commanders can generate a consistent run game. Against Miami in the joint practice, they were more effective throwing the ball. In the preseason opener, rookie running backs Kaytron Allen and Robert Henry Jr. combined for 160 yards rushing and two touchdowns. But Washington managed just 10 yards in four carries by Allen in the first quarter. Sometimes it was the block; other times it was the run. Regardless, Washington needs this area to develop. Quinn said the run game on both sides of the ball is not yet where it needs to be. But he’s not surprised it’s taking longer on offense. “That’s to be expected,” he said. “But we’re making progress. The combinations, the speed off the ball, we’re not where we will be, but I would say in terms of the targeting of where we’re going to, who’s blocking who, we’re making progress.” To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Sports Illustrated Commanders Injury Report: 15 Players Dealing With Injuries Ahead of Lions Game Rachaad White joined Washington’s growing injury list Thursday, while Dan Quinn also provided updates on Trey Amos, Nick Allegretti, and Johnny Newton [This was published prior to report of Daron Payne suffering a minor injury on Thursday] To read more of this article, CLICK HERE The Athletic (paywall) Washington Commanders camp observations: Injury list grows, the plan for Detroit and more As of Friday morning, at least 15 Commanders are confirmed to be recovering from or still working their way back from injuries. (Teams are not required to report injuries until Week 1 of the regular season.) The majority of Washington’s injuries aren’t believed to be long-term issues. Coach Dan Quinn expressed optimism earlier this week that Mariota will be available for Week 1. Payne’s injury, which was not disclosed, is believed to be minor. But as the list grows, concern follows. The disappointing [2025 season] prompted the Commanders to overhaul many aspects of their operations and personnel, but it also shaped Quinn’s approach this year. Even during the offseason program, he tried to give players with the least experience more reps so he could get a better sense of the team’s depth and just how much the backups could handle. The plan for Detroit Quinn said “a good amount of starters will get some playing time” on Saturday in Detroit. He declined to say who or how much, but noted that many of the 26 players who sat out the preseason opener against Miami will get more looks this weekend. Whether that includes quarterback Jayden Daniels remains to be seen. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Sports Illustrated 3 Overreactions From Day 14 of Commanders Training Camp Overreaction No. 2 — Washington Is Back to Square One at Center For clarity, Allegretti returned to practice this week only to experience more calf tightness and get pulled. After seeing Good-Jones against Miami’s defensive line , we can all agree it is not a good idea for him to take the field against the Philadelphia Eagles and those monsters on the interior they have in Jalen Carter and Jordan Davis. This discussion is no longer about whether Allegretti can play the position; it’s about whether he has taken enough practice reps to make the calls and build chemistry with the offensive line. One thing to remember: this isn’t the same type of shutdown that Allegretti got at the beginning of camp . This came with clean imaging of his calf and a word from the coach that they plan on reevaluating the situation Sunday. This overreaction carries a bit more truth value: Washington absolutely needs Good-Jones or another option ready to function as a legitimate Plan B because Allegretti hasn’t been available consistently enough to assume everything will suddenly stabilize. Washington is not back to square one yet, but the center position remains unresolved until Allegretti can stack practices instead of simply returning for one at a time. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE From Commanders Roundtable: Matt Gulbin stuck out in his first unofficial NFL appearance where he gets a chance to potentially build on that after Dan Quinn confirmed the rookie will draw snaps at guard to evaluate his positional versatility along the interior offensive line. Julian Good-Jones, meanwhile, has drawn the bulk of snaps in Allegretti’s absence while the team added a pair of depth pieces in camp after inking Daniel Brunskill and Trey Hill. The question isn’t about depth anymore — it’s at the top of the room. While head coach Dan Quinn and players have raved about the IQ and leadership of Allegretti, becoming an impact NFL center over a 17 game span is a question mark. And after suffering a pair of injuries before playing in any game action, whether Allegretti can last the full season is a growing question. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Commanders.com Training camp notebook | ‘A good amount’ of Commanders starters will play vs. Lions There has been significant speculation on whether the Commanders will play their starters against the Lions, and Quinn did provide an answer. He said that “a good amount of starters” will get some playing time, although who will play and how much is still being determined by the staff. Jayden Daniels is one of the players Quinn is unsure about, saying that he will make a decision once he knows about the health of everyone else around him. On the decision about who will play in the preseason, Quinn said it will be determined on a player-by-player basis rather than an entire group in terms of which positions could benefit more from getting action against the Lions. While he said he’s interested in seeing positions like the receivers and cornerbacks, he wants to see what certain players do with the opportunity to get more snaps in a game scenario. There has been some debate on how much time the Commanders’ players should get in the preseason and whether their workload is worth the risk of injury. There is certainly value to it; not only do the Commanders have a new scheme on both sides of the ball, they also need to go through the act of tackling, running plays and other routine actions in a game. Quinn would like to get his players as many snaps as possible, but he and the team like to customize according to each player’s needs as much as possible. The most important angle they consider is whether the amount of work each player gets is the most beneficial to their development. title: Washington Commanders 91-man 2026 preseason Game 2 roster/depth chart
summary: Reviewing the roster limit As you are probably aware, the NFL CBA allows each team to have 90 players on its offseason roster, but it also makes provisions for a 91st player who joins the team via the International Player Pathway (IPP) program. For the last several years, the Commanders have made use of this […]
full_text: Reviewing the roster limit As you are probably aware, the NFL CBA allows each team to have 90 players on its offseason roster, but it also makes provisions for a 91st player who joins the team via the International Player Pathway (IPP) program. For the last several years, the Commanders have made use of this IPP exemption, as they have again this season, so Washington’s offseason roster limit is once again 91 players. Washington’s 91st player via the IPP is currently edge rusher TJ Maguranyanga , who spent the 2025 season on the Commanders roster. Surprising number of roster changes since the Dolphins game In the four days that followed the Dolphins game, the Commanders announced eight roster moves. Released/waived (2) K Jake Moody Most people were surprised, not by the result, but by the timing of the end of Washington’s kicker competition. After the release of Jake Moody, undrafted rookie place kicker Drew Stevens was declared the winner of the roster spot that the two had been competing for since OTAs. Now, Stevens will have two preseason games to build his confidence and cement his spot as the permanent kicker on a team that has signed 20 guys to the role in the past 25 seasons. P Matt Haack Another non-surprise came when the team released punter Matt Haack , who had been signed to punt during camp while Tress Way recovered from a pectoral injury he sustained during a “flex off” with former Redskins player and now-Hollywood actor Terry Crews . Injured Reserve (2) When a player is placed on injured reserve during training camp, he is ineligible to return to play for the team that season, though he can be waived with an injury settlement and play for another team when healthy. RB Jerome Ford was put on IR with a hamstring injury. WR River Cracraft was put on IR with an unspecified injury. Outside of the regular season and playoffs, NFL teams are not required to provide details about player health or injuries, though details will likely be reported by local media eventually. Both players were long shots to earn a roster spot in their respective crowded position groups, and with the move to IR, neither will don the burgundy & gold again in the 2026 season. Signed (4) RB Craig Reynolds With Jerome Ford headed to IR and Jeremy McNichols out for “weeks” according to Dan Quinn, the team needed depth at the running back position. Craig Reynolds entered the NFL initially as an undrafted player with the Washington Redskins in 2019. More relevant to his recent signing, however, is the five years he spent with the Detroit Lions, where he was teammates in 2021 and 2023 with the Commanders current offensive coordinator David Blough. TE Tre’ McKitty Tre’ McKitty recently won the UFL championship with the Louisville Kings. His performance over the spring season—including two crucial catches in the UFL championship game—reignited NFL interest and earned him a successful workout with Washington. McKitty was a highly touted third-round pick by the Los Angeles Chargers in 2021, and Washington is providing a “now or never” opportunity to see if his raw athletic traits can finally be unlocked at the NFL level. DT Maurice Hurst II Defensive lineman Johnny Newton will miss several months after having surgery to repair a torn pectoral muscle . Maurice Hurst II was signed to step directly into defensive rotations and absorb reps during padded and non-padded practices and the remaining preseason schedule. Hurst brings 65 games of NFL experience across his stints with the Raiders, 49ers, and Browns. Over the last three seasons in Cleveland, he proved to be an efficient rotational piece when healthy, accounting for 39 tackles, two sacks, and an interception. LB Krys Barnes Linebacker Jordan Magee has been dealing with a shoulder injury following the Dolphins game. Ale Kaho also got banged up against Miami but seems to be okay. Either way, the Commanders needed a reliable, healthy body to step into the second-team defensive rotations immediately. Unlike many late-preseason additions who are unproven, Barnes brings 75 games of NFL experience and 33 career starts across his time with the Packers, Cardinals, and Panthers. Having a veteran who has recorded multiple 80-plus tackle seasons ensures a higher floor for the defense if injuries linger. Accounting for Laremy Tunsil & Johnny Newton While Friday’s chart lists 91 players, we know already that two of those players, LT Laremy Tunsil and DL Johnny Newton , will not be on the active roster in Week 1. Timing counts for a lot with players who suffer major injuries in training camp. Here’s a quick explanation of the considerations for placing a player on IR under the relevant NFL rules: 1. The Pre-Cutdown Rule (Season-Ending) As mentioned above, if the Commanders place Tunsil or Newton on IR during training camp before the final 53-man roster reduction deadline on Aug. 30, the player is automatically ruled out for the entire season . He would not be allowed to practice or play for Washington at any point during the year. While Tunsil and Newton have already undergone surgery, head coach Dan Quinn said that doctors have not yet determined the recovery timeline for either player. If doctors determine, in the coming days, that Tunsil and/or Newton will not be able to return to play prior to mid-February, then the Commanders might choose to exercise this option. 2. The Cutdown Day Exception (Designated to Return) NFL rules allow teams: a. to designate, on cutdown day (Aug. 30), up to two injured players to return from IR during the season b. alternatively, the team can carry a player onto the initial 53-man roster and move him to IR the following day (Aug. 31st) opening up a roster spot; the only reason to do this would be if the team needed to designate two other players to return at the time the initial roster was set on Aug. 30. (Option A is almost certainly the one that the Commanders would choose in Tunsil’s case, probably Newton as well) This approach (either option a or b) allows the player (Tunsil/Newton/both) to keep his season alive since it leaves the door open for him to return after sitting out a minimum of four games (obviously, in these two cases, it would be closer to four months than four games). If doctors determine that the player’s (Tunsil’s/Newton’s/both) return to play could happen prior to mid-February, then the Commanders might choose this option to keep all possibilities on the table. The only cost to the team is the opportunity to carry one or two more players on the training camp roster between now and Aug. 30. Not your typical depth chart The chart below is only a depth chart insofar as it assigns players to positions and stacks them in an order. The primary purpose of the chart is to keep track of the 91 guys that currently comprise the training camp roster, not to predict game-day alignments. You will note, for example, that I have 12 offensive position stacks and 13 defensive position stacks on the chart despite the fact that a team can only field 11 players at one time. You will also note that each player’s name appears only once regardless of the fact that he may play in multiple alignments or positions ( e.g., an interior offensive lineman who can play center and both guard spots will appear at only one of those positions, not all of them ). Again, this is by design, since the goal is to provide handy visual reference of the 91 individual players while also offering an overall snapshot of team strength and depth. The bias, though, is to provide a visual list of the full roster, not so much to create a game-ready depth chart. Finally, you will also note that, where players are capable of playing more than one position (and likely to do so on game days), my decision on where to align them may be very different from your idea of where they belong. title: 2026 NFL season: Ranking the best, worst positional groups
summary: Which team has the best running backs? The shakiest edge rusher room? We ranked all 32 teams in 10 different position groups.
full_text:
When analyzing NFL rosters , it's important to keep relativity in mind. It's easy to say a team is in "good shape" or "loaded" at a particular position, but each unit is only as good as it is relative to the league's 31 other teams.

 That might seem like common sense, but you would be surprised by what you can learn sitting down and objectively grading and/or ranking each positional unit of all 32 teams. This is a project I've done each offseason, which has led to many interesting revelations, including the likely breakouts of teams such as the 2020 Buccaneers , 2022 Eagles and  2023 Dolphins .

 Here are position-by-position unit rankings for all 32 teams this season  covering the 10 key offensive and defensive groups. At the bottom, I've included an overall ranking weighted based on positional importance (for example, it's more crucial to be elite at quarterback than at running back). I also gave brief outlooks on the best and shakiest units at each position, as well as intriguing groups worth keeping an eye on. Note that these are 2026 rankings rather than long-term outlooks.

 Let's take a look, starting at quarterback.

 

 
 Jump to: 
 QB | RB | WR | TE | OL 
 DT | Edge  | LB | CB | S 
 Overall outlook 

 
 

 Quarterback 
 

 

 Best: Buffalo Bills 
 After having Baltimore's  Lamar Jackson  in this spot last year , I'm giving the edge to 2024 NFL MVP Josh Allen  this time around. Allen has finished no lower than seventh in QBR in each of the past six seasons (third or better in four of them). He remains a major factor with his legs, leading all QBs in carries, rushing yards and rushing TDs last season. Incredibly, only running back  Derrick Henry (44) has more rushing TDs than Allen (41) over the past three seasons.

 

 Shakiest: Arizona Cardinals 
 Kyler Murray is gone, leaving Jacoby Brissett as the probable Week 1 starter. Brissett racked up strong counting stats in 12 starts last season (3,366 passing yards, 23 TDs), but Arizona throwing at a league-high rate (partially due to always being behind) was a primary factor. Brissett finished 24th among 28 qualified quarterbacks in QBR (41.2). Gardner Minshew II and third-round rookie Carson Beck could also get some run if Brissett struggles.

 

 Unit to watch: Atlanta Falcons 
 Outside of Cleveland, the only QB battle around is between  Michael Penix Jr . and Tua Tagovailoa . The No. 8 overall pick in 2024, Penix has yet to emerge as a capable starter. He has totaled 14 touchdown passes in 14 games, and he had a league-low 23.1% off-target rate before his ACL tear in Week 11 of last season. Meanwhile, Tagovailoa has flashed at times during his career, but Miami took on a record $99.2 million in dead money to move on from him after a disappointing 2025 season.

 

 
 Running back 
 

 

 Best: Indianapolis Colts 
 Close one here, but  Jonathan Taylor gets the nod. He's one of the league's best backs and handles a massive bulk of the team's touches. Taylor had a terrific 2025 campaign in which he led the NFL in carries (323) and touchdowns (18), while also finishing third in rushing yardage (1,585). Once a minimal part of the Colts' passing game, Taylor also ranked the top-10 among backs in routes, targets, catches and receiving yards, setting career highs in each. This all happened despite a big dip in production after quarterback Daniel Jones  was  injured in Week 14.

 

 Shakiest: Jacksonville Jaguars 
 There's upside here, but this group is unproven. With Travis Etienne Jr . gone, 2025 Day 2 picks Bhayshul Tuten and LeQuint Allen Jr . will team up with journeyman Chris Rodriguez Jr . to form a three-headed committee. Tuten made some highlight plays as a rookie, but he was limited to 83 carries and 14 targets. Rodriguez has been effective as a rusher (career 4.6 yards per carry), but the sample is small (198 carries) and he's not a receiving option (six career catches). Expect Allen (23 carries, 11 targets as a rookie) to see occasional work in passing situations.

 

 Unit to watch: Seattle Seahawks 
 Super Bowl MVP Kenneth Walker III signed with the Chiefs and Zach Charbonnet tore his ACL in January, leaving Seattle's backfield with a much different look in 2026. Rookie Jadarian Price  -- the final pick of the first round -- could emerge as a breakout, but he's obviously an unknown and has minimal experience as a pass catcher. Holdover George Holani and journeyman Emanuel Wilson will battle for reps until Charbonnet makes his return.

 

 
 Wide receiver 
 

 

 Best: Cincinnati Bengals 
 There were a few strong candidates here, but none can match Cincinnati's duo of  Ja'Marr Chase  and  Tee Higgins . In 2024, Chase became the first player in league history to reach 1,700 receiving yards and 17 TD catches in a single season. Last season, he became the third receiver to produce 120-plus catches and 1,400-plus yards in multiple campaigns. Higgins is arguably the league's best WR2, and he has the fourth-most TD catches in the league over the past two seasons (21).  Andrei Iosivas is a capable No. 3 option; fourth-round rookie Colbie Young is already making a play for a Year 1 role.

 

 Shakiest: Miami Dolphins 
 The Tyreek Hill / Jaylen Waddle era is over in Miami, leaving the rebuilding Dolphins with a major short-term hole at the position. I say "short term" because they invested 2026 draft resources into the position:  Chris Bell (Round 3), Caleb Douglas (Round 3) and Kevin Coleman Jr . (Round 5). But it's hard to project the Year 1 impact for these rookies, especially since Bell is returning from a torn ACL . The likes of Malik Washington and newcomers Tutu Atwell and Jalen Tolbert are best suited for situational/depth roles, but they could be the Dolphins' starting trio most of this season.

 

 Unit to watch: Tennessee Titans 
 The Titans invested heavily at the position during the offseason, signing Wan'Dale Robinson (one of four receivers with 90-plus catches in each of the past two seasons) to a four-year, $70 million deal and selecting Carnell Tate with the No. 4 pick in April. That duo will team up with veteran Calvin Ridley  in the starting lineup, second-year players Chimere Dike and Elic Ayomanor should add solid depth.

 

 
 Tight end 
 

 

 Best: Las Vegas Raiders 
 An injury-riddled 2025 campaign is not enough for us to overlook superstar Brock Bowers . The 2024 first-round pick began his career with an elite stat line of 112 receptions, 1,194 receiving yards and five touchdowns. He remained dominant despite missing five games in 2025, posting 64 receptions, 680 receiving yards and seven touchdowns -- all three of which ranked top 10 at the position. The 23-year-old is a strong bet for a big bounce-back with Kirk Cousins and/or Fernando Mendoza under center in 2026. Michael Mayer and former Carolina starter Ian Thomas add terrific depth.

 

 Shakiest: Miami Dolphins 
 Greg Dulcich was solid for this team down the stretch last season, but the reality is that he's a 26-year-old journeyman with 67 career receptions who would be a depth piece on most rosters. Instead, he'll work as the Dolphins' top receiving option at the position. Rookies  Will Kacmarek (Round 3) and  Seydou Traore (Round 5), as well as fourth-year veteran  Ben Sims , will be in the mix for snaps.

 

 Unit to watch: Los Angeles Rams 
 Coach Sean McVay has pivoted his scheme to rely heavily on the tight end position, so it's no surprise that the team used its past two second-round picks at the position ( Terrance Ferguson in 2025 and Ohio State's  Max Klare in 2026). Tyler Higbee is back for his age-33 campaign, while veterans Colby Parkinson and Davis Allen will also get run. Don't be surprised if Ferguson finishes third on the team in catches this season.

 

 
 Offensive line 
 

 

 Best: Denver Broncos 
 This was an easy call after the Broncos led the NFL in both pass block and run block win rate in 2024 prior to finishing top-eight in both categories last season. Incredibly, Denver will have the…

title: MHJ is all smiles so far through Cardinals preseason
summary: Harrison has played well in August and hopes his first 1,000-yard receiving season is right around the corner.
full_text:
TEMPE, Ariz. -- A couple of weeks ago,  Arizona Cardinals  receiver Michael Wilson noticed something different in his teammate and fellow receiver Marvin Harrison Jr .

 He was smiling more.

 Wilson said it's not that Harrison has been happier, adding that Harrison is just a happy person. It's that he's showing it more.

 "Whether he's caught five balls or no balls or one ball in practice, he's smiling," Wilson said.

 "So, it's just good to see Marv smiling a lot because when his energy is right and his attitude is right ... I'm going to keep saying it: He's one of the best receivers in the NFL from a talent perspective. And, so, it's good to see him smiling and having fun playing football.

 "Because, at the end of the day, football is a fun sport and we've all been playing. I've been playing since I was 8 years old. And the reason why I still love to play because it's fun. At the end of the day, it's fun."

 Whether having more fun will turn into Harrison's first 1,000-yard season of his young career or even the best season he has had since getting drafted fourth in 2024 is yet to be seen. Harrison said this week that he feels pretty good after suffering injuries to his feet that hampered him last season.

 But it's not how Harrison has started this training camp, but how he has finished. And it has put a chip on Harrison's shoulder.

 A couple of drops early in camp went viral, leading to the typical backlash that frequents social media. Harrison saw it, and he understands it.

 "It's easy to look at the results," he said. "I know whether if I don't make a play that someone thinks I should have made, they're going to post it, and it's going to do what it's going to do in the social media era. And that's OK.

 "For me, it's just I'm worried about my process, know what I do each and every single day to prepare myself for practice, prepare myself for games on Sunday. And what the result's going to be, the result's going to be. But I know Monday through Saturday, I'm going to do the best I can to make sure I put my best foot forward."

 Since those drops, Harrison has been consistent through practice and his one preseason action this year against the Raiders last week. He caught a touchdown pass on what he called an "impressive" and "crazy throw" from quarterback Jacoby Brissett that resulted in a "distraction drill catch for me."

 It was part of what Harrison described as a "good camp" for him.

 "I made a lot of plays, explosive plays," he said. "I feel like I've definitely, as far as the run game, been more involved in the run game. I feel like we've had a great camp. I think not only myself, just as an offense. It's been fun out there, and I had a lot of fun in the offense, but I would say I had a pretty good camp so far."

 As camp progressed, Brissett saw Harrison be patient with his progress.

 "I think he's taken tremendous steps as far as understanding this is a long process," Brissett said. "The end result is not going to be tomorrow. And that's a battle. That's a battle for him, me, everybody on the team. The hard part is you want the results now. You want to go out there and do everything the right way. But that's why we're in the room that we're in, and we have the opportunity to go out there and play in a National Football League because we know we can.

 "It's just a matter of now we got to sustain that competitive edge on a day-in-and-day-out process."

 New coach Mike LaFleur has seen "steady improvement" out of Harrison throughout camp but wasn't concerned about the drops. If they continue during the regular season, that might change, but for camp, LaFleur was more worried about why they happened and how Harrison corrected it.

 The two have developed a quick rapport and need just a hand signal for LaFleur to communicate to Harrison, especially about get-off. LaFleur flashes it when he wants to see Harrison have more body length off the line.

 "Because once he gets going, he's a big dude, right?" LaFleur said of the 6-3, 220-pound receiver. "And if I'm a DB standing there knowing I got a big dude that could run by me or can stop on a dime, that's tough. If we're upright out of our stance, well, you've already lost yardage right there."

 To do that on every play comes down to having the right mentality, Harrison said. But LaFleur has already helped Harrison with his get-off.

 "Especially for me, just kind of where my routes usually are deeper down the field," Harrison said. "Obviously, those first 5 to 10 yards is making everything look full speed. He definitely helped me in those routes."

 LaFleur is a bit concerned that Harrison might be getting bored in meetings because football makes sense to him on a level it doesn't to most other players, partly a product of being raised by a Hall of Famer wide receiver. LaFleur described Harrison as "super intelligent, super smart" and is someone with whom the coaches enjoy working, LaFleur added.

 LaFleur doesn't have a reference point to say whether Harrison is happier or smiling more, but he has seen a steadiness from Harrison every day. That's just Harrison trying to be himself, trying to be positive every day, the receiver said. With that comes trying to be a good example for his teammates, especially the younger ones.

 Harrison is not consciously smiling more or trying to come across as happier. It's just happening.

 "It's just something," Harrison said, "I'm just being myself."

title: As season opener nears, Falcons still don't have a QB1
summary: Michael Penix Jr. hasn't been cleared to fully practice, and Tua Tagovailoa has struggled. Not ideal for Atlanta.
full_text:
Tua Tagovailoa will not start at quarterback Saturday in the  Atlanta Falcons ' second preseason game; that much we know about the team's quarterback hierarchy. And that's about it with just over three weeks from the Falcons' opener at Pittsburgh on Sept. 13.

 When will Michael Penix Jr . (knee) be allowed by doctors to practice fully? Unclear.

 What does Tagovailoa have to show coach Kevin Stefanski to win the job? Uncertain.

 When will Stefanski decide on the Week 1 starter against the Steelers ? Unsure.

 The Falcons play a preseason game at the Indianapolis Colts on Saturday afternoon. Undrafted rookie Jack Strand and veteran Cooper Rush will get all the snaps at quarterback. Tagovailoa did his work in Indy already, participating in 11-on-11 team sessions in joint practices Wednesday and Thursday. Penix, as he has done in Flowery Branch, Georgia, worked in 7-on-7s.

 

 Stefanski said he prefers to play starters in the first and third preseason games. Tagovailoa did not wow last week in a 27-7 loss to the Denver Broncos , and he acknowledged that afterward. He'll likely get a chance next week -- against his former team, the Miami Dolphins , at Hard Rock Stadium.

 By then, maybe Penix is at least closer to being cleared for 11s in practice. He said early in training camp that he might be cleared in four weeks, which would be Wednesday. By then, maybe Stefanski is closer to choosing his Week 1 starter, too.

 "You put thought into it, but also, those decisions and those type of things, we'll cross that bridge when we get there," Stefanski said. "But in the meantime, feel very, very comfortable with what we've done to date. Feel really comfortable with the guys, the work they put in."

 Stefanski said Tagovailoa was "good" in joint practice against the Colts, but the team's protection needed some cleaning up, and "the quarterback obviously plays a role in that, as well." That was an issue in last week's preseason game. Tagovailoa was 3-of-5 for 22 yards, and all four of his targets were short passes to tight end  Kyle Pitts Sr . Tagovailoa didn't look completely comfortable, and the Broncos got plenty of pressure.

 On Wednesday, Tagovailoa threw an interception and fumbled a snap. He also fumbled the second snap of the game last week against the Broncos.

 

 Penix hasn't faced any pressure other than a yoga ball the Falcons have used to simulate a pass rush during practices. Eventually, he will be back and competing for the starting job. Stefanski said he views every position -- every role -- as being up for grabs in a competition. And those competitions keep going throughout the season. If Penix isn't ready for Week 1, it doesn't mean he can't get cleared and then do enough during the season to earn the spot.

 Falcons quarterbacks coach Alex Van Pelt said Penix has looked "really good" in 7s, but he's not ready for other players to be around his legs at this point.

 "Throwing it really well right now," Van Pelt said. "I love his footwork. We've done a lot of under-center work with him in these 7-on-7 periods to get him comfortable from under center. I'm just really proud of the way he's progressed. Can't wait for him to get back."

 Once he does, there will be more clarity. At least Tagovailoa and Penix will be operating as equals, able to do the same things. That should make it easier for Stefanski to judge, easier for him to make a decision on who gives the Falcons a better chance to win Week 1 and beyond.

 But time is ticking and there's no guarantee Penix will be back in time to start Week 1.

 Tagovailoa was asked Wednesday if he thinks there's enough time between now and the first game of the regular season to get where he wants to be operating this offense.

 "Well, I don't think you have a choice," Tagovailoa said. "At the end of the day, when it's game time, it's game time. You better be ready."

title: Ravens' Jesse Minter leads team in rapping Eminem's 'Lose Yourself'
summary: The newly minted Ravens head coach led his team in a rousing rendition of the 2002 classic at a team dinner.
full_text:
The Baltimore Ravens believe Jesse Minter is the head coach to lead them to the Super Bowl. What the players didn't know until Thursday night was that he could also lead them to rap.

 Minter brought down the house -- or, in this case, the restaurant -- when he grabbed the mic and belted out Eminem's "Lose Yourself" at a team dinner in Minnesota. In his untucked buttoned-down shirt, Minter confidently delivered verse after verse, creating the most unforgettable moment of the Ravens' week that included joint practices and a preseason game against the Minnesota Vikings .

 

 In what looked to be a true bonding experience, the players stood around Minter and joined in shouting the lyrics with their 43-year-old head coach. Wide receiver Ja'Kobi Lane put the impromptu performance on his social media livestream.

 

 Although Minter's rapping was a surprise, his musical selection was not. At a fan event four months ago, Minter was asked to name what musical artist he would see if he could attend just one concert. His answer? Eminem .

 Minter was named the fourth head coach in Ravens history in January, replacing John Harbaugh after 18 seasons. The players have talked all summer about how Minter has brought new energy and positive vibes to the team, which was evident when he delivered a rap instead of a pep talk at dinner.

title: 2026 NFL preseason Week 2: Game takeaways, analysis
summary: Week 2 of the NFL preseason is underway, and our NFL Nation reporters are tackling the biggest looming roster questions coming off each game.
full_text:
Week 2 of the  2026 NFL preseason kicked off Thursday, giving us more insight into position battles and the push to make 53-man rosters before the cut-down deadline Aug. 30. Action began with two games Thursday before Friday's three games, with severe weather rolling through Jacksonville late in the fourth quarter -- causing league and team officials to end the game because of lightning at the two-minute warning. Things will continue with 10 on Saturday before the first Sunday night game of the season to wrap things up.

 What are the biggest questions for the teams after each game? What have we learned about how the depth charts are shaping up? And what solutions could present themselves based on preseason play in Week 2?

 Our NFL Nation reporters picked out what you need to know about big roster decisions and more coming off Week 2 of the preseason.

 
 Quick links: 
 Full schedule | Where to watch 
 Depth charts  | Sign up to play fantasy 

 

 

 Friday's games 

 Jets 17, Steelers 0 
 

 Jets: Who's the No. 2 quarterback?  Rookie Cade Klubnik could've erased any doubt with another strong game, but it was a middling performance -- five drives, no points and only four plays in Pittsburgh territory. Klubnik (10-for-14, 75 yards) got a taste of real football, as the Steelers played many of their starters for two series. The organization probably will choose Klubnik as  Geno Smith 's backup. If the Jets explore outside options, now would be the time.

 In other battles, incumbent safety  Andre Cisco , battling Dane Belton for the starting job, helped his chances with an interception, but it came with the second-team defense. Belton got the start and made four tackles. Rookie Omar Cooper Jr . and Isaiah Williams are locked in a close battle for the WR3 position. Cooper got the start this week, but had only one catch for 9 yards. Williams had a fumble that was recovered by the Jets.  -- Rich Cimini 

 Next game:  vs New York Giants  ( Aug. 28, 7:30 p.m. ET )

 

 Steelers: Which position gets reduced to accommodate four quarterbacks? Mason Rudolph seemingly solidified his spot as QB2 without playing a snap as Will Howard struggled, and rookie Drew Allar failed to replicate his explosive preseason debut. Unless the Steelers try to sneak Howard through on the practice squad, it seems more and more likely that they'll keep four quarterbacks, and that would mean numbers have to be reduced somewhere else on the roster. Two potential groups to watch are the offensive linemen and safeties because of the position flexibility of veterans such as  Brock Hoffman  and Jalen Ramsey .  -- Brooke Pryor 

 Next game:  at Buffalo Bills  ( Aug. 28, 7 p.m. ET, NFL Network )

 

 Panthers 34, Jaguars 17 
 

 Panthers: Is there a second starting-caliber inside linebacker on the roster? Carolina didn't play Devin Lloyd , so Trevin Wallace and Claudin Cherelus  both started Friday. Neither defender has gained an advantage in their position battle this summer, and the depth behind Lloyd could be upgraded before Week 1.

 Similar to tight end, it wouldn't be surprising to see the Panthers search for a veteran free agent linebacker before or after the cut-down deadline next week.  -- Mike Kaye 

 Next game:  vs. Houston Texans ( Aug. 28, 7 p.m. ET )

 

 Jaguars: What will they do at running back?  LeQuint Allen Jr . is out for the rest of camp because of a soft tissue injury. If that lingers into the regular season, the Jaguars will need someone behind Chris Rodriguez Jr . and Bhayshul Tuten . That'll be either veteran Ameer Abdullah , who ran for 45 yards and had three catches for 37 yards against the Panthers, or undrafted rookie J'Mari Taylor . Taylor, who ran for 78 yards and a touchdown in Week 1, had little success Friday (3 yards, 4 carries). Both have had their moments in camp, so it might come down to which player the Jaguars believe they can risk adding to the practice squad.  -- Michael DiRocco 

 Next game:  vs. Tampa Bay Buccaneers  ( Aug. 28, 7:30 p.m. ET )

 

 Packers 33, Broncos 13 
 

 Packers: Do they have to find a way to keep four running backs? Even if  Josh Jacobs ' legal issues don't lead to a suspension by the NFL, the Packers might want to keep four running backs because Pierre Strong Jr . could be their best option as a kickoff returner. He ripped off a 68-yard return in the first half and showed he can handle some carries, too. He rushed for 37 yards on eight carries (a 4.6-yard average), including gains of 12 and 7 yards on consecutive plays. Behind Jacobs, the Packers will keep MarShawn Lloyd , and they like Chris Brooks as a third-down back because of his pass blocking. If Jacobs gets formally charged and/or suspended before the opener, they will almost certainly keep Strong.

 One question that appears to be answered is whether rookie kicker Trey Smack can handle the job. Despite some shaky days in practice -- he has nine missed kicks on the Ray Nitschke practice field this summer -- he has been successful in the preseason games. After going 3-for-3 last week (including a 58-yarder and not including another 58-yarder that was wiped out by a penalty), he made field goals of 51, 59, 43 and 38 yards against the Broncos to stay perfect in two games.  -- Rob Demovsky 

 Next game:  vs. Arizona Cardinals  ( Aug. 28, 8 p.m. ET )

 

 Broncos: What will they decide to do at safety?  In an attempt to add some experience behind starting safeties Talanoa Hufanga and Brandon Jones , the Broncos signed veteran safety Taylor Rapp this week. Rapp's arrival indicates that the Broncos want to bolster the depth chart on defense. Among the reserve safeties, Devon Key -- an All-Pro special teams selection last season -- has been the most consistent in game/practice snaps on defense. Two of the other backups -- JL Skinner and Tycen Anderson -- project as largely special teams players and haven't been nearly as consistent. And some of the defense's issues that happened when Jones was out of the lineup last season are still fresh in the coaches' minds. The Broncos have difficult decisions behind the starters at inside linebacker and the offensive line as well.  -- Jeff Legwold 

 Next game:  vs. Minnesota Vikings  ( Aug. 28, 9 p.m. ET, NFL Network )

 

 
 Thursday's games 

 49ers 41, Chargers 17 
 

 49ers:  What is the state of the receiver and guard depth charts?  The battle for receiver roster spots has been hard to decipher, but Jacob Cowing helped his cause significantly Thursday night due to his special teams contributions. Cowing returned a punt 83 yards for a score and is the most reliable punt return option on the roster. That should help him land on the initial 53-man roster, even if it means saying goodbye to a more proven veteran.

 Elsewhere, it's still unclear whether the Niners have a starting-caliber left guard, with rookie Carver Willis getting the start against the Chargers. Willis, Connor Colby and Robert Jones have been competing for that spot, but none of them has done enough to separate from the others. Austen Pleasants also entered the mix Thursday, creating more questions at the position.  -- Nick Wagoner 

 Next game: at  Las Vegas Raiders  (Aug. 27, 8 p.m. ET, ESPN Unlimited)

 

 Chargers:  Is Jake Slaughter ready to be the starting center?  The biggest news of the week for the Chargers was the injury to center Tyler Biadasz , who suffered an ACL injury to his left knee Tuesday and is out indefinitely.

 Slaughter, a second-round rookie, will likely begin the season as the Chargers' starting center, where he played all his college snaps. He got his first shot at that job Thursday night, playing nine snaps. He allowed zero pressures, according to NFL Next Gen Stats.  -- Kris Rhim 

 Next game: vs.  Los Angeles Rams  (Aug. 27, 10 p.m. ET, NFL Network)

title: Why Lions, NFL coaches believe Super Bowl chances are real
summary: If you don't believe Campbell & Co. that the Lions will be contenders, ask Sean McVay, Matt LaFleur and others.
full_text:
DETROIT -- When Dan Campbell arrived for the NFL's annual league meeting in March, no one would have guessed he was three months removed from one of his most disappointing seasons as the  Detroit Lions ' coach.

 Instead, those who saw him at the Arizona Biltmore in Phoenix were more preoccupied with his hair, which along with his goatee was considerably longer than anyone covering the team since 2021 could remember.

 "You know what? I just haven't cut it," Campbell joked. "I haven't cut it. I cut the sides, but I haven't."

 

 His relaxed look mirrored the calm confidence with which he discussed his team while answering questions from reporters alongside his coaching peers. He talked about his team heading into the 2026 season -- expressing his belief in the staff and the roster that he and general manager Brad Holmes had built.

 "We've been going. It's been fun. Been fun. Brad and I have been -- we've been back in the bunker just going at it," Campbell said. "It's been fun. It really has. Kind of a little bit of a rebirth, actually."

 His Lions were in need of the mini reset. They had won 15 games in 2024 and 12 the season before that, cementing themselves as one of the NFC's top contenders along the way. But in 2025, after losing both coordinators and eight coaches overall, they won just nine games and missed the playoffs for the first time since 2022.

 This offseason, some change was inevitable. The biggest: Campbell brought in former Arizona Cardinals offensive coordinator Drew Petzing to replace John Morton, whom the Lions fired in January after the first-time OC struggled to give Detroit an offensive identity. Detroit also put the finishing touches on a two-year renovation of the offensive line by moving All-Pro Penei Sewell from right tackle to left, adding Cade Mays in free agency and drafting tackle  Blake Miller  with the No. 17 selection.

 

 Otherwise, the team that enters the 2026 campaign is largely made up of the same nucleus that helped push the Lions to so much success. And Detroit has doubled down by locking down two of its young stars in running back Jahmyr Gibbs and linebacker Jack Campbell  with lucrative contract extensions. Those signings followed new deals they've given to other homegrown talents over the past three years and raised their overall investment in extensions to more than $1 billion over that span.

 Dan Campbell said the commitment to the current roster, combined with the organization's recent track record of success, is why he and the Lions remain confident their championship window remains open despite last season's setback.

 "Our window is not closed. It's not closed. That was the whole reason why we did this. We fell short last year. But needed to get in [the playoffs], and now it's about the matchups, where you're playing and who you're playing," Campbell told ESPN of his team, which is  favored by DraftKings to win the NFC North and have the fifth-best odds to win the conference . "We want to be able to do that every year, and sometimes, I'm just saying is what happens is, you want to go all-in for one player, well how do you know that one player doesn't get hurt?

 "Or how do you know the three players behind him don't get hurt and now you've got no depth. Whereas, let's just get a unit together that we feel like can compete every year and then it's about in that moment, we're making those plays and finding a way to win that game."

 And they are not alone in their assessment of the team. Asking about the Lions' prospects revealed a consensus from top coaches around the NFL -- from the  Los Angeles Rams ' Sean McVay to the  Green Bay Packers ' Matt LaFleur -- that the 2026 Lions are not the 9-8 team the league saw last season.

 Here's what the Lions and others around the league are saying about Detroit's Super Bowl worthiness in 2026.

 

 

 Part of the reason for Detroit's uncharacteristic 2025 campaign was the turnover on the coaching staff. After finishing 15-2 in 2024, the Lions most notably lost offensive coordinator Ben Johnson and defensive coordinator Aaron Glenn, who took head coaching jobs with the Chicago Bears and the  New York Jets , respectively. Those two departures were big losses for the team. But an underappreciated aspect that contributed to its struggles last season was the sheer number of coaches Campbell had to replace. 

 Campbell: "Well, you learn. But I don't think anybody necessarily tells you, 'Hey, be ready to lose [eight] coaches in one year.' Of course, that's the plan. You're going to lose some guys, you do it right and then the next guy, you can promote or you can go find guys. But when you're talking about [eight coaches], that's a tall task. But you owe it to the players, you owe it to the organization to find the best guy.

 

 "So, I feel like those pieces we added last year, for the most part, really fit what we're about and are good for us."

 McVay: "I think it's a champagne problem. When you end up losing coaches for the reasons that you're talking about with Dan, that means you're doing really well. People want to try to replicate. Or people in your building that are in leadership roles, they want to have them lead or take elevated steps in their career.

 "What I would say is it's a blessing. What I've really leaned into for us is what's been really fortunate is you get exposure to new people. New ideas."

 Glenn: "It's a really good problem to have because usually when you're losing coaches like that, that means you're doing well."

 LaFleur: "I do think that is a challenge, obviously. [Campbell] lost both of his coordinators, and there's a little bit of learning curve there and sometimes you have some growing pains, but I still think they're an elite team."

 

 In Johnson's three years as OC, the Lions established one of the NFL's most dangerous and prolific offenses. In 2024, his unit scored a franchise-record 564 points and led the league in scoring for the first time since 1954. Since 2022 -- the year Johnson took over playcalling duties midseason -- the Lions are tops in the NFL in scoring and total offense. While they still managed 481 points last season, they failed to establish an offensive identity outside of home run plays, and Morton, who replaced Johnson, was relieved of playcalling duties in November. In January, the Lions fired Morton and hired Petzing, who'd spent the previous three seasons as OC of the Cardinals. 

 Campbell: "I feel like the addition with Drew Petzing is going to be great for us. I think it's going to get us centralized. Back to being centralized more on offense."

 McVay: "This league is so volatile, great coaches get let go every year and great coaches become available. And I think when you show your place is a developmental staff that'll invest in the human being and help them get to places that Dan and I were fortunate enough to get to, you attract high-caliber people and you've got to lean into it."

 

 

 The Cardinals ranked second in the NFL in rushing yards per attempt (4.92) and ninth in total rushing yards (6,399) during Petzing's three years of calling plays in Arizona. And while Detroit's average yards per carry remained steady from 2024 to 2025 (4.7 to 4.6), the team's attempts, rushes per game and rushes of 10 or more yards per game all dipped last season. 

 Petzing, on what he wants from his offense in Detroit: "It needs to be physical, it needs to be tough, it needs to be difficult to defend and it needs to be multiple at times.

 "It's not going to all run through one person, it's not going to run through one personnel, it's going to change week to week. I think that's important in this league. Defensive coordinators, I think, do things at a really high level. They watch tape, they understand scheme. So, I think that's a big part of what we need to be on offense."

 Gibbs on Petzing: "He's nice. Smart. He's demanding of us, but he knows we can do it. He puts a lot on our plate, but like I said, he…

title: Jordan Morgan gets his shot at the Packers' left tackle job -- finally
summary: The 2024 first-round pick is ready to step in to protect quarterback Jordan Love for Green Bay.
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. --  Aaron Banks knows a bit about what  Jordan Morgan  went through early in his NFL career. Banks was a high draft pick forced to play out of position with mixed results early in his career, only to move back to his natural spot and become a full-time starter.

 That's one reason Banks has a keen interest in Morgan.

 The other is that they will line up next to each other on the Green Bay Packers ' offensive line this year with Banks at left guard and Morgan -- finally -- at his preferred left tackle position.

 For two seasons, the Packers force-fit Morgan into guard -- with 10 of his 13 career starts coming at either left or right guard -- after they picked him at No. 25 overall in the 2024 draft out of Arizona, where he played almost exclusively left tackle.

 

 It reminded Banks of how his career began: as a second-round pick (No. 48 overall) by the  San Francisco 49ers  in 2021 who thought for sure he would play his preferred left guard spot. Instead, they practiced him at right guard, and he couldn't get on the field. He played just five offensive snaps as a rookie. Meanwhile, Laken Tomlinson played 1,091 out of 1,091 offensive snaps at left guard.

 "Me and J-Mo have some similarity," Banks said. "I came in my rookie year, they put me at right guard. I wasn't very good at right guard. But I came back that second year, [Tomlinson] had departed in free agency and what they told me was, 'Hey, it's your job to lose.'

 "And I think that's the mindset that he's come in with -- like I'm not going to lose this. I'm doing everything I can to solidify myself as the left tackle for this team, and not just that but to challenge himself every day to be the best version of himself that he can be."

 While Morgan played nearly 750 snaps last season after 186 as a rookie, he didn't get his first shot at left tackle until last year's regular-season finale at Minnesota when LaFleur rested several starters in advance of the playoffs. Morgan played 51 snaps at left tackle against the Vikings. But come the playoff game, it was back to right tackle, where he filled in for an injured Zach Bako-Bewele .

 Coming out of college, some NFL teams viewed him as a guard because of his short-ish arms. They measured 32⅞ inches, which is below some teams' threshold of 34- or 35-inch arms to play tackle.

 

 Morgan would hear none on it. On the first day of his rookie minicamp back in 2024, he laid out his plan.

 "I'm trying to show that I'm a true left tackle and show I'll be out there on the edge to protect the quarterback," Morgan said.

 Instead, the Packers stuck with Rasheed Walker for two more seasons. Walker had taken over for David Bahktiari, whose career ended because of recurring knee injuries one game into the 2023 season. Walker kept the starting job despite a strong training camp by Morgan last summer.

 It was a season of inconsistency on the offensive line last year, culminating with a poor performance in the playoff loss to the Bears. It prompted the Packers to finally view it as time to give Morgan his shot, and they let Walker leave in free agency (he signed with the Carolina Panthers on just a one-year, $4 million contract).

 "I think we're very comfortable with him there," general manager Brian Gutekunst said. "He's going to have to go out and do it over full season and year in and year out, but he's done a really nice job through the spring, really nice job so far. I'm looking forward to getting some more reps here in the preseason and then get ready for the regular season.

 "We think he's got a super-bright future to be a really good player in this league. I'm sure he'll go through his ups and downs like they all do at that position because that's one of those positions where you're going to have some of that. But yeah, I'm excited for him."

 

 While there has been some shuffling on the offensive line during training camp, it hasn't been at left tackle. It's been Morgan the entire time.

 "I think it's one of those things where I just want to get to the games and see how we just keep building and how he looks out there," quarterback Jordan Love said. "But definitely got a lot of confidence in him, a lot of trust. That's one of those things where my back's going to be to him all game. So got to have that confidence that he's going to hold it down, and he's been doing great things."

 In Morgan's preseason debut last week against the Steelers, he did not allow a pressure in 22 snaps. But it was a run block that stood out the most. Morgan got to the second level and flattened cornerback Jamel Dean .

 "That is what the expectation is, and it's funny you bring that play up because I'm going to show that one [in the team meeting]," LaFleur said the day after the game. "That's something that we've definitely been stressing to not only the offensive line, but to every position. Football's an imperfect game, but the thing that you do control is your effort and physicality, and that is exactly, that is a play that I want to highlight."

 It was a play by someone who looked like they'd been waiting two years for their chance.

 "From OTAs to training camp, he's just been bought in and relentless working on his technique, doing stuff after practice, asking questions," Banks said. "Just really intentional in the way he's approach it -- not just practice but walk-throughs, meetings, everything we're doing. I just personally feel like I've seen a big leap of, I'm not going to say maturity because I don't think J-Mo's immature, but just growth from him from a mental standpoint, from an approach to the reps he's getting in practice to the individual drills, everything.

 "From last year to this year, it's all been positive in my eyes."

title: Chargers rookie Akheem Mesidor paving way for Ottawa NFL players
summary: Ottawa is having a moment in the NFL. And the city's first first-rounder Akheem Mesidor hopes to usher in the next generation.
full_text:
VICTOR TEDONDO WOKE Akheem Mesidor out of his sleep.

 It was around 2015 when Tedondo, the coach of the Gridiron Academy, was taking Mesidor and some other players in his minivan on an over 800-mile drive from their hometown of Ottawa, Canada, to a high school football camp at the University of Indiana.

 Tedondo began training Mesidor at the football academy when he was 8 years old, becoming one of the most impactful coaches in Mesidor's development. "These car rides were always the worst," Mesidor said, because it was when Tedondo critiqued players. And they were particularly bad for whomever was sitting exactly where Mesidor was: in the passenger seat next to Tedondo.

 "Akheem, you're about to go play against some real dogs. You think you're good?" Tedondo asked.

 "Yeah."

 "Does your mom tell you you're good?"

 "Yeah."

 "You f---ing suck," Tedondo said.

 "I did not like him," Mesidor laughed. "A lot of people didn't like him but once you started doing better and performing, he started easing off. The more of a dog you were, the less you heard."

 

 At that camp in Indiana, Mesidor, then 14, was playing inside linebacker, but he lost in three consecutive one-on-one reps, and Tedondo pulled him and forced him to play on the defensive line. From that point on, that's where Mesidor has played, evolving into one of college football's best outside linebackers at the University of Miami and a first-round pick (No. 22) by the Los Angeles Chargers in this year's draft.

 Mesidor is the first Ottawan drafted in the NFL draft's first round, a feat he credits in part to the many uncomfortable minivan rides and grueling training sessions with Tedondo. Defensive end Brian Belway became the first Ottawa-born player to appear in an NFL regular-season game in 1987, and it took 30 years for the next.

 Now, Mesidor is the latest of an influx of NFL players to come from Canada's capital. Among active players, Mesidor joins New England Patriots linebacker Jesse Luketa , Chicago Bears defensive tackle Neville Gallimore , Rams outside linebacker Wesley Bailey and Miami Dolphins defensive tackle Rene Konga . They believe they're only scratching the surface of the talent back home.

 "I take a lot of pride in coming from Ottawa because a lot of people don't do it," Mesidor told ESPN. "... We have dogs in Ottawa. The kids just need guidance, and they need people who believe in them."

 
 

 IT'S JUST BEFORE 9:30 a.m. at the Chargers facility on the 11th day of training camp, and Mesidor is the only player on the team's practice field. Practice doesn't begin for another half hour, but he's already in a deep sweat and going through swipe-rip pass-rush moves. Mesidor is one of the first players on the field each day, maintaining a pre-practice routine since he was drafted that has impressed his teammates and coaches.

 Mesidor has grown accustomed to the extra work. He also swims as a part of his training, a routine that began at Miami to help shed weight after transferring there from West Virginia in part because he wanted to shift from the interior defensive line to edge rusher, where he feels most comfortable.

 "He's the first one on the field every time. He goes about it like a pro," Chargers outside linebacker Tuli Tuipulotu said. "He's very locked in. He knows what he needs, what he wants, and that's what we love."

 Mesidor's time at different positions on the defensive line made him attractive in the draft process for his versatility, and his six years in college helped him develop a refined set of pass-rush moves.

 "When he puts his hand down on the ground at the defensive end, the five technique, there's flashes of elite," Chargers coach Jim Harbaugh said. "The initial quickness, the strength, very polished in his arsenal of what he can do."

 

 This version of Mesidor seemed impossible back at Gridiron Academy. "When it came down to physical training, he was not really about it," Tedondo reflected, "but he loved football."

 That love for football brought Mesidor and Tedondo together. Tedondo introduced himself to Mesidor when Mesidor was in elementary school. At that time, Mesidor was playing for the youth football club North Gloucester Giants, and Tedondo was coaching the Orléans Bengals. Tedondo recalls blowing out the Giants in a game. But Mesidor caught Tedondo's attention.

 "It was his tenacity. He just kept fighting," Tedondo said. "A lot of young kids just gave up because they didn't have that mental toughness, that resiliency at that age to keep fighting. And Akheem just kept fighting."

 After that game, Tedondo, then 22 years old, asked Mesidor to train at his academy. Over the next decade, Tedondo became a father figure to Mesidor, who had grown up without one present in his life. But the relationship wasn't always smooth sailing.

 Mesidor evolved into a good football player, but he had fallen behind his peers who had begun receiving Division I offers as freshmen and sophomores. Tedondo said that Mesidor trailed his peers because he hadn't committed to the work outside of football -- lifting, conditioning and his diet.

 After attending a camp at the University of Michigan before his sophomore year, Mesidor watched how coach Harbaugh -- who coincidentally is now Mesidor's pro coach in L.A. -- offered another Gridiron player, Kenny Mestidor, a scholarship to play football at Michigan.

 Already frustrated by his progress and peers seemingly passing him by, Mesidor decided he wanted to quit football. He got a job at Domino's Pizza and stopped training for a few weeks at the academy. At the same time, Mesidor's personal life was in turmoil: He struggled in school, his single mother struggled to make ends meet, his brother was in a drug-induced coma, and he had a sister dealing with legal troubles.

 But after a conversation with Tedondo, Mesidor learned that the most realistic way to change his situation was through football.

 "He used to run away from struggle," Tedondo said. "He used to run away from his life in a sense because he was dealt with a lot at home. But from that moment, everything started clicking."

 Soon, Tedondo began finding Mesidor training at the academy before he got there. It was there that Mesidor began doing many of the things he does now -- arriving early to practice, staying late, doing extra work in the weight room -- and as a junior, he received his first Division I offer from Syracuse. For his senior season in 2019, Mesidor transferred to Clearwater Academy International in Florida, hoping to gain more exposure.

 He dominated, finishing with 18 tackles for loss, 92 tackles and 10 sacks, while cementing himself as a four-star recruit and receiving 20 Division I offers.

 Mesidor eventually committed to the University of West Virginia, but Tedondo continued to push him from afar. Starting during his freshman year in 2020, Tedondo would call Mesidor before games to remind him that he belonged. The calls continued when Mesidor transferred to Miami as a junior.

 

 Then one night Mesidor didn't answer.

 "He didn't need it anymore," Tedondo said.

 Mesidor laughs now when he hears this story. He doesn't remember ignoring Tedondo, but admits that his process, which began in college, is to ignore whomever is calling his phone the night before a game.

 "I don't answer him. I don't answer my mom. I don't answer my girl," Mesidor said with a smile. "I just don't like really talking to anybody, being on the phone. It's my quiet time. It's time for me to relax before the game."

 Over three seasons at Miami, Mesidor evolved into Ottawa's highest drafted prospect. In his final season at Miami in 2025, he led the team with 17.5 tackles for loss and 12.5 sacks as the Hurricanes made it to the College Football Playoff National Championship game. His production and work ethic made the Chargers fall in love with him during the draft process.

 "We interviewed him and you just felt that in the room," Chargers general manager…

title: Dolphins less interested in winning joint practice than improving
summary: The Dolphins had some highlights against the Giants, but coach Jeff Hafley had his eyes on one-on-one battles.
full_text:
MIAMI GARDENS, Fla. -- The Miami Dolphins' final joint practice of the summer was a mixed bag, depending on whom you ask.

 The Dolphins hosted the New York Giants on Thursday, in what Giants linebacker Brian Burns called a "dominant" showing for the visitors. The Giants' pass rush, led by Burns, Abdul Carter , Kayvon Thibodeaux and Chauncey Golston , combined for at least six sacks Thursday in addition to several pressures.

 Giants coach John Harbaugh referred to his team's pass rush as "ferocious," while Dolphins center Aaron Brewer thought Thursday's practice was "good competition."

 "I felt like it was a good battle. They had some wins, we had some wins," he said. "So I feel like it was just some good competition out there. Once I watch the tape, I'll see how we did overall, but it felt like a solid day."

 Thursday marked the second of two joint practices the Dolphins scheduled for this preseason, following last week's practice with the Washington Commanders .

 With the NFL's youngest team in terms of average age, the Dolphins' focus during these practices isn't necessarily on winning the day. First-year coach Jeff Hafley said he's more interested in seeing how his players perform in one-on-one matchups than he is in outscheming Miami's opponent.

 "I'm not looking to see if we can outsmart a coaching staff in a preseason practice. I mean, I don't think that gets our players any better," Hafley said. "Like I said, just imagine I spent all this time the next two nights trying to draw up a blitz and getting a free runner off the edge. What does that tell us about our players? That they can run off the edge in a period where you're not even going to sack the quarterback and it looks cool? Like, that's not important to me.

 "What's important is building the foundation the right way. I want to see who can go up against their really good edge rushers and block them one-on-one. ... This year in these joint practices, it's trying to figure out who we are, what we have, get our players better, get them more confident, push them to compete rather than try to outscheme, confuse and beat the New York Giants in a football practice. That would be more ego and that would be a selfish move on my part than it would be about our team and trying to get them better, if that makes sense."

 Miami turned in a handful of highlights during Thursday's practice. Running back De'Von Achane broke a long run thanks to lead blocks from fullback DJ Herman and tight end Will Kacmarek . Quarterback Malik Willis also fooled New York's pass rush with a play-action fake and hit rookie wide receiver Kevin Coleman Jr . for a first down -- Coleman took a hit from former Dolphins safety Jevon Holland but was able to complete the catch.

 Rookie linebacker Jacob Rodriguez also intercepted Giants quarterback Jaxson Dart . It was a busy day for the second-round pick, who played a larger role with starter Jordyn Brooks sidelined and Tyrel Dodson forced out of practice for an undisclosed reason.

 

 "It's something that's very unique to the NFL -- you don't ever do this growing up," Rodriguez said of joint practices. "Coming out here and still working through plays and serious competition that you need full-speed reps at, but you're getting it against a different look. Some of the issues our offense present us every day are different from what the Giants present.

 "I think it's just a really good mesh of everybody in the NFL, that brotherhood of us being here trying to get better before the season starts."

 The Giants and Dolphins play Saturday night at Hard Rock Stadium in both teams' penultimate preseason finale.

 Hafley said before practice that he had an idea of who will play in Saturday's game, but it would depend on Thursday's workload.

 "Everybody should be ready to play," Hafley said. "I think it's really important for me and for us to see how many reps our guys get today, and then am I willing to put certain guys out who might get 40, 45 reps, you know, two days later? So I got to be careful on that. But I have a certain idea."

title: Cam Skattebo still top option in crowded Giants backfield
summary: With the addition of Najee Harris, it's difficult to predict New York's backfield carries at this point.
full_text:
EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. -- The New York Giants ' running back room got a bit more crowded this week with the signing of Najee Harris . He is a four-time 1,000-yard rusher looking to prove once again that he's a high-level back.

 Harris took three days to get into live drills. He received three carries during joint practices Thursday with the Miami Dolphins .

 But Harris isn't joining the Giants to be the fourth option behind Cam Skattebo , Tyrone Tracy Jr . and Devin Singletary . He was brought in under the premise that he's going to be a significant contributor, even though a source told ESPN he signed a one-year minimum salary $1.215 million deal with no guaranteed money.

 Harbaugh and the Giants seem ready to let it play out.

 

 "I mean, football's competitive, the NFL's competitive, and we're building the strongest team we can," Harbaugh said. "And [Harris is] a really good football player. So that's it."

 Skattebo has been the first running back up most days at practice this summer (including at Thursday's joint practice) and was the starter in the Giants' preseason opener Saturday even though he is coming off an open fracture of his right ankle . He ran well against the Minnesota Vikings , to the point Harbaugh said he looked like the pre-injury Skattebo of last season. Harbaugh conceded Skattebo is not "100% twitchy and explosive yet," but he's getting there and substantial progress has happened in training camp practices.

 So, the second-year running back who scored seven total touchdowns in eight games during his rookie season remains the Giants' top option. 

 Tracy has also been a regular working with starting quarterback Jaxson Dart this summer. He was the first running back up at Tuesday's practice and remains part of the mix. His missed block that sent Dart to the blue medical tent Saturday left Harbaugh unhappy, but it hasn't eliminated him from the Giants' plans. It could, however, light a fire under the third-year back.

 Tracy has two straight seasons with 1,000-plus yards from scrimmage in his first two professional seasons. His blocking also hasn't been a problem. Tracy's pass block win rate of 83.3% was comparable to Singletary (84.6%) last season and significantly better than Skattebo (66.7%).

 

 The Giants' signing of Harris wasn't in direct response to Tracy's preseason gaffe. The team had been in contact with Harris' representative for months and the workout was scheduled last week, sources told ESPN.

 Harbaugh prefers a deep and physical running back room, and Harris fits the mold at 6-foot-1 and 242 pounds.

 "He's an experienced back. Anybody that's watched him play knows what type of a back he is," the Giants coach said. "He's a downhill runner, physical runner. I've played against him a lot. I have a good feel for who he is as a player.

 "Everybody that's been around him, my brother [ Los Angeles Chargers coach Jim Harbaugh], [senior offensive assistant Greg Roman], [former Pittsburgh Steelers coach] Mike Tomlin, love him as a teammate. So, excited for the possibilities."

 This seems to be among the reasons Harris chose the Giants; he knows if he shows the form he had in Pittsburgh prior to tearing his Achilles, he'll jump up the depth chart. It's not out of the realm of possibilities that Harris is getting a significant number of carries several weeks into the 2026 season.

 "I want opportunity. I think this is a good opportunity here," he said. "The style of play that they're heading toward is the style of play that aligns with me. Harbaugh coming from the AFC North, me playing against him a lot of times, I know the type of style of football he wants. ... I think that just coming here is a good opportunity, and I'm willing to just put my foot in there and help out in any way I can."

 

 At this point, Singletary shouldn't be counted out. He is second to tight end Isaiah Likely in catches during live drills this summer on passes thrown from Dart. He also ran well in the preseason opener.

 The four capable running backs make it hard to predict the Giants' backfield carries at this point. The unproven Eric Gray and Damon Bankston are also on the active roster.

 Harbaugh isn't averse to keeping four running backs. The  Baltimore Ravens  had four on their Week 1 roster last season, and that was with Derrick Henry as their feature back.

 Four backs could be necessary as injury protection for Skattebo, even though he "felt great" being out there in a game environment on Saturday. Skattebo said he didn't even think about the injury. But multiple executives have expressed to ESPN reservations about him remaining healthy long term considering his size and style of play. It was a contributing factor to the former Arizona State player being selected in the fourth round of the 2025 NFL draft despite being one of the most productive players in college football.

 Now, at least, with the addition of Harris, the Giants have significant insurance for Skattebo and motivation for Tracy.
