title: 2026 Seattle Seahawks training camp: Latest intel, updates
summary: Catch up on our daily updates from Seahawks training camp, including intel on QBs, position battles and potential breakouts.
full_text:
The 2026 NFL training camps have kicked off around the league, and our team reporters are on the ground each day following all the action. The  Seattle Seahawks ' camp is taking place in Renton, Washington, and Seahawks reporter Brady Henderson has the latest intel on standouts, highlights, position battles, depth chart movement, cut decisions and, of course, the quarterbacks room.

 What follows is everything we are seeing and hearing at Seahawks camp. What is new with the defending Super Bowl champions? Who are the breakout players to watch, especially for fantasy football? And which players on the roster bubble could make the final 53?

 Catch up on all the updates, including the Packers' top camp performer and biggest lingering question as preseason games begin.

 
 Camp previews for all 32 NFL teams 

 
 

 

 Latest news from Seahawks camp 
 
 CB Trevon Diggs signing 1-year deal with Seahawks 
 Sources: Seahawks still plan on signing Terrion Arnold 
 Cooper Kupp's latest route? Opening a new coffee shop 
 Seahawks, Witherspoon reach extension: 4 years, $132M, sources say 
 Seahawks' DeMarcus Lawrence confirms 2026 season his last 
 Facing charges, Terrion Arnold set to join Seahawks 
 WR Tory Horton healthy after cracking tibia last season 
 Seattle Pro Bowl DL Williams confirms deal talks 
 Seattle's Nick Emmanwori has ankle surgery, expected to play W1 
 Who are the Khoslas? Meet the family set to buy the Seahawks 
 
 

 Friday, Aug. 21 

 The Seahawks spent a second-round pick on safety Bud Clark after losing Coby Bryant in free agency, but don't pencil the rookie into the starting lineup just yet. Ty Okada doesn't look like he's giving up that job any time soon.

 "We love Ty," linebacker Ernest Jones IV said Friday after Okada provided a highlight of Seattle's joint practice against the Tennessee Titans . "I think where Ty has grown is that he's just more in command in his voice and speaking up when things aren't right. He's also just taken a next level to his game being ahead of plays and being that safety in the back that you depend on."

 Okada was dependable last season. The 2023 undrafted free agent gave Seattle starting-caliber play while Bryant and Julian Love missed a combined 11 games with injuries. But Friday's practice brought more evidence that Okada can also provide some playmaking when he jumped an over-the-middle throw from Cam Ward for a pick-six.

 "It was a really great call," Okada said. "I was coming down over the middle. I tried to get his eyes off of me and then on a crossing route, I was able to read it, play off of him, go out there and make a play. It felt good."

 Clark, the 64th overall pick, intercepted 15 passes over his final four seasons at TCU. But the ball production that was his calling card in college has yet to come alive with Seattle. It's among the reasons why Okada has taken almost all of the reps with the No. 1 defense, as all signs point to Seattle rolling with him opposite Love in their starting lineup.

 "He's got a ton of confidence," coach Mike Macdonald said. "He's taking on more of a leadership role, too, in terms of really holding our younger guys to a higher standard, which is great. We need that right now from those guys. From my stance, he's playing really good football."

 Other observations:  

 
 RB George Holani got most of the reps with the No. 1 offense as top pick Jadarian Price (lower body soreness) continues to ramp back up after missing over a week of training camp. "It's not responsible to give him a thousand carries after being down for a minute, but I'm eager to watch the tape," Macdonald said. "I was looking forward to seeing him play today." 
 OLB Derick Hall is also working his way back from an undisclosed injury (Macdonald does not readily give injury information) that sidelined him for several days. Hall was in uniform Friday and went through early warmups before taking it easy for the remainder of practice. 
 

 

 Thursday, Aug. 20 
 What is Trevon Diggs ' mindset after joining the Seahawks?

 "I just want to come here, compete, earn my keep," the former Dallas Cowboys cornerback said Wednesday, "just do everything I can to earn a spot here and help this team win."

 Exactly what the Seahawks have in mind for Diggs will become more clear when the details of his one-year deal emerge. The fact that they were not initially reported seems telling in and of itself. So does the ending of Diggs' tenure in Dallas last season, as well as what he said after arriving at Seahawks headquarters about how he wants to "earn" a spot in Seattle.

 Nothing about the situation suggests the Seahawks view Diggs as an immediate, surefire upgrade to their current options at CB3. Rather, he looks like someone who could reinforce Seattle's secondary depth for now, and potentially work his way into a bigger role.

 With the Seahawks off to Nashville Thursday for a joint practice and a preseason game against the Tennessee Titans , the Diggs signing invites a day-after look at Seattle's cornerback room.

 The only real certainties are that the newly-extended Devon Witherspoon and Josh Jobe  -- whom Seattle re-signed in March -- will fill the top two spots. Noah Igbinoghene seems to have at least a slight edge over Nehemiah Pritchett in the battle for the No. 3 job.

 The Seahawks seem to think that Terrion Arnold could eventually be an upgrade there, but with a stay on the commissioner exempt list coming and a suspension potentially to follow, there's no telling when he'll be available. Julian Neal figured to be part of the No. 3 cornerback competition when the Seahawks drafted him in the third round, but he's been sidelined for much of camp with an undisclosed injury. While Neal has been in uniform in recent days and took part in the walkthrough Wednesday, rookies who miss as much time as he has tend to fall far behind.

 The Diggs signing might have as much to do with Neal's extended absence and strengthening the bottom of the depth chart than it does the question of whether Seattle will be vulnerable at CB3 regardless of who wins that job.

 Below them are seventh-round picks Andre Fuller and Michael Dansby , who have each cooled off after strong starts to training camp. They've always seemed like candidates for the practice squad more than the 53-man roster. The Seahawks had a fifth-round grade on Fuller, but the fact that each lasted to the seventh round suggests there's a good chance Seattle could get them through waivers.

 Seattle recently placed Shemar Jean-Charles on season-ending injured reserve, but he wasn't likely going to make the 53-man roster even if he'd stayed healthy.

 More observations: 

 
 G Bryce Cabeldue was on the field for the walk-through Wednesday after going down with a neck injury Tuesday. He appears to be OK. 
 The Seahawks will hold one practice against the Titans on Friday. They'll practice by themselves on Friday before the preseason game Sunday. 
 

 

 

 Tuesday, Aug. 18 
 There are so many ways in which Mike Macdonald coaches the Seahawks differently from his predecessor, and this week is about to bring another example.

 Whereas Pete Carroll was staunchly against joint practices -- he never held one in 14 seasons in Seattle -- Macdonald is a proponent. It's why the Seahawks will head to Nashville on Thursday to practice against the Tennessee Titans on Friday, two days before their preseason game at Nissan Stadium.

 The Seahawks held joint practices in each of Macdonald's first two seasons -- in Nashville in 2024 and against the Packers in Green Bay last summer.

 Macdonald sees a best-of-all-worlds appeal in getting reps against another team in the controlled setting of a practice, where the two sides can simulate certain situations, and where the quarterbacks are not to be touched. Teams can also run plays that they wouldn't call in preseason games lest they put them on film for the rest of the league to see.

title: Commanders need to show how far they've come vs. Lions
summary: Third-year QB Jayden Daniels is looking like he did in 2024, but can a revamped defense hold up its end?
full_text:
ASHBURN, Va. -- After three weeks of training camp, the Washington Commanders have seen what they hoped for from their quarterback and, most of the time, from their defense. They've also seen an offensive line that has been reshuffled because of one big injury, and because of that they still need to see their run game evolve.

 The Commanders play at the Lions in a preseason game at noon Saturday. It's a chance for Washington to build momentum, though it's uncertain how many starters will play or for how long. It's also an opportunity to learn more about the Commanders and the direction they might take once the season begins.

 They need to improve on a 5-12 season, and so far -- after one joint practice and a preseason game -- there have been signs that provide hope, and some that warrant caution.

 Washington coach Dan Quinn said he likes the "competitive makeup" of the camp practices. He also likes the details of what he has seen in different situations: fourth down, two-minute drills, red zone work.

 But there are big-picture takeaways as well.

 Quarterback Jayden Daniels looks sharp 

 All offseason, the two words heard most from those who know Daniels well were these: "Locked in." The result has been a standout camp. He impressed Miami's coaches in the joint practice, both during one-on-one drills and in full-team work, with his accuracy. One coach also pointed to his athleticism -- sometimes in subtle ways, like his ability to slide, and other times to extend plays.

 Daniels did not play in the preseason opener, and Quinn isn't sure yet if his starters will play vs. Detroit. Earlier in the week he said a lot of it would be based off how much work Daniels received in practice, and he took more snaps than usual Tuesday and Wednesday.

 But, regardless, he said they're seeing what they had hoped to from Daniels.

 "I love that he's decisive," Quinn said. "He's got a unique ability to put the ball in the right location. I like that he's in a system that he is now at the line of scrimmage working more things. That might be the biggest difference between the last couple of years and this year is him at the line of scrimmage and working through. He's done a good job with cadence. That's not something that we've done here before. Those are a few of the things that don't show up on the stat sheet that he's doing a really good job with."

 Offensive coordinator David Blough , who has been with Daniels since his arrival in 2024, said they've tracked every throw he has made over the last three years. Blough's conclusion: "He's as accurate as he's ever been. It's just a testament to asking him to do something different and him wanting to grow and evolve."

 It helps that Daniels has a full complement of receivers, unlike last summer, when Terry McLaurin was holding in. Another wideout expected to help, Noah Brown , was injured most of camp. The result: an offense that lacked any rhythm. Daniels' season was then derailed by multiple injuries, limiting him to four full games.

 "I felt like this last year, so I wasn't hurt around this time last year," he said. "It's a new year. I want to compare what I did my first two years."

 

 Offensive line questions 

 Washington entered training camp feeling good about its offensive line, anchored by left tackle Laremy Tunsil and with four returning starters. Right tackle Josh Conerly Jr . finished strong as a rookie, and right guard Sam Cosmi would be another year removed from a torn ACL.

 Because of that, and with a change in schemes, the Commanders had hoped to develop a strong run game.

 But the reality has been tougher. With Tunsil out after surgery on his torn triceps (no timetable for his recovery has been given, a team source said), Washington needed to slide Brandon Coleman to left tackle -- and remove him from the competition to start at left guard. Coleman and Chris Paul both were solid in the two series they played in the preseason opener vs. Miami.

 But the question will be whether the Commanders can generate a consistent run game. Against Miami in the joint practice, they were more effective throwing the ball. In the preseason opener, rookie running backs Kaytron Allen and Robert Henry Jr . combined for 160 yards rushing and two touchdowns.

 But Washington managed just 10 yards in four carries by Allen in the first quarter. Sometimes it was the block; other times it was the run. Regardless, Washington needs this area to develop.

 The difficult part is that Nick Allegretti , the favorite to start at center, has participated in just two full practices this summer because of a strained calf.

 Allegretti said the line understands the run game concepts and the last step is improving the three-man combination blocks -- getting used to different defensive looks.

 Quinn said the run game on both sides of the ball is not yet where it needs to be. But he's not surprised it's taking longer on offense.

 "That's to be expected," he said. "But we're making progress. The combinations, the speed off the ball, we're not where we will be, but I would say in terms of the targeting of where we're going to, who's blocking who, we're making progress."

 The defense will be aggressive 
New coordinator Daronte Jones worked under the uber-aggressive Brian Flores for three seasons in Minnesota, serving as his pass game coordinator. It shows. The Commanders have been aggressive in practice, sending blitzes from all over. Their aggressiveness helped them against Miami, a team that lacks much firepower on offense, in the joint practice. But one Dolphins coach pointed specifically to the defense as a reason Washington could be good this season.

 "The biggest thing with this defense is you're no longer a reactor," safety Jeremy Reaves said. "Most defenses in the NFL you're just trying to stop offenses. This defense dictates what they do so now they play on your terms, not vice versa."

 But Quinn wasn't happy with their early showing in the preseason game, when mostly backups played -- though linebacker  Sonny Styles , who is expected to start, did play, as did key reserve Leo Chenal .

 Against Detroit, Quinn wants to see more of that attacking mentality transfer to each game. Washington did not show in the game what it has been doing in practice, though it did send some defensive backs on occasion. But in Minnesota the inside linebackers were aggressive in creeping up to the line and showing blitz -- and either rushing or dropping; that wasn't the case in the preseason game. Neither Styles nor Chenal showed that look.

 However, Quinn wants to see a mindset develop.

 "I just didn't love the urgency that we played with," he said. "It just wasn't as downhill and aggressive like I saw from the practice. I wanted to see more of that."

 Also, in Quinn's first two seasons combined in Washington the Commanders rank 31st in takeaways with only 27. They took the ball away three times against Miami and have emphasized that in practice, with players often punching down on the ball in the runner's arms and working on this in drills.

 Styles, who played 14 snaps last week, told Quinn he wants to get "downhill" better. Styles has shown his sideline-to-sideline speed and he can drop deeper than most linebackers because of his safety background and ability to close fast on passes ahead of him. But he also knows he must be a strong defender filling gaps. That's why his goal is basic.

 "Just starting really fast," he said. "I've got to work on keeping better footwork, hands, all those different things. I'm going to keep getting better."
